full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner was issued on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure challenging the judgment and decree dated 4-11-1992 (decree signed on 10-11-1992) passed by the Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur in Title Appeal Number 153 of 1989 allowing the same on reversing those dated 30-8-1989 passed by the Assistant Judge, Bhanga, Faridpur in Title Suit Number 91 of 1986 decreeing the suit. 

2. The petitioner instituted the suit in the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Bhanga, Faridpur for specific performance of contract. His case, in brief, was that the land as described in the schedule of the plaint belonged to defendant number 1 Abdul Hamid Matubbar, predecessor of opposite parties number 1-10. He executed an agreement with the plaintiff on 30-10-1978 to sell 91 decimals of land for a consideration of Taka 20,000 (twenty thousand), out of which Taka 18,000 was paid as earnest money. It was stipulated that he would execute and register the sale deed receiving the remaining consideration of Taka 2,000 (two thousand) within Boishakh-Chaitra, 1392 BS. It was further stipulated that if the defendant refunded the earnest money (Taka 18,000) within the month of Chaitra, 1391 BS, the agreement for sale would be returned. Since, the defendant did not refund the money, the plaintiff requested him on 1-4-1986 to receive the remaining consideration, and execute and register a sale deed, but he refused. Hence the suit. 

3. Defendant number 1's two sons. namely, Rajob Ali Matubbar and Chand Miah Matubbar were added as defendants number 3 and 4 and they contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. Their case, in brief, was that defendant number I did not receive money from the plaintiff and also did not execute any agreement for sale. The agreement was a forged and created one. Defendant number I was financially solvent and he had no reason to sell the property. He had already transferred the suit land to these defendants by registered gift deed number 2185 dated 13-6-1972. These defendants were possessing the ponds situated on the suit land by rearing fishes. 

4. Defendant number I also filed a written statement on similar averment affirming the transfer of the suit land to his sons by way of registered gift deed dated 13-6-1972. Thereafter, defendant number 1 died and his remaining heirs were substituted by order dated 29-3-1989 and they also contested the suit adopting the said written statement by filing an application dated 16-7-1989. 

5. On the aforesaid pleadings, the trial court framed issues, namely, (i) whether the suit was maintainable in its present form and manner, (ii) whether the suit was barred by limitation, (iii) whether the sale agreement in question was executed by defendant number 1 on 30-10-1978 in accordance with law, and (iv) whether the plaintiff was entitled to the relief of specific performance of contract as prayed for. 

6. In course of hearing, the plaintiff deposed as PW 1, where he supported the plaint's case as reproduced above stating that the defendant number l's son Jonah Ali and some other persons, namely, Ohab, Danesh, Mamun and Siraj Mir were present at the time of execution of the sale agreement. The negotiation for sale was held at the house of Siraj Mir. He himself paid the money to defendant number 1 in presence of the attesting witnesses and also the scribe of the sale agreement, Suriya Kumar (PW 3). 

7. In cross-examination, PW 1 stated that he could not recollect the date of execution of the sale agreement and could also not say about the denomination of the currency that was given as consideration money. 

8. PW 2 Siraj Mir, an attesting witness to the sale agreement in question, deposed supporting the plaintiff's case and payment of earnest money amounting to Taka 18,000 at the time of execution of the sale agreement. 

9. PW 3 Suriya Kumar, scribe of the agreement for sale proved his signature thereon. He stated that the executant Hamid signed it in his presence, but could not recollect whether the earnest money was paid in his front. 

10. PW 4 Danesh Sharif stated that he was present at the time of negotiation before execution of the sale agreement. There was a settlement for sale of 89 decimals of land. He knew the suit land and claimed himself to be the owner of adjacent land. 

11. On the other hand, defendant number 1 (ka) Jonab Ali Matubbar deposed as DW 1. He outright denied the plaintiff's case claiming the sale agreement to be a forged and created one. He asserted that the plaintiff did never possess the suit land. He denied his signature, which was allegedly put on the sale agreement as an attesting witness. He further stated that the plaintiff was his maternal uncle, who was a person of bad reputation and so many criminal cases were pending against him. He could not submit the original gift-deed containing the signature of his father, because those were seized by the Anti-Corruption Office. His father did not sign the sale agreement, nor did he receive the earnest money. He affirmed the written statement filed by his father (defendant number 1) and asserted that PW 4 Danesh had no land adjacent to the suit land. The land appertaining to plot number 2770 belonged to Amjad, Latif and him. He denied the suggestion that the gift deed was collusive. 

12. The defendant side examined three local witnesses namely, DW 2 Mannan, DW 3 Shorab Matubbar and DW 4 Azraf Ali. All of them deposed in support of the defendants case and asserted their (defendants') physical possession over the suit land. 

13. After conclusion of hearing, learned Assistant Judge decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff by judgment and decree dated 30-8-1989 (decree signed on 5-9-1989). Being aggrieved, the defendants preferred Title Appeal Number 153 of 1989 in the Court of District Judge, Faridpur. Learned Subordinate Judge, Faridpur ultimately heard the appeal and allowed the same by the impugned judgment and decree reversing those of the trial court. In that event, the plaintiff-petitioner moved in this court with the present revisional application and obtained the Rule. 

14. Mr. Saidul Alam Khan, leaned advocate for the petitioner submits that the plaintiff proved his case by producing the written agreement for sale, examining two attesting witnesses and the scribe of the sale agreement, and also by examining a local witness (PW 4). The plaintiff clearly proved the payment of earnest money to defendant number 1, Abdul Hamid Matubbar. The trial court, on proper consideration of the evidence on record, decreed the suit but the appellate court, on usual variation in the oral evidences of the plaintiff's witnesses disbelieved the contract and allowed the appeal. 

15. Mr. Khan further submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract, the validity of sale agreement and payment of consideration money are the prime considerations, which the plaintiff has been able to prove in this case. In a suit for specific performance of contract, there is no scope to examine the title of a third party and to refuse specific performance on that ground. In support of his submission, Mr. Khan refeis to the case of lbrahim Khalil vs Mujibir Rahman, X ADC (2013) 72. 

16. I have considered the submission of the learned advocate and gone through the record. Since this a judgment of reversal. I have gone through the evidence and other materials available in the lower courts' files. It appears that defendant number I (ka) Jonab Ali Matubbar (DW 1) was an attesting witness to the sale agreement dated 30-10-1978, who denied his signature thereon. He stated that the original gift deed dated 13-6-1972 was seized by the then Bureau of Anti-Corruption (now Anti-Corruption Commission) in connection with a criminal case that was lodged against the plaintiff. The defendants side produced the original seizure list with photocopies of the original gift deed dated 13-6-1972 with another gift deed, and eleven rent receipts showing payment of rent against the suit land. For unknown reason, the said documents except the rent receipts were not exhibited/marked. These documents are still lying in the trial court's file, which I have examined and found that the sale agreement and gift deed are bearing the left thumb impressions (for short, LTI) of defendant number 1, Abdul Hamid Matubbar on their back pages. The written statement filed by him is also bearing his left thump impression on its front pages. So, there was sufficient scope to compare the LTIs of defendant number 1 from the said two documents calling the gift deed from the then Bureau of Anti-Corruption and arrive at a decision whether he had executed the sale agreement in question. 

17. It is important to notice that defendants number 3 and 4 were added in the suit and contested the same claiming their title and physical possession over the suit land on the basis of gift deed dated 13-6-1972 executed and registered by the same vendor (defendant number 1) long before execution of the sale agreement dated 30-10-1978. In such a case, if the suit is decreed without determining their case on merit, would they be non-suited as against the present plaintiff? In the present case, defendant number 1 himself denied the sale agreement and stated that he had gifted the property to his sons by registered Oft deed dated 13-6-1972. DW 1 deposed affirming the said gift and DWs 1-4 affirmed their possession over the suit land. In such a case the trial court ought to have examined the title and physical possession of defendant number 1 in the suit property and been extra cautious in giving the decree on the basis of an unregistered sale agreement. 

18. Section 25(a) of the Specific Relief Act disqualifies a person from specific performance of contract, who knowing himself not to have any title to a property, contracts to sell it. However, such contract makes him liable for payment of damages. On the effect of section 25 of the Act, we find the case of Bajrang Lal Agarwala vs Aksed Ali Shaikh, 35 DLR 110. In this case, the plaintiff instituted a suit for specific performance of contract, where an application for addition of party under Order I, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by a third party, who claimed title and possession over the suit land. Learned trial judge rejected the application. Challenging the rejection order, the applicant moved in the High Court Division with a revisional application and obtained Rule. A Division Bench heard the Rule and made it absolute. In passing the judgment, ATM Afzal, J (as his lordship then was) speaking for the court observed:—
"In a suit for specific performance the general Rule is that a stranger to the contract cannot be sued upon it. Only the parties to the contract are, according to that Rule, necessary and sufficient parties. But the general rule is subject to certain modifications. For instances strangers are made parties as an exception to the rule in cases of novation; and in cases where it is desirable to avoid multiplicity of stilts. 
"... the petitioner's presence is very much necessary because he claims to be in possession of the suit property. If his possession is proved, no decree for possession can be passed against him and the suit for specific performance would fail although a suit for damages may lie against the vendor....' 

19. We also find the case of Sh. Barkatullah and another vs Khawaja Mohammad Ibrahim, 22 DLR (SC) 419, 424 where there was a contract for leasing out a shop between the plaintiff and defendant number 1. Before handing over the possession, a dispute over fixing the monthly rent of the shop arose between them. The defendant leased out the shop to a third party and also put him in possession. The plaintiff instituted the suit for specific performance of the said contract for lease. The trial court dismissed the suit on the findings amongst others that the third party, who was in physical possession of the shop and was carrying on business there, was a necessary party to the suit. On an appeal, the appellate court reversed the judgment and on second appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court affirmed the judgment of the appellate court. The matter was taken to the Supreme Court of Pakistan, where the Supreme Court granted special leave and after hearing allowed the appeal and restored the judgment of the trial court. In so doing, the Supreme Court of Pakistan observed:—
" ... As a general rule the second lessee cannot be sued upon the contract to which he was not a party i.e. no decree for possession can be passed against him. The suit for specific performance would therefore fail though a decree for damages may be passed against the lessor for breach of contract. However, if the second lessee is in possession and has notice of the contract on which the suit is based, he would then be sued upon and a decree for possession passed against him…….” 

20. It is to be kept in mind that the decisions of the Supreme Court of Pakistan passed before emergence of Bangladesh are having binding effect on the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, High Court Division. (reliance placed on Temb Ali vs Sved Ullah, 75 DLR (AD) 233: Siddique Farazi vs State, 73 DLR 79 and Ahmed Nazir on behalf of AKM Golan Kaffir vs Bangladesh through Seeretaty, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh, 27 DLR 199, 224). 

21. In the case of Ibrahim Khalil and others as cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, the title of an ejmali land was subsequently devolved upon two SA recorded tenants, namely, Gurudas Sarker and Debendra Mondal, Defendants number 1, whose title was derived from Debendra Mondal, entered into an agreement for sale with the plaintiff. Defendants number 4-9 were co-sharers of the suit land having ejmali title therein derived from Gurudas Sarker, who tried to resist the plaintiff's claim of specific performance (see paragraphs 4 and 13). The executants of the sale agreement (defendants number I and 2 did not contest the suit, but defendants number 4-9. The trial court dismissed the suit, while the High Court Division being appellate court decreed the same and the Appellate Division upheld the High Court's judgment on the grounds that the executants of the sale agreement did not contest the suit, the contesting defendants number 4-9 were co-sharers of the suit land and the issue of their independent title was beyond the scope of adjudication in a suit for specific performance of contract. In the cited case, there was alternative remedy to bring a suit for partition praying all necessary reliefs on the part of the defendants number 4-9. Moreover, whether defendants number 1 and 2 in the cited case had exclusive title and possession over the land under contract and defendant number 1 was disqualified under section 25 of the Specific Relief Act, were not raised and discussed there. 

22. In the case in hand, defendants number 3-4 were added by court's order, which was not challenged by the plaintiff. The proposed vendor (defendant number 1) filed written statement denying the execution of the sale agreement, his legal heirs contested the suit on the basis of his written statement and the suit land was not ejmali in nature. The defendants claimed title and possession over the self-same suit land from the same person by a gift deed registered long before execution of the unregistered sale agreement of the plaintiff. The bar also failed to bring into notice of the court its previous decision given in the case of Sh. Barkatullah and another. So, on many counts, the decision cited by the learned advocate for the petitioner is distinguishable with the case in hand. 

23. In view of the discussions made and the decisions cited above, we can safely hold that under exceptional circumstances, a third party's claim of physical, possession and prima-facie title can be adjudicated on merit in a suit for specific performance of contract, where he is already made a party and claims independent title and physical possession over the subject matter of the contract. This will help avoid multiplicity of litigations and future complications. 

24. Under the facts and circumstances of the present case, I think it would be just and proper to send the suit cm remand to the trial court for determination of the genuineness of the sale agreement in question by comparing the LTIs of defendant number 1, Abdul Hamid Matubbar as put on the back pages of agreement for sale dated 30-10-1978 and those of the original gift deed dated 13-6-1972, or that on the front pages of his written statement, which is lying with the record, if the gift deed is not found available. Before that, for exercising the discretionary power of the court in granting the relief of specific performance, physical possession and prima-facie title of defendants number 3 and 4 should also be determined taking into consideration the registered gift deed dated 13-6-1972 for the purpose of complete adjudication of the dispute and also to avoid multiplicity of litigations.
 
25. In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the suit is sent back on remand to the trial court for determination of physical possession and prima-facie title of defendants number 3-4 over the suit land and validity of sale agreement dated 30-10-1978 (Exhbit-1) comparing the thumb impressions of defendant number 1 Abdul Hamid Matubbar by an expert in the manner stated above. 

26. On receipt of this judgment, the trial court will serve fresh notice upon the plaintiff as well as the contesting defendants, frame an issue as to whether defendants number 3 and 4 had physical possession and prima-facie title over the suit land and adjudicate the same. The plaintiff will take necessary steps for expert examination of the thumb impressions of deceased defendant number 1 in the manner stated above within 04 (four) months from receipt of this judgment. 

Send down the records. 

End.

parties:
Naimuddin Mondol @ Namiruddin -------Defendant No.2-Respondent-Petitioner 
vs
1. Md. Abdus Sattar ------ Plaintiff-Appellant-Opposite Party
2. Government of Bangladesh, and others ------- Defendants-Respondents-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Kazi Md. Ejarul Haque Akondo, J : This Rule, under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, was issued in the following terms—
"Record be called for, and let a Rule be issued calling upon opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 26-11-2012, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Naogaon in Title Appeal No. 283 of 2011 allowing the appeal by reversing and setting aside those dated 28-9-2011, passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Damoirhat, Naogaon in other Class Suit No. 32 of 2004, and decreed the suit should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper." 

2. The present opposite party No. 1 as the plaintiff filed the instant suit before the Court of Learned Assistant Judge, Damoirhat, Naogaon against the present petitioner and other opposite parties as the defendants for a declaration that the people have the easement right over the suit land. 

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the suit land is the property under Khas Khatian No. 1 of the Government. In the remark column of the said khatian it has been written useable by the people and in the CS Khatian there was a remark 'eidgah' in the remark column for which the suit land had not been given on pattan. The suit property is a ditch, pond and eidgah. A mosque has been built in some portion of the suit land. The local people use the land for a long period from time immemorial. But in the RS Khatian, there was no remark in the remark column of the plot as useable by the people. Defendant Nos.1-2 on 15-12-2003, refused the easement right of the people, hence the plaintiff filed the instant suit on the consent of all for declaration of the easement right over the suit land. 

4. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land is the khas land of the Government. It has been recorded in the CS, SA, and RS Khatians in the name of the Government in Khas Khatian No. 1. There is no scope of building a mosque or an eidgah illegally in the suit land. 

5. Defendant No. 2 filed a separate written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land is the khas land of the Government, and he got the same from the Government by way of settlement, enjoying the property by mutating his name, and paying rent. He gifted 25 decimals of land to build a mosque thereon, and hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

6. Defendant Nos. 3-4 also filed a separate written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable, but did not contest the case by adducing any evidence. 

7. During the trial, the plaintiff examined 03 witnesses and produced documentary evidence, and on the other hand, the defendants examined 04 witnesses and produced documentary evidence to prove their respective cases. 

8. After the conclusion of the trial the learned Assistant Judge. Dhamoirhat, Naogaon by judgment and decree dated 28-9-2011, dismissed the suit on contest against the contesting defendants and ex-parte against the rest. 9. Being aggrieved by the said impugned judgment and decree dated 28-9-2011, the plaintiff as the appellant preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Naogaon, and the same was numbered as Title Appeal No. 283 of 2011. After hearing the appeal the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Naogaon by judgment and decree dated 26-11-2012, allowed the appeal by setting aside those of the Trial Court on contest against respondent No. 2 and ex-parte against the rest, and decreed the suit. 

10. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said impugned judgment and decree dated 26-11-2012, defendant No. 2 as the petitioner had preferred this civil revision before this Court and obtained the instant Rule. 

11. Anyway, Mr Md Iqbal Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for defendant No.2 petitioner submits that the learned Judge of the Trial Court considering the facts and circum-stances of the case and the evidence on record rightly dismissed the suit of the plaintiff but on appeal, the learned Judge of the Appellate Court below without controverting the findings of the Trial Court erroneously passed the impugned judgment and decree. 

12. He further submits that the learned Judge of the Appellate Court below on misreading and non-consideration of the material facts on record passed the impugned judgment and decree though there was no continuation of the easement right of the plaintiff. He also submits that PW-1 himself gave evidence before the Court to the effect that he never performed Eid prayer in the suit land, but the learned Judge of the Appellate Court below only taking into consideration the CS record passed the impugned judgment and decree, and thereby committed an error of law which is liable to be set-aside for the ends of justice. 

13. Conversely, Mr. Pirjada Syed Abu Hanifa 1bna Jamal Md. Alam the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Md Sultan Mahmud, Advocate on behalf of plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 submits that admittedly the suit land originally belonged to the Zamindar namely Shankarpur Zamindary Estate directly under the proprietorship of the Zamindari and rightly recorded in the CS Khatian' in the name of the Zamindar who dedicated the suit land to the Muslim mass people for their eidgah as well as for general use and accordingly, the said intention/dedication published in the CS Khatian in its remark column. 

14. He next submits that this is not a customary easement; rather, it's an easement that was created by way of taking the suit land from the original owner of CS record who gave the same to the Muslim mass people for their eidgah as well as general use, and once it was given/ dedicated for such use and recorded in the CS record, there is no authority to delete/return the said property from the rights of Muslim mass people and to give it settlement to any person for his personal use by depriving the mass people. 

15. He also submits that the suit land which is being used by the Muslim mass people has been given to one person who only paid Taka 129 and, as such, for the better interest of the masses the suit land is required to remain open for their use. He lastly submits that some portion of the suit land has been transferred to a mosque which is a clear violation of the terms and conditions of the settlement executed by the Government. 

16. On the other hand, Mr. Prahlad Debnath, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, appearing for opposite party No.2-Government submits that initially the instant suit was filed by 2% of the local people as the plaintiffs but subsequently, plaintiff No. 2 withdrew himself from the suit by applying. He also submits that after filing the case a notice was published in the daily newspaper but no one came forward to add themselves as a party in the case. He further submits that the land of plot No. 5848 has been given to the defendant-petitioner by way of settlement by executing a hukumnama. He next submits that an Advocate Commissioner was appointed by the Court to inquiry the suit land physically and after physical examination, the Advocate Commissioner submitted a report before the Court opining that there was no existence of eidgah in the suit land; rather, there were dwelling houses, trees, etc. 

17. Heard the learned Advocates for the contending parties and perused the materials on record. However, at the time of hearing of the Rule, we heard Mr. Swapan Kumar Dutta, an Advocate of this Court as Anticus Curiae for proper adjudication of the matter. 

18. Mr. Dutta in the course of his submissions contends that it appears that during the trial, the Trial Court decided to issue No. 2 separately in favor of the plaintiff. While the Court decided to issue Nos. 1, 3 & 4 jointly against the plaintiff. In deciding all those issues the learned Trial Judge took all the oral and documentary evidence of the contending parties including the commissioner's report and held that, at present, there is no existence of eidgah in CS and RS plot Nos. 5848 and 8419, and long before the same has been converted to the private land of defendant No. 2, who obtained the same vide Lease Order of the P.S. Case No. 1136 of 1969-70 (exhibit-'G'), Letter of Allotment of PS Case No. 1136 of 1969-70 dated 13-1-1979 (exhibit-'H'), and registered Kabuliat No. 1727 (exhibit-`1'). He mutated his name and got Khatian No. 1071 (exhibit- T), paid Government dues and got DCR (exhibit-'K'), and paid rent [exhibit- 'L'—'L(7)']. 

19. He next contends that defendant No. 2 donated 25 decimals of land from the CS and RS plot Nos. 5848 and 8419 in favor of "Purba Jahanpur Jame masjid" by registered deed of gift No. 7096 dated 1-8-1992, a Mosque and an aujukhana were established thereon. The Advocate Commission report 'exhibit- X(1)1 and the sketch-map thereto [exhibit- X(2)] proved the said facts. The plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 did not even file any written objection against the said commissioner's report. The plaintiff (PW-1) also admitted that he performed prayer in the "Purba Jahanpur Jame masjid". In that view of the facts, there cannot be any existence of eidgah for public use in the said land as claimed by the plaintiff, and thus the learned Trial Judge dismissed the suit on the contest but the Appellate Court below mistakenly shifted the onus of proof upon the defendants because there is no iota of evidence on the part of the plaintiff to show that the suit property is still being used as eidgah continuously and uninterruptedly. 

20. He further goes on to submit that it is very important to mention here that the claim of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1, being the nature of a discontinuous easement as contemplated in section 5 of the Easements Act, 1882 is to prove the uninterrupted and continuous use of it as such strictly by the public at large. Otherwise, he could not come within the ambit of the definition of section 4 of the Easements Act, 1882 for having a decree as prayed for. The provisions of sections 4 and 5 of the Easements Act, 1882 are quoted below for ready reference-
4. "EASEMENT" DEFINED—An easement is a right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses, as such, for the beneficial enjoyment of that land, to do and continue to do something, or to prevent and continue to prevent something being done, in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land not his own. DOMINANT AND SERVIENT HERITAGES AND OWNER—The land for the beneficial enjoyment of which the right exists is called the dominant heritage, and the owner or occupier thereof the dominant owner; the land on which the liability is imposed is called the servient heritage, and the owner or occupier thereof the servient owner. 
5. CONTINUOUS AND DISCONTINUOUS, APPARENT AND NON-APPARENT EASEMENTS—
Easements are either continuous or discontinuous, apparent or non-apparent. A continuous easement is one whose enjoyment is or may be, continual without the act of man. 
A discontinuous easement is one that needs the act of man for its enjoyment. 
An apparent easement is one the existence of which is shown by some permanent sign which, upon careful inspection by a competent person, would be visible to him. 
A non-apparent easement is one that has no such sign. 

21. Defendant No.2 was able to prove his case by oral and series of exhibited documents (exhibits-A to L (7)]. The learned Advocate Commissioner also exhibited his report and sketch-map [exhibits-X(1) and X(2)] which also supported the case of the defendant-petitioner that since 1979 he has been using the suit property as his private property and donated some lands vide registered deed of gift No. 7096 dated 1-8-1992 for construction of a mosque named "Purba Jahanpur Jame Mosjid" and these clear and unequivocal facts frustrated the very foundation of the plaintiff's case. 

22. He lastly contends that by claiming the easement right over the suit property the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 wanted to harm the absolute right of the local Muslims in the 25 decimals of land which they acquired by a registered deed of gift No. 7096 dated 1-8-1992 as because if the suit is decreed as prayed for the absolute right of the masses will be negated and will be divested to the Government. 

23. On scrutiny of the evidence on record, it appears that admittedly, the suit land along with then Zamindar namely "Shankarpur Zamindary Estate" i.e. directly under the proprietorship of the Zamindar, and during the CS operation, their names were recorded in CS Khatian No. 1 and the same was finally published in their names and subsequently on 14-4-1956, the entire land devolved upon the Government by the cessation of zamindary system. During the SA and RS operation, the suit land along with other lands was recorded in the name of the Government in its Khas Khatian No. 1, and permanently settled the suit land in favor of the petitioner under PS Case Nos. 198/1964-65 and 1136/1969-70 respectively. The petitioner mutated his name, paying rent, and enjoying the property. 

24. It also appears that PW-1 along with other PWs admitted in their cross-examinations that all the inhabitants of Zahanpur perform their holy Eid at Eshwarpur eidgah instead of Zahanpur eidgah (the suit eidgah), and there is no existence of the eidgah as claimed by the plaintiff. The plaintiff failed to establish the case that he and other persons of the locality enjoying and possessing the suit land as eidgah as mandated by the Easements Act; rather, the plaintiff admits in his cross-examination that he and his full brother Md. Zafar Ali purchased a part of the suit property by registered deed No. 3388 dated 18-6-2021. In the premises, it appears that the learned Trial Judge rightly held that once upon a time there was an eidgah and subsequently the same has been abolished by operation of law. After abolishing the zamindary system all lands in the khas possession of the then Zamindar which appertain to their estates, vested absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances as per section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950 and thus, the Government acquired the suit land as their khas land by operation of law and subsequently, settled the same in favour of defendant No. 2-petitioner by accepting salami and rents vide exhibit Nos. A-L. Thereafter, the petitioner gifted 25 decimals of land for constructing a Mosque vide deed No. 7096 dated 1-8-1992 which was apparent in the Advocate Commissioner's report dated 15-10-2004, and accordingly, the learned Trial Judge rightly dismissed the suit on elaborate discussions. 

25. The nature of the suit land has already been changed over time, and the. Government rightly settled the same to the defendant-petitioner, who has been enjoying the property for a long time as private land other than eidgah and thus, the continuity of the easement right has been frustrated. The settlement of the Government cannot be nullified by the mere claim of the plaintiff, who was not able to prove his case. There are as many as 4 plots out of which the alleged eidgah is in one of the plots, but there is no claim regarding the land of the other 3 plots. 

26. Because of the above, it appears that the learned Judge of the Appellate Court below on an erroneous view passed the impugned judgment and decree reversing those of the Trial Court and thereby committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice. 

27. Given the above, I found substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and that of the learned Amicus Curiae, and merit in the Rule. Accordingly, the Rule succeeds.  
28. As a result, the Rule is made absolute without cost. 

29. The impugned judgment and decree dated 26-11-2012, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Naogaon in Title Appeal No. 283 of 2011 allowing the appeal by reversing and setting aside those dated 28-9-2011, passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Damoirhat, Naogaon in Other Class Suit No. 32 of 2004, and decreed the suit is hereby set-aside. The original Other Class Suit No.32 of 2004 is dismissed. 

Send a copy of this judgment along with the LCR to the Court below at once. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 2nd day of June, 2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3767 of 2004)
full_judgment:
Abu Bakar Siddiquee, J: This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated the 2nd day of June, 2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3767 of 2004 making the Rule absolute. 

2. The facts relevant to dispose of the appeal, in short, are that the appellant as plaintiff instituted the original suit being No. 101 of 2000 in the Court of Assistant Judge Chowddagram, Cumilla for declaration of title and khas possession, alleging, inter alia, that one Abdul Gazi was the original owner of the suit land. During Chakla Roshnabad settlement operation, the CR Khatian was recorded in his name. Abdul Gazi died leaving behind four sons as his heirs, namely, Wazuddin, Miazan, Abdul and Alimuddin. By amicable arrangement, Alimuddin and Abdul got the land of first schedule and while owning and possessing 14 decimals land of the suit plot, Alimuddin died leaving behind four sons, namely, Tajul Islam, Saku Mia, Bazlur Rahman and Ibrahim and one daughter, Asia Khatun. At the time of SA operation, Khatian No. 106 was prepared in their names. By amicable arrangement, Saku Mia got 4 decimals land from the suit plot and he died leaving behind one daughter, namely, Bachuni Bibi, by his first wife and two sons (plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2) and two daughters named Amena and Tafura, by his second wife, Jobeda Begum. After that, Jobeda died leaving behind two daughters and two sons (plaintiff, Nos. 1 and 2). Among the heirs, the plaintiffs got the suit land by amicable partition and built shops on the suit land and have been possessing the same through tenants. Accordingly, the plaintiffs got their names recorded in 4 decimals land (3 decimals from plot No. 591 and 1 decimal from plot No. 597). Defendant No. 2 sold ½ decimal land to Safu Mia, son of Sekander Ali by a registered deed of sale dated 18-1-1982. The plaintiffs' suit land is on the northern side of the land sold by defendant No. 2. Defendant No. 1 sold ½ decimal land to Bhola Mia, son of Hosson Ali by a registered deed of sale dated 6-3-1989. The plaintiffs filed a suit for permanent injunction against the defendants who having been infuriated by the Filing of the suit dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit land. Hence, this suit-has been filed. 

3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that Alimuddin, original owner of the suit land, died leaving behind four sons, namely, Bazlur Rahman, Saku Mia, Tajuddin and Ibrahim and one daughter, Asia Khatun. Each son got 6½ decimals land and daughter got 3½ decimals land. By amicable arrangement, Ibrahim got his share from the northern side, Bazlur Rahman got from southern side and Asia got from southern side of the suit land. The plaintiff got 3 decimals land as the heir of Saku Mia from western side of the suit land. Ibrahim sold out his share to his brother, Md Bazlur Rahman by a deed of sale dated 18-4-1953. After that, Bazlur Rahman died leaving behind two sons (defendant Nos. 1 and 2). Asia Khatun sold 1½ decimals land out of 3½ decimals land to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by a deed of sale dated 10-10-1980. Later on, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 sold out their shares to various persons by different deeds of sale except 1 decimal land and they have been possessing one decimal land by erecting shop. The plaintiff has no right, title and possession in the suit land. 

4. The defendants filed additional written statement alleging, inter alia, that they have been owning and possessing the suit land with other land by inheritance and by purchase. They sold out some portion of land to various persons on different dates. Meanwhile the market value of the suit land has been increasing day by day. For that ieason, the plaintiff dispossessed defendant Nos. 1 and 2 from the suit land in the first part of 1980. As such, arbitration was held and the Arbitrator ordered the plaintiff to hand over the possession of the suit land in favour of the defendants. Accordingly, the plaintiff handed over possession of the suit land in favour of the defendants. At that time, the plaintiff did not take any step in Title Suit No. 80 of 2000. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have been possessing the suit land. The statements made in the plaint are false and fabricated and that they have prayed for dismissing the suit. 

5. On the other hand, the plaintiff filed a written objection against the additional written statement denying all the facts and stating that there was no arbitration as alleged by the defendants. 

6. The trial Court decreed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 15-9-2003. 

7. Against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 preferred Title Appeal No. 213 of 2003 in the Court of the District Judge, Cumilla. On transfer, the appeal was heard by learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Cumilla, who by his judgment and decree dated 15-6-2004 dismissed the appeal affirming those of the trial Court. 

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed Civil Revision No. 3767 of 2004 before the High Court Division. The learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute. 

9. Against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division, the plaintiff-appellant filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1618 of 2009 and leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant:—
"I. Whether the suit land is specified and demarcated by its boundary and the trial Court and the Appellate Court concurrently found that the plaintiff was in possession of such specific land and that the suit is very much maintainable in its present from and the High Court Division misconceived the law requiring partition to the same and as such, the impugned judgment passed on such erroneous finding is liable to be set-aside. 
II. Whether because of subsequent dispossession, the petitioner did not proceed with the suit for permanent injunction filed by him and again filed the present suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession and the High Court Division misconceived the said facts and because of dismissal of the suit for permanent injunction disbelieved the plaintiffs previous possession and thus passed the impugned judgment which required to be interfered with by this Division. 
III. Whether admittedly the suit property is a shop in nature but the High Court Division without any material on record held that it is the only paternal homestead of the defendant-respondent and thus came to erroneous decision which is liable to be set-aside." 

10. Mr Khair Ezaz Maswood, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the suit land is specified and demarcated by its boundary and the. trial Court and the Appellate Court concurrently found that the plaintiff was in possession of such specific land and that the suit is very much maintainable in its present from and the High Court Division misconceived the law requiring partition of the same and, as such, the impugned judgment passed on such erroneous finding is liable to be set-aside. He further submits that because of subsequent dispossession, the plaintiff-appellant did not proceed with the suit for permanent injunction filed by him and again filed the present suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession and the High Court Division misconceived the said facts and because of dismissal of the suit for permanent injunction disbelieved the plaintiffs previous possession and thus passed the impugned judgment which is required to be interfered with by this Division. He lastly submits that admittedly, the suit property is a shop in nature but the High Court Division without any material on record 'held that it is the only paternal homestead of the defendant-respondent and thus came to erroneous decision which is liable to be set-aside. 

11. None appeared to represent respondent Nos. 1-2. No one appeared for respondent Nos. 3-19 to support the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. 

12. We have heard the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant and also perused the materials on record. 

13. The suit land originally belonged to one Abdul Gazi who died leaving behind four sons in Wazuddin, Miazan, Abdul and Alimuddin. 

14. The plaintiff-appellant has come with an allegation that aforesaid Alimuddin and Abdul acquired 0.28 acre land from CR Khatian No. 9 by way of amicable arrangement among the co-sharers. It has been further alleged that said Alimuddin as owner in possession over 0.14 acre land died leaving behind Tour sons in Tazul Islam, Soku Mia, Bazlur Rahman and Ibrahim and one daughter in Asia Khatun. It has been further alleged that Soku Mia alone acquired 0.04 acre land by way of amicable arrangement among the brother and sister and thereafter Soku Mia died leaving behind one daughter in Bechuni Bibi by his 1st wife and two sons, plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and two daughters in Amina Begum and Tafura Begum by his second wife Jobaida who subsequently died leaving behind two sons (plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and one daughter in Tafura). It has been also alleged that the plaintiff Nos. l and 2 acquired entire 0.04 acre land which have been recorded under plot No. 430 by way of amicable arrangement among the co-sharer and they constructed a homestead and shops therein and thereafter have been possessing the same by engaging Abul Kasham Dealer, Dr. Nazir Ahamed and Probir Mistry as monthly tenant. It has been further alleged that during RS operation 0.03 acre land has been recorded under plot No. 599 and 0.01 acre has been recorded in plot No. 597. It has been further alleged that defendant No. 2, Abdul Awal, transferred 0.05 decimal land to one Soku Mia son of Sekandar Ali by a Kabala dated 18-1-1982 and defendant No. 1 sold other 0.05 decimal land to one Bhola Mia son of Hossain Ali by a Kabala dated 6-3-1989 but all of a sudden defendant Nos. l and 2 threatened the plaintiff with dispossession from 0.03 acre of land under plot number 599 and, as such, plaintiffs were compelled to institute a suit being No. 80 of 2000 for permanent injunction, but on receiving the summons of that case, the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff from that land and building by ousting their varatia. Thereafter it has been alleged that the appellant plaintiff requested the defendant to quit the aforesaid land and building in their favour but they denied it and, as such, the plaintiff-appellants were compelled institute the present suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession after withdrawing the suit for permanent injunction. 

15. Respondent Nos. land 2 (contesting defendants) denied the aforesaid contention of the plaintiff and counter claimed that their father Bazlur Rahman is the son of Alimuddin who is one of the sons of original owner Abdul Gazi and, as such, his father inherited 0.62/9 acre land and also purchased the share of another co-sharer Ibrahim by Kabala dated 18-4-1953. They further alleged that after the death of their father they purchased they recorded 0.01½ acre from another co-sharer Asia Khatun by Kabala dated 10-10-1980, but they sold out the said land elsewhere and they have been possessing only 0.01 acre land from the suit plot but the alleged fact of acquisition of 0.4 acre by the plaintiff from their father is downright falsehood and construction of building and letting out the same to anybody is also a false story. It has been further alleged that the plaintiffs present suit is not at all maintainable in its present from since they have filed another suit on the same cause of action. 

16. Let us proceed to examine the evidence on record and see therefrom as to how far the plaintiffs have been able to prove their case. 

17. It is an established principle that plaintiff in order to succeed must establish his own case to obtain a decree and weakness of defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff. 

18. Asraf Ali while deposing as PW1 stated that his predecessor Soku Mia acquired 0.04 acre land from previous plot No. 430 out of which 0.03 acre has been recorded under RS plot No. 599 and 0.01 acre has been recorded under RS Plot No. 597. He also deposed that their predecessor Soku Mia acquired the aforesaid 0.04 acre land from SA Plot No.430 and the plaintiffs inherited the same as have been alleged by them. The genealogical table as has been furnished the plaintiffs has not been challenged by the defence, but the acquisition of entire 0.04 acre land by amicable arrangement has been challenged by the defence. The defendants claimed that they have sold out their share excepting their 0.01 acre land in which they have claimed their right, title and interest in this case. In this respect defendant No.2, Abdul Awal, while deposing as DW1 stated that excepting 0.01 acre land they have sold out other land under suit jote to others, but he has not disclosed the name and quantum of land sold. Thus the defendants failed to show as to how much land, they have transferred in this case, to whom, nor they filed those transfer deeds and, as such, we are unable to ascertain as to whether the defendants have any right, title, interest over 0.01 acre land as has been claimed by them. Not only that, the defence have come with an allegation that they have sold out the land to stranger purchasers against whom the plaintiffs are entitled to get protection from section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act wherein it has been enacted that original co-sharer of the suit jote are entitled to an order of injunction against stranger purchaser in respect of possession of the homestead land. In this respect the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant has cited a decision enunciated in the case of Md Muktar Ahmed vs Mir Md Hussain reported in 9 DLR page 119 wherein it has been held that:—
"A member of an undivided family can maintain a suit for injunction restraining a stranger-purchaser of a portion of a joint property from taking possession of the property. 
Instead of availing himself of that right that is, his bringing of a partition suit for a specific possession of share if such purchaser tries to take forcible possession, a co-sharer can bring a suit for injunction restraining such a transferee from entering into possession of the undivided dwelling house." 

19. In the instant case, the plaintiff-appellant at first instituted a suit for permanent injunction and alleging that during pendency of that suit the defendants dispossessed the plaintiffs and, as such, the plaintiff has instituted the present suit seeking declaration of title and recovery of khas possession after withdrawing the previous suit for permanent injunction. Although the contesting defendants are not stranger but they indulged some strangers to enter into the suit jote and at last the defendants claimed only 0.01 acre of land from the suit jote. 

20. SA Motin Mazumder a survey knowing Advocate was appointed with a view to survey the suit land. The point for ascertainment by the survey knowing Advocate was as to whether the suit land described in schedule lg(K) of the plaint attracted with suit plot and the said fact should be ascertained after relement of those plots. 

21. In his report the Advocate Commissioner clearly shows that the land described in the schedule lg(K) is clearly attracted with the land appertaining to plot No. 430 and area of land is 0.00661 equivalent to ¾ decimal in place of 0.01 acre. 

22. This commissioner report has been accepted by the trial court and, as such, it has been admitted in evidence. PW2 Dr. Nazir Ahamed deposed that he was rendering his business as physician in the suit premises after taking the suit shop as varatia from the plaintiff and thereafter he surrendered the possession of the suit shop in favour of one Probir Babu amicably. He further deposed that the defendant dispossessed the plaintiff on 25-9-2000 from the suit shop. PW3, Probir Mistry, also corroborated the fact of such dispossession. PW4, Abdul Hai, deposed that he saw the plaintiff to possess the suit shop after engaging Abul Kalam, Dr. Nazir Ahmed and Probir Mistry as varatia but on 25-9-2000 the defendant ousted those varatia and thereby dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit premises. DW2, Samsul Alam Muzamder, is one of the mediators who deposed that Dr. Nazir and Probir Mistry were the varatia of the suit premises and he asked them to vacate the same. DW3, Harez Chowdhoury, is another mediator who deposed that before the fact of dispossession Dr. Nazir Ahmed and Probir Mistry were the varatia of the suit premises. 

23. Those facts and circumstances and evidence on record lead us to hold that the plaintiff-appellant was in possession of the suit premises before dispossession as has been alleged on 25-9-2000. 

24. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant argued that the suit land is specified and demarcated by mentioning the contiguous land holder and both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiffs were in possession on such specific portion of land and that the suit is very much maintainable in its present form but the High Court Division misconceived in holding that the facts of the case demanded to file a suit for partition. 

25. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant has cited the decision enunciated in the case of Amir Hanzza vs Abdul Ali and others reported in 4 .MLR (AD) 1999 page 425 wherein it has been held that: — 
"Section 42 suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession of suit land maintainability of suit without seeking partition. 
When the plaintiff succeeded in establishing his title to and his possession in the suit land separately recorded in his name before he was dispossessed there from and the suit is instituted well within limitation and the findings of the trial court are based on well reasoning supported by consistent evidence on record and the findings are affirmed by the appellate court as well as by the Provisional Court the decree so awarded cannot be interfered with merely on the ground of maintainability for not seeking partition in addition thereto." 

26. We also hold the view that there is no embargo to maintain this type of suit without seeking partition where the suit land is specifically well demarcated. 

27. Because of subsequent dispossession, the appellants did not proceed with the suit for permanent injunction filed by them and again filed the present suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and the High Court Division erroneously held that the suit is not maintainable because of dismissal of the suit for permanent injunction and disbelieved the plaintiffs' previous possession and thus passed the impugned judgment which is required to be interfered with by this Division. 

28. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant argued that the High Court Division as a revisional Court has hardly any jurisdiction to set-aside the concurrent findings of fact by the trial court as well as appellate Court without discussing any fault in the factual finding by the said Court. 

29. It is settled principle that a Court of revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure can interfere with the findings of fact of the lower appellate Court which is the last Court of facts, only in exceptional circumstances when the findings are shockingly perverse or these are vitiated by non-reading of the material evidence or mis-construction of any important documents affecting the merit of the suit. But in the instant case, we find that the appellate Court below as final Court of facts made a threadbare discussion and left no stone unturned, hence there was no room for mis-appreciation or misreading or any scope to no-consideration of evidence on record. 

30. Thus, it appears that the learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division erroneously disagreed with the finding of the appellate Court below. 

Accordingly, we find merit in the appeal. Thus, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment and order delivered by the learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division was set-aside. Consequently, the judgments and orders passed by the learned Judges of the Court's below are hereby restored. 

End.

Mr. Yousuf Ali, D. A. G with Ms. Kamrunnahar Lipy, A.A.G with Ms. Israt Jahan, A.A.G with Mr. Billal Ahmed Majumder, A.A.G -------- For the appellant
Mr. Md. Sherder Abul Hossain with Mr. Md. Saiyedul Islam, Advocates --------For the respondents
parties:
Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Cumilla. ----- Defendant No.1-appellant.
Vs.
Md. Jamal Mia and others -------- Plaintiff-respondents.
full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal, J: This first appeal at the instance of the defendant No. 1- appellant is directed against the judgment and decree dated 28.02.2018 (decree signed on 06.03.2018) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Cumilla in Title Suit No. 135 of 2010 decreeing the suit.

2. Material facts relevant for disposal of the appeal, briefly, are that the respondent No.1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 135 of 2010 in the court of the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Cumilla impleading the Government as defendant praying declaration of title in the suit land and to correct the wrong record of right stating, inter-alia, that one Minnat Ali was the original owner of 20 decimal of land of Dag No.526 and his name has been included in C.S. Khatian No.2 as unpermitted possessor in the remark column. Minnat Ali possessed the suit land as illegal occupant. He died leaving behind 8 sons and 2 daughters respectively. Thereafter his son Shamsu got the said land in question by way of amicable settlement and subsequently he gifted the same to the plaintiff on 29.01.2008 by registered Kabala No.557/08. Thereafter plaintiff has been possessing and enjoying the property in question by fishing by developing surrounding areas of the said land till date but at the time of R.S record, the suit land has been recorded in Khatian No.1 wrongly. The said land in question has never been possessed and controlled by the East Pakistan Government and as the value of the land has been increased now and accordingly he came to learn about the wrong record on 05.09.2009 and hence, the suit.

3. The Government defendant Nos. 1-3 entered appearance in the suit and filed written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint stating, inter-alia, the suit is misconceived, incompetent and not maintainable in law, the plaintiff has/had no right, title and possession over the suit land. The suit property originally belonged to Khawja Habibullah and others and the predecessor of the plaintiff, Minnat Ali took possession of the suit land without taking permission from the real owner, Khawja Habibullah and others before preparation of C.S. Khatian and possession Minnat Ali was also recorded in the comment column of C.S. Khatian No. 2 as illegal occupant. After publishing C.S. Khatian Minnat Ali, the predecessor of the plaintiff left the suit property with uncared condition and after abolishing the Jamindari system the suit land measuring 20 decimal under dag No. 526 and other land adjacent land became vested in the Government. The plaintiff filed the case on false averments and as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Joint District Judge on the pleadings of the parties framed the following issues for determination:- 
i. Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form and manner? 
ii. Whether the suit is bad for defect of parties? 
iii. Whether the suit is barred by limitation? 
iv. Whether the plaintiff has right, title and possession over the suit land? 
v. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree, as prayed for?

5. At the trial plaintiff side examined as many as 3 witnesses and exhibited some documents while the defendant side examined 1 witness namely DW1 to prove their respective cases.

6. The learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Cumilla after hearing the parties and on considering the materials on record by his judgment and decree dated 28.02.2018 decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff.

7. Aggrieved thereby, the Government of People’s Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Cumilla, Defendant No.1-Appellant has preferred this appeal.

8. Mr. Md. Yusuf Ali, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the appellant in the course of argument takes us through the evidence and materials on record and then submits that admittedly C.S khatian was recorded in the name of Bharot Samrat, S.A khatian, B.S khatian and R.S khatian were also recorded in the name of Deputy Commissioner, Cumilla on behalf of the then Pakistan Government now the Bangladesh Government and the Government is now possessing the suit land. He further submits that the claim of the plaintiff is that the predecessor of the plaintiff was an unauthorized possessor of the suit land and it is on record that after publishing C.S khatian in the name of Government the predecessor of the plaintiff Minnot Ali left the suit land keeping it as abandoned and since then he had no possession in the suit land and when the SAT Act came into force in the year 1950, suit land became the khas land and recorded in the name of the Government. The learned Deputy Attorney General further submits the trial court wrongly found that suit land was partitioned between the sons and daughters of Minnot Ali although the plaintiff could not submit any document regarding such partition. Since Minnot Ali had no title, the heirs of Minnot Ali Samsu Mia also had no title, so the transfer registered deed No.557 dated 29.01.2008 in favour of Zamal Mia executed by Samsu Mia has no legal basis and the said transfer has been done without any title and without any lawful authority whatsoever. He further submits as per C.S, S.A and B.S khatian, it is found that suit land is "nal" land and the Government is in possession over the suit land till date but the learned trial Judge wrongly found that the suit land is pond and the plaintiff used to farming fish. He further submits that the Defendant-Appellant in their written statement stated that so called registered deed No. 557 dated 29.01.2008 is forged, void and created and on going through the said deed it is evident that J.L. No, khatian No, quantum of land and Dag No, are not identical with C.S. S.A and B.S khatian. More so, there is only one witness in the said deed and the said witness is identifier also, which proves that it is a created forged deed although the learned trial court without considering all these vital aspects of the case from a correct angle gave wrong finding that heirs of Minnot Ali possessed the suit land without permission of the owner and after the death of Minnot Ali, his son Samsu Mia has been possessing the suit land and subsequently Samsu Mia gifted the suit land to his son Zamal Mia in spite of fact that Minnot Ali and his son Samsu Mia had no title in the suit land. Title less illegal owner cannot transfer the land to anybody by the registered deed and that registered deed is illegal and it has no value in the eye of law and as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set-aside.

9. Mr. Md. Sherder Abul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff respondent, on the other hand , submits that it is admitted facts by both the parties that the suit property originally belonged to Khawja Habibullah and others and the predecessor of the plaintiff, Minnat Ali took possession of the suit land without taking permission from the real owner, Khawja Habibullah and others before preparation of C.S. Khatian and this possession was also recorded in the comment column of C.S. Khatian No. 2. That C.S. Khatian was finally published in the year of 1926 and since then the plaintiff successively maintaining possession till today which is evident from the subsequent S.A, R.S. and B.S Khatian. In all those Khatians in comment column it has been written that plaintiff's predecessor was in possession without permission. So at least after expiry of 12 years from 1926 Minnat Ali accrued adverse title in the suit land as per provision of Section 28 read with Article 142 of the Limitation Act. He further submits that the Section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provided the list of property which will retain by the Government and in that list there is no mention about the land which was recorded in the name of private persons in C.S. Khatian prepared under the provision of section 3.B(5) of Bengal Tenancy Act and it is apparent in the C.S. Khatian No. 2 that it was recorded in the name of Khawja Habibullah and others as owners, so the entry of S.A. record in the name of Deputy Collector on behalf of East Pakistan Government and the defendant could not say as to how and in what procedure the Government of East Pakistan accrued the ownership in the suit property either in their written statements or producing any scrap of document and as such, the entry of S.A. and R.S. Khatian are baseless. Finally, Mr. Sherder Abul Hossain submits, the defendant asserted in the written statements that after publication of C.S. Khatian Minnat Ali left the suit property with uncared condition for earning his livelihood, as such the Government became owner of the suit land. In this respect the defendants did not adduce any corroborative witness or evidence to substantiate their case. Moreover there is provision in section 92(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for acquiring title by the Government in any abandoned property by filing a Miscellaneous Case and finally publishing Gazette Notification and the said act was effected from 14.04.1956 and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has no retrospective effect, so the claim of the defendant is beyond the purview of any law and as such the entry of S.A, R.S. and B.R.S. Khatian are wrong and not binding upon the plaintiff.

10. To effectively deal with the contentions raised by the learned Advocates for both the parties before us it would be convenient for us to decide first how far the learned trial Judge was justified in decreeing the suit. It is found that the respondent as plaintiff instituted the suit praying the following reliefs:
(ক) আরজির ১ম তপছিলোক্ত ভূমিতে বাদী দান সূত্রে মালিক মর্মে এক ঘোষণার ডিক্রী দিতে,
(খ) আরজির ২য় তপছিলের আর,এস ১নং খতিয়ান সম্পূর্ণ বেআইনী, তঞ্চকী, বানোয়াটি, অকার্যকরী ভিত্তিহীন এবং উহা দ্বারা বাদী বাধ্য নয় মর্মে ঘোষণার ডিক্রী দিতে,
(গ) মোকদ্দমার খরচ ডিক্রী দিতে,
(ঘ) আদালতের ন্যায় বিচারে বাদীগণ আর যে, যে, প্রতিকার পাওয়ার অধিকারী হয় তাহার পাওয়ার আদেশ দানে সুবিচার করিতে মর্জি হয়।

11. In order to resolve the dispute let us advert to the evidence of PWs and sole DW-1. At the trial the plaintiff respondent examined as many as 3 (three) witnesses to prove its case out of which PW-1, Md. Jamal Miah stated in his deposition that :
আমি বাদী। নালিশী ১ম তফশীলের জমির মালিক ছিল মিন্নত আলী, তৎনামে CS ২০নং খতিয়ান হয়। খতিয়ানে ৫২৬ দাগে মিন্নত আলী দখল লিপি আছে। মিন্নত আলী দখলে থেকে মরণে ৮ পুত্র, ২ কন্যা ওয়ারিশ হয়। তৎপুত্র আমপু মিয়া মিন্নত আলীর জীবদ্দশায় মারা যায়। মিন্নত আলীর ওয়ারিশগণ দখলে থাকাবস্থায় মিন্নত আলীর পুত্র সামছু মিয়া নালিশী তফশীলের জমি আপোষে এককভাবে প্রাপ্ত হন। তিনি আমার পিতা। আমার পিতা গত ২৯-১-০৮ তারিখে ৫৫৭ নং দাগ দলিলে আমাকে উক্ত জমি হস্তান্তর করে। আমি জমিতে মালিক দখলকার আছি।
This witness also stated that :
জমিতে বিবাদী সরকারের কোন স্বত্ব দখল নাই। BS ১নং খতিয়ানে সামছু মিয়া অনুমতি দলকার লিপি আছে।
In cross examination the defendant side could not able to discover anything as to the credibility of this witness on the matter to which he testifies. 

12. PW-2, Moslem stated in his deposition that :
আমি বাদী, বিবাদী ও নালিশী জমি চিনি। নালিশী জমিতে মাছের চাষ করে বাদী। এর আগে নাল ছিল। তখন বাদীর বাবা ফসল চাষ করত। বাদীর দাদাকে দেখিনি। আমার জন্মের পর থেকে বাদীকে দখলে দেখে আসছি। সরকার জমি দখল করে না। আমার বাড়ি নালিশী জমির দক্ষিণ পাশে।
This witness also stated that :
সরকার নোটিশ দেয়ার পর শুনেছি যে, জমি খাসের।
PW-3, Giashuddin stated in his deposition that :
আমি বাদী, বিবাদী ও নালিশী জমি চিনি। নালিশী জমিতে বাদী মাছ চাষ করে। বাদী আমার চাচা, মিন্নত আলী, আমার দাদা আকিজউদ্দিন বেপারীর বাবা। নালিশী জমিতে CS জরীপ হতে ফসল চাষে দখলে ছিল। মিন্নত 'আলীর বাড়িতে আমরা থাকি। বাদী তার নানা বাড়িতে থাকে। আপোষে নালিশী জমি শামছু মিয়া পায়। শামছু মিয়াও জমিতে চাষাবাদ করত। বাদী পিতা হতে দানমূলে দখলে আছে। সরকারের দখল জমিতে নেই।

13. On the other hand, sole DW -1, Land assistant officer, stated in his deposition that- 
"নালিশী দাগের ২০ শতক জমি সহ মোট ২০.৯৪ একর জমির মূল মালিক ছিল তালুকদার হয়ে কিশোরের অধীনে নবাব খাজা হাবিবুলস্নাহ গং। তাদের নামে CS ২নং খতিয়ান হয়। উক্ত মালিকদের বিনা অনুমতিতে ৫২৬ দাগে মিন্নত আলী দখলকার থাকায় খতিয়ানের মন্তব্য কলামে সেভাবেই লিপি আছে। নালিশী দাগের জমিতে সরকার মালিক দখলকার থাকাবস্থায় BSDP ১নং খতিয়ান বর্তমানে চূড়ান্তভাবে সরকারের নামে লিপি হয়েছে। বাদীগণের কোন স্বত্ব দখল জমিতে নেই।"
This witness also stated in his cross examination that : CS
CS দাগ ৫২৬; বিনা অনুমতিতে দখল মিন্নত আলী দাগের মন্তব্য কলামে লিপি আছে।

14. On assessment of the above quoted evidence PWs and DW-1, it appears that PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 all of them testified in one voice that the predecessor of the plaintiff respondent possessed the suit land. Name of Minnot Ali, the predecessor of the plaintiff was recorded in CS khotian and Dag No. 526 as possessor. The sole DW-1 also admitted in his evidence as to possession of Minnot Ali in the suit land. Dw-1 in his evidence also could not disclose that as to how and under what way the Government acquired the suit land.

15. On close perusal of the record, it is found that the suit property originally belonged to Khawja Habibullah and others and the predecessor of the plaintiff, Minnat Ali took possession of the suit land without taking permission from the real owner, Khawja Habibullah and others before preparation of C.S. Khatian and this possession was also recorded in the comment column of C.S. Khatian No. 2 and C.S. Khatian was finally published in the year of 1926 under the provision of Section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act and since then the plaintiff successively maintaining possession till today which is found from evidence and materials on record. Section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provided the list of property which will retain by the Government and in that list there is no mention about the land which was recorded in the private persons in C.S. Khatian prepared under the provision of Section 3.B(5) of Bengal Tenancy Act and it is apparent in the C.S. Khatian No. 2 that it was recorded in the name of Khawja Habibullah and other as owners so the entry of S.A. record in the name of Deputy Collector on behalf of East Pakistan Government and the defendant could not say as to how and in what procedure the Government of East Pakistan accrued the ownership in the suit property either in their written statements or producing any scrap of paper and as such the entry of the suit land in S.A. and B.S. Khatian are baseless.

16. The defendant-Government asserted in the written statements that after publication of C.S. Khatian Minnat Ali left the suit property and went away from the suit land for earning his livelihood and thus the Government became owner. In this respect the defendants did not adduce any corroborative witnesses or evidence to substantiate their case. Besides, there is provision in the Section 92(3) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for acquiring title by the Government in any abandoned property by filing a Miscellaneous Case and finally publishing Gazette Notification and the said act was effected from 14.04.1956 and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has no retrospective effect, so the claim of the defendant is beyond the purview of any law as such the entry of the land in question in S.A, R.S. and B.R.S. Khatian are wrong and not binding upon the plaintiff-respondent.

17. It is found that the C.S. Khatian No. 2 was prepared in the name of Khawja Habibullah and others and Minnat Ali took possession of the suit land without their permission before publication of C.S. Khatian and the matter was noted in the C.S. Khatian No.2 and C.S. Khatian was published in the year of 1926 and Minnat Ali continued his possession within the Knowledge of the real owner Kawja Habibulla, as such after expiry of 12 years i.e. in the year of 1938 Minnat Ali accrued title and it is well settled that "In order to claim title by adverse possession it is incumbent upon a person to prove that he has been in continuous possession of the disputed property over the statutory period of 12 years. Ref. 49 DLR (AD) 61.

18. Adverse possession is a legal process that allows someone to gain ownership of a property without the legal owner's permission. It's based on continuous occupation of the property or in other words, in Bangladesh, adverse possession law states that someone can gain ownership of land if the rightful owner doesn't evict them within 12 years. This means that long-term occupation of a property can lead to ownership without the need for documents.

19. In this case, we have already noticed that the plaintiff has been able to show his unbroken possession in the suit land for the last 80 years and this long-term occupation of a property can lead to ownership without the need for documents. Therefore, we think, there is a good deal of persuasion in the submission of the learned counsel for the plaintiff respondent.

20. On perusal of the impugned judgment, it appears that the trial court below after a detailed discussion of the attending circumstances borne out by records came to conclusion that :
উপরোক্ত সাক্ষ্য প্রমাণ পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায় যে, নালিশী জমিতে বিবাদী সরকার পক্ষের মালিক হওয়ার বা দখলে থাকার কোন কারণ নাই। পক্ষান্তরে বাদীর পূর্ববর্তী মিন্নত আলী সিএস রেকর্ডের পূর্ব হতেই বিনানুমতি দখলকার হিসেবে নালিশী জমি ভোগ দখল করে স্বত্বের মালিক হয়েছেন এবং তার মৃত্যুর পর তার ওয়ারিশদের মধ্যে আপোষ বন্টনে তার পুত্র সামছু মিয়া নালিশী জমি ভোগ দখল করেছেন। সামছু মিয়া হতে দানপত্র দলিল মূলে বাদী মালিক দখলকার হয়েছেন। বাদীপক্ষ নালিশী জমিতে তার স্বত্ব ও দখল প্রমাণ করতে সক্ষম হয়েছেন।

21. This being purely a finding of fact based on proper assessment of the evidence and materials on record that the plaintiff has been able to prove his unbroken possession and title in the suit land before publishing C.S. record. Therefore, we find no substance in either of the contentions as raised by the learned Deputy Attorney General.

22. The learned trial Judge appears to have considered all the material aspects of the case and justly decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 28.02.2018, we find no reason to interfere therewith.

23. In any view of the matter, having regard to the fact as aforesaid, this appeal must fail.

24. In the result, the appeal is dismissed. In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.

Send down the LC Records at once.

End.
