full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon opposite party Nos. 1-13 to show cause as to why judgment and decree dated 14-3-2013 passed by learned District and Special Judge, Rajshahi in Title Appeal No. 94 of 2007 disallowing the appeal and affirming judgment and decree dated 27-2-2007 passed by learned Assistant Judge, Charghat, Rajshahi in Other Suit No. 46 of 1990 decreeing the suit in-part should not be set-aside. 

2. During issuance of Rule, the operation of the impugned judgment and decree was stayed for a period of 3(three) months which was extended time to time. 

3. Facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule, are that Ismail Sonar, the predecessor of opposite party Nos. 1-13, as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 155 of 1922 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Rajshahi against Gulzar Ali Sonar and others in which the present petitioner was defendant No. 34 praying for a decree of partition of 0.89 acre land claiming eight anna four gonda share upon deducting 0.07 acre land there from. The suit was transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Charghat, Rajshahi and renumbered as Other Suit No. 46 of 1990. The case of the plaintiff is that 0.89 acre land as described in the schedule to the plaint belonged to Emran Sonar in eight anna share, Jarimon Bibi in three anna four gonda share, Sabjan Bewa in sixteen gonda share and Kamani Bewa in four anna share and accordingly, CS Khatian No. 220 was prepared and finally published in their name. Sabjan Bewa died leaving behind one daughter Jamiron Bibi and husband Emran Sonar. Jamiron Bibi died leaving behind three sons Koshimuddin Sonar. Abdul Hamid, Abdul Kader and four daughters Sokina, Hamidon, Samina and Maleka (defendant No. 30). Abdul Kader died leaving behind five sons (defendant Nos. 12-16). one daughter (defendant No. 17) and one wife (defendant No. 18) as his heirs. Abdul Hamid died leaving behind three sons (defendant Nos. 8-10) and one daughter (defendant No. 11). Kashimuddin Sonar died leaving behind three sons (defendant Nos. 1-3), three daughters (defendant Nos. 4-6) and one wife (defendant No. 7). Hamidon died leaving behind two sons (defendant Nos. 22-23), one daughter (defendant No. 24) and husband (defendant No. 23). Sokina died leaving behind one son (defendant No. 19) and two daughters (defendant Nos. 20-21). Samina died leaving behind husband (defendant No. 25), one son (defendant No. 26) and two daughters (defendant No. 27-28). Kamani Bewa died leaving behind one son Abdus Shukur, who died leaving behind two daughters (defendant Nos. 31-32) and one wife (defendant No. 33). Thereafter, Emran Sonar died leaving behind one son, the plaintiff. In the aforesaid way the plaintiff inherited eight anna and four gonda share out of 0.89 acre suit land. The plaintiff has got his ancestral homestead in Plot No. 1912 and out of his share he sold 0.07 acre land of Plot No. 1873 to Sairuddin long ago who got his joma separated from the original jote by mutation and, as such, he was not impleaded in this suit. Said 0.07 acre land would be deducted from the share of the plaintiff. 

4. Kasimuddin (predecessor in interest of defendant Nos. 1-7), Sokina (predecessor in interest of defendant Nos. 19-21) along with defendant Nos. 8-12, 18, 31 and 33 sold 0.26 acre land out of total 0.89 acre land by registered sale deed dated 3-9-1969 to Answer Ali Sonar and five others (who are sons of defendant No. 34). Though said kabala dated 3-9-1969 was ostensibly in the name of his sons but in fact. defendant No. 34 purchased said 0.26 acre land in the benami of his five sons. The plaintiff instituted Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 in the Court of Sadar Munsif, Rajshahi for getting said land through pre-emption. Defendant No. 34 was opposite party No. 31 in that case. The purchasers of said kabala end their father Younus Soner (defendant No. 34) contested said case by filing separate written objections and both parties adduced evidence to prove their respective case and the trial Court vide judgment and order dated 27-6-1979 allowed the pre-emption case. As per said judgment dated 27-6-1979 the right, title and interest of opposite party purchasers in respect of said 0.26 acre land vested in the petitioner (plaintiff of this suit). It was observed in that judgment that the petitioner may get possession of the disputed land only after filing a regular suit for possession. 

5. It has further stated that the father of the plaintiff, Emran Sonar left his house situated in the suit land for some times and went to Abdulpur for his treatment and the plaintiff also went with his father to look after him and at that time the plaintiff's father entrusted with the suit property including the house standing thereon to one Bashanto Kumar. The plaintiff and his father stayed at Abdulpur for a few months where his father died and he was buried there. Thereafter, the plaintiff came to his ancestral house and has been residing there. During temporary absence of the plaintiff and his father in the suit land and misusing the trust given upon him, Bashanto Kumar created certain documents in his name in respect of the suit jote and subsequently, created sale deed being No. 7799 dated 9-10-1952 by which it was purported to transfer some portion of the suit land to Younus Sonar (defendant No. 34). Defendant No. 34 never claimed title to said land and, as such, his possession of that portion is nothing but permissive and by such possession and on the basis of that sale deed dated 9-10-1952 he did not acquire any title to the suit land. The question of title to and possession of 0.26 acre land of defendant No. 34 was decided and became final in said pre-emption case and, as such, defendant No. 34 is debarred from claiming title to said land. The suit property is ejmali property of the plaintiff and the defendants except defendant No. 34 and the suit property was never portioned by metes and bounds. Cause of action of the suit arose on 27-6-1979 when judgment was passed in the pre-emption case and, as such, the plaintiff was constrained to file the present suit for partition. 

6. Out of the defendants, only defendant No. 34 contested the suit by filing written statements contending that the suit was not maintainable, barred by limitation and there was no community of interest between the parties for partition of the suit property. The positive case of the defendant was that the CS recorded tenants voluntarily surrendered their rayoti right to the superior landlords from whom Bashanto Kumar took pattan and paid rent to the landlords. The plaintiff took settlement of 0.23 acre land from the suit jote from Bashanto Kumar and erected dwelling house therein and thereafter, SA Khatian No. 157 and RS Khatian No. 134 were prepared and finally published in his name. Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land out of the suit property along with other land measuring total 2.305 acre by registered sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-5-1952 to Younus Sonar (defendant No. 34). While Younus Sonar was owning and possessing said 0.59 acre land from the suit jote separate SA Khatian No. 155 and RS Khatian No. 117 were prepared and finally published in his name. The plaintiff has no right, title to or interest in 0.59 acre land and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

7. To prove their respective case, the plaintiff adduced three oral witnesses and defendant No. 34 adduced three oral witnesses and both of them produced documentary evidence. The trial Court, upon considering the evidence and materials on record, decreed the suit in-part allotting total 0.49 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff by judgment and decree dated 27-2-2007. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree, defendant No. 34 preferred Title Appeal No. 94 of 2007 before the learned District Judge, Rajshahi which was transferred to learned Special District Judge, Rajshahi for disposal who, upon hearing the parties, disallowed the appeal by affirming judgment and decree of the trial Court vide judgment and decree dated 14-3-2013. Being aggrieved by said judgment and decree of the Court of appeal, defendant No. 34 has preferred this revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule and order of stay, as stated above. During pendency of this Rule the petitioner died and his heirs have been duly substituted. 

8. Mr. Julfiquir Bulbul Chowdhury, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner by taking me to the judgments and decrees of the courts below submitted as follows: 
1. As per chronological admission of the plaintiff there is no community of interest between the plaintiff and defendant No. 34 in the suit property and, as such, the present suit for partition is not maintainable. 
2. Though CS record was prepared and finally published in one Khatian but during SA and RS operation the land of CS Khatian was separated and three separate SA Khatians and three separate RS Khatians have been prepared and finally published out of which one SA Khatian and its corresponding RS khatian have been prepared and finally published in the name of defendant No. 34 and two other separate SA Khatians and its two separate RS Khatinas have been prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff and, as such, the plaintiff is not a co-sharer of defendant No. 34. Moreover, in the plaint the plaintiff himself stated that defendant No. 34 was not a co-sharer in the suit holding. 
3. There is no cause of action of filing this partition suit inasmuch as in one hand, the plaintiff asserted in the plaint that he has no community of interest with defendant No. 34 and on the other hand stated ( in paragraph 4 of the plaint) that the cause of action of the suit arose after judgment was pronounced in Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 and, as such, the claim of the plaintiff is self contradictory leading to no cause of action for filing this partition suit and the plaintiff upon camouflage of partition suit is trying to bypass the finding and decision of Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 and, as such, this suit is a testing suit which should have been buried at its inception as being not maintainable. 
4. It is settled principle of law that the plaintiff is to prove his own case to get a decree in his favour but in the instant case the plaintiff could not prove his title to and possession in the suit land which have been observed by the Courts below but both the Courts below upon misconception of law allotted 0.26 acre land as per fruitless judgment of the pre-emption case. 
5. No title was passed in respect of 0.26 acre land in favour of the plaintiff by judgment of the pre-emption case because admittedly, the sellers of the pre-emption case had no possession when the alleged sale deed No. 3969 dated 3-9-1969 was purportedly executed and registered and that during execution and registration of the sale deed defendant No. 34 was in possession of said land which has been observed by the learned Judge while passing judgment in the pre-emption case. 
6. Defendant No. 34 purchased 0.59 acre land including 0.26 acre land from Bashanto Kumar by registered sale deed dated 9-10-1952 following which separate SA and RS Khatians have been prepared and finally published in his name and he has been paying rents to the jaminders and thereafter, to the Government and has been possessing 0.59 acre land continually and uninterestedly from 1952 and, as such, defendant No. 34 acquired title therein by adverse possession and the right, title or interest, if any, of the CS recorded tenants have been extinguished and the plaintiff could not acquire title through CS recorded tenants. 
7. Tough defendant No. 34 admitted title of the plaintiff in respect of 0.23 acre land but since the present suit for partition is not maintainable, the plaintiff is not entitled to any decree in this partition suit. 
8. The Court of appeal, upon misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record and upon misconception of law, illegally allotted 0.26 acre land in the saham of the plaintiff and in doing so did not discuss any evidence of the parties and accordingly, committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

9. Mr. Md. Ekramul Islam, learned Advocate appearing for opposite party Nos. 1-13 submitted as follows: 
1. The Court of appeal as the last Court of facts upon considering the evidence and 
materials on record, concurrently held that the plaintiff is entitled to 0.26 acre land on the basis of judgment of the pre-emption case and such finding cannot be reversed in revisional jurisdiction. 
2. Though defendant No. 34 claimed that the CS recorded tenants surrendered the suit property to the superior landlords and thereafter, Bashanto Kumar took settlement from them but he could not prove such plea by adducing creditable evidence and, as such, defendant No. 34 could not acquired title to 0.59 acre land by sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-10-1952 from Bashanto Kumar. 
3. The rent receipts which have been produced by defendant No. 34 and marked as Exhibits-Ga, Ga-1 and Ga-3 are forged documents and since those are private documents and exhibited without formal proof, those cannot be considered as evidence in favour of defendant No. 34. 
4. Since 0.54 acre land of CS and SA Plot No. 1912 corresponding to RS Plot No. 4003 has not partitioned by metes and bounds, publication of said land in separate SA and RS Khatians in the name of plaintiff and defendant No. 34 did not cease their co-sharership and, as such, the par ties have community of interest in the suit property and the suit is maintainable. 
5. Though sale deed dated 3-9-1969 was ostensibly in the name of the sons of defendant No. 34 but in fact purchaser was defendant No. 34 who purchased the same in the bename of his sons and accordingly, possession of defendant No. 34 is to be considered as possession of the pre-emptiees-purchasers and, as such, defendant No. 34 became co-sharer in common as the predecessor of his sons. 
6. It is settled principle of law that remedy of a co-sharer out of possession of the joint property, is available in a suit for partition and accordingly, the plaintiff has rightly filed the suit. 
7. By dint of judgment and order passed in Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 the plaintiff got right and title of the pre-emptees in his favour and as per observation of the Court the plaintiff has filed this suit for his remedy which tantamount to be an execution case for getting possession of the pre-empted land. 
8. Defendant No. 34 by adducing evidence could not establish the ingredients for proving his adverse possession in 0.59 acre land and, as such, he could not acquire title to said 0.59 acre land by adverse possession. 
9. The Court of appeal, upon proper consideration of evidence and materials on record, rightly affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court and, as such, interference is not called for by this Court. 

10. In support of their respective contentions learned Advocates have referred to some decisions of this Court and the Hon'ble Appellate Division which will be considered later. 

11. I have heard the learned Advocates, perused the judgments of the Courts below, the pleadings of the parties, the documents adduced by them and other materials available on record. 

12. Apart from adducing three oral witnesses the plaintiff produced CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1), the application of Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 (Exhibit-2), the judgment and order passed in the pre-emption case (Exhibit-3), certified copy of RS Khatian Nos. 117, 133 and 134 (Exhibits-4 series) and SA Khatian Nos. 156 and 157 (Exhibits-5 series). On the other hand, defendant No. 34 adduced three oral witnesses and also produced Jamindary rent receipt (Exhibit-Ka), the rent receipt showing payment of rent by Emran Sonar to Bashanto Kumar (Exhibit-Kha series), rent receipts showing payment of rent by Ismail Sonar (Exhibit-Ga series), one pattani receipt (Exhibit-Gha), twelve rent receipts showing payment of rent to the Government (Exhibit-Uma series), the original sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit-Cha), certified copy of SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Chha), certified copy of RS Khatian No. 117 (Exhibit-Ja), order passed in a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and application filed therein (Exhibits-Jha and Neo). 

13. Admittedly, 0.89 acre land appertaining to 0.07 acre of CS Plot No. 1873, 0.28 acre of CS Plot No. 1911 and 0.54 acre of CS Plot No. 1912 belonged to the father of the plaintiff in eight anna share and three others in eight anna share as CS Khatian was duly published in their name which has been proved by certified copy of CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1). The plaintiff claimed eight anna four gonda share after deducting 0.07 acre land out of total 0.89 acre land of CS Khatian No. 220. His case is that his father Emran Sonar had eight anna share in the suit land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1) and he also inherited four gonda share from his wife Sobjan Bewa and after his death the plaintiff inherited eight anna and four gonda share from the suit jote. The plaintiff also claimed title to 0.26 acre land on the basis of judgment dated 27-6-1979 passed in Pre-emption Case No. 19 of 1970 and to prove the judgment, he produced its certified copy (Exhibit-3). On the contrary, defendant No. 34 contended that the CS recorded tenants voluntarily surrendered their raiyoti right to the superior landlords and after surrender, Bashanto Kumar took settlement and paid rent to the landlords and thereafter, Ismail Sonar (the plaintiff) took settlement of 0.23 acre land from Bashanto Kumar and constructed dwelling house therein and thereafter, SA Khatian No. 157 [Exhibit-5 (Ka)] and its corresponding RS Khatian No. 134 [Exhibit-4(Kha)] were prepared and finally published in his name. His further contention is that Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land along with other land to him by registered sale deed No. 7799 dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit-Cha) and thereafter, separate SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Cha) and its corresponding RS Khatian No. 117 [Exhibit-Ja (4)] have been prepared and finally published in his name and he has been owning and possessing the same uninterruptedly, on payment of rent for more than 12 years. 

14. PW1 Abdus Salam is the son of the plaintiff, Ismail Sonar, deposed in support of the plaint. In cross-examination he stated,— 
“আমার পিতা কি করেছে না করেছে তা আমি কিছুই বলতে পারব না। ...মামলার জমি আর.এস জরীপ কয়টা দাগ হয়েছে তা আমি বলতে পারব না। আর.এস জরীপে কোন দাগে কতটুকু জমি তা আমি বলতে পারব না। কোন শরীক কোন দাগের কতটুকু জমি দখল করে তা আমি বলতে পারব না। কয় কাঠা জমি দখল করি তাও আমি বলতে পারি না। ..ইউনুস সোনার কতটুকু জমি দখল করে আছে তা আমি বলতে পারি না। কতটুকু জমি ফিরে পাবার জন্য মামলা করেছি তা আমি বলতে পারি না। .... ইউনুস জমি খাচ্ছে সেই খাজনা দেয়। মামলার জমির খাজনাপত্র আমি কোন দিন দেই নাই। .... জমি কার ছিল কি হয়েছে কি ঘটেছে তা আমি বলতে পারি না।"

15. PW2 Abdus Sattar, deposed in support of the case of the plaintiff, stated in his cross-examination that the plaintiff possesses 14/15 decimal land. Upon Evaluation of the evidence of the PWs, the trial Court held that the PWs could not prove the case of the plaintiff rather, they deposed adversely to the plaintiff and admitted that defendant No. 34 had possession in the suit land and that the plaintiff could not adduce any evidence to show that defendant No. 34 was a permissive possessor under the plaintiff or his predecessor. The trial Court finally came to conclusion that the plaintiff could not prove his claim. However, the trial Court found title to and possession in 0.23 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 in favour of the plaintiff as per admission of the defendant No. 34. The Court of appeal, it appears that, did not discuss oral or documentary evidence of the parties independently but concurred with the findings of the trial Court. The plaintiff did not challenge the adverse findings of the Courts below by preferring any appeal before higher forum. Accordingly, it is to be presumed that he accepted the findings and decision of the courts below that he acquired title to 0.23 acre land as per admission of defendant No. 34 and that the CS recorded tenants including the father of the plaintiff surrendered tenancy right to the superior landlords from whom Bashanto Kumar took settlement afresh and then settled 0.23 acre land to the plaintiff and on the basis of such settlement SA Khatian No. 157 and its corresponding RS Khatian No. 134 were rightly prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff in respect of 0.23 acre land and that the plaintiff could not prove permissive possession of defendant No. 34. 

16. Now question arises whether the plaintiff is entitled to saham of 0.26 acre land on the basis of judgment dated 27-6-1979 passed in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1970. In this regards, the court of appeal concurrently held that though vendors of sale deed dated 3-6-1969 had no possession of 0.26 acre land at the transfer and defendant No. 34 was in possession therein but as per judgment of pre-emption case right and title of 0.26 acre land has been vested to the pre-emptor (the plaintiff of present suit) and, as such, he is entitled to saham of 0.26 acre land. 

17. Now question arises as to whether the plaintiff is entitled to 0.26 acre land in view of the judgment passed in pre-emption case. The plaintiff produced certified copy of judgment of the pre-emption case, marked as Exhibit-3, from which it reveals that the plaintiff of present suit as petitioner filed the pre-emption case to enforce the right of pre-emption of 0.26 acre land purported to be sold by opposite party Nos. 7-16 of that case (who were the heirs of CS recorded tenants) vide sale deed dated 3-9-1969 in favour of the sons of defendant No. 34. On the other hand, opposite party Nos. 1-6 and 31 (present defendant No. 34) and 38, 39 contested the pre-emption case by filing three separate written objections. In that pre-emption case opposite party Nos. 1-6 and 31 contended that they never purchased 0.26 acre land from opposite party Nos. 7-16 and the disputed deed dated 3-9-1969 was collusive and without any consideration. Defendant No. 34 of this suit contended in that pre-emption case that he purchased 0.59 acre land including 0.26 acre land along with other lands in 1952 and he was owning and possessing the same and the petitioner of the pre-emption case was not a co-sharer of the disputed holding and opposite party Nos. 7-16 had no saleable interest in 0.26 acre land. Both parties adduced evidence in that case and upon considering the evidence, the trial Court held that there was a sale in respect of said 0.26 acre land and the pre-emptor (the plaintiff) was a co-sharer to the disputed land and finally observed and gave verdict as follows: 
"Out of the vendors some Md. Matiar Rahman and Serajuddin Sarker appearing as PWs 2 & 3 respectively have admitted that they (OP Nos. 7 to 16) sold the disputed land to OPs 1 to 6 but at the time of disputed sale they had no possession in the disputed land. Further they have admitted that the disputed land is being possessed by OP 31. Younus Sonar. In view of the above evidences of PWs. 2 & 3 it appears that the OP-Vendors (OPs 7 to 16) had no possession in the DL when they sold it to OPs 1 to 6 and, as such, it is obvious that the OPs 1 to 6 simply obtain the disputed deed without getting possession of the DL. So I am inclined to hold that the Petr. is not to get possession of the pre-empted land without a regular suit for possession. 
In view of the above it follows that the Petr. is entitled to get relief as prayed. 
Hence 
Ordered 
That the Miscellaneous Case be allowed on contest without cost against the contesting OPs and exparte also without cost against the rest. 
The right, title and interest of the OP-purchasers what they got from their vendors, OPs 7 to 16 in respect of the disputed land do vest in the Ptr. The Ptr. may get possession of the disputed land only after a decision in a regular civil suit for possession." 

18. Neither of the parties challenged said judgment and order passed in the pre-emption case. The above observation made it clear that when 0.26 acre land was purported to be sold by the heirs of CS recorded tenants, they had no possession therein and the so called purchasers could not get possession of the said land and that opposite party No. 31 (defendant No. 34 of this suit) was in possession of said 0.26 acre land. It is settled principle of law that mere registration of sale deed without delivery of possession by the vendee does not operate to pass title to the vendee or to pass any interest in the land purported to have been sold to him. Since during execution and registration of so called deed of sale dated 3-9-1969 the vendors had no possession of 0.26 acre land, the pre-emptee purchasers could not acquire title or right to said 0.26 acre land and the said deed of sale was a paper transaction only and accordingly, the pre-emptor could not step into the shoes of the purchasers of the deed on the strength of judgment passed in the pre-emption case (Exhibit-3). As per said judgment, defendant No. 34 was a third party stranger to the suit jote and was in possession of 0.26 acre land prior to execution and registration of sale deed dated 3-9-1969. 

19. In this case, it appears that the trial Court after evaluating rent receipts (Exhibits-Kha series and Uma series) and original sale deed dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit Cha) as well as SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Chha) and RS Khatian No. 117 (Exhibit-Ja) observed that after purchase in 1952 defendant No. 34 has been paying rents of the suit land to the jaminders and thereafter, to the Government. But without giving any finding in regards acquisition of title to 0.59 acre land by defendant No. 34, the trial Court erroneously held that the plaintiff would get saham of 0.26 acre land from CS Plot No. 1911 as per judgment of Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1970. The Court of appeal committed the same error and illegally allotted 0.26 acre land. 

20. Now question arises whether defendant No. 34 could prove his title to and possession in 0.59 acre land including 0.26 acre land. 

21. As mentioned earlier, the trial Court after evaluating rent receipts (Exhibits-Kha series and Uma series) and original sale deed dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit Cha) as well as SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit-Chha) and RS Khatian No. 117 (Exhibit-Ja) produced by defendant No. 34 observed that after purchase in 1952 defendant No. 34 has been paying rents of the suit land to the jaminders and thereafter, to the Government which has been upheld by the Court of appeal. Defendant No. 34 produced original sale deed dated 9-10-1952 (Exhibit-Cha) from which it appears that Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land and rent receiving interest of 0.23 acre land to defendant No. 34. This sale deed dated 9-10-1952 is more or less admitted by the plaintiff in the way that Bashanto Kumar had no saleable interest to transfer said 0.59 acre land to defendant No. 34 because he was a permissive possessor under the plaintiff. But both the Courts below as well as the Court who passed judgment in the pre-emption case found that the plaintiff or the petitioner in the pre-emption case could not prove the fact of permissive possession. Moreover, sale deed dated 9-10-1952 was attained 30 years of age at the date when it was tendered to evidence on 23-9-1997, original "of which was produced from proper custody and, as such, as per section 90 of the Evidence Act it is to be presumed as genuine document and that the signature and every other part of the document is genuine. As per section 92 of the Evidence Act oral or extraneous evidence to contradict the terms of contents of a document is inadmissible. However, the plaintiff did not adduce any oral or documentary evidence to prove that Exhibit-Cha was a product of forgery. As per recital of sale deed dated 9-10-1952, Bashanto Kumar was a tenant of 0.28 acre land of CS Plot No. 1911 and 0.54 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 under Putia Jaminder of Rajshahi. The plaintiff was under-tenant from Bashanto Kumar in respect of 0.23 acre land out of 0.54 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 and Bashanto Kumar transferred entire land of his khas possession and rent receiving interest of 0.23 acre land to defendant No. 34 and handed over possession of 0.28 acre land of CS Plot No. 1911 and 0.31 acre land of CS Plot No. 1912 in favour of defendant No. 34. Since sale deed dated 9-10-1952 is an old document of avove 30 years, as per section 90 read with section 91 of the Evidence Act, the recital of the deed dated 9-10-1952 are presumed to be correct. Moreover, during SA operation said 0.59 acre land was recorded in the name of defendant No. 34 in SA Khatian No. 155 (Exhibit Cha) and 0.23 acre land was recorded in the name of the plaintiff in separate SA Khatian No. 157 (Exhibit-5 Ka) and thereafter, their corresponding RS Khatian No. 117 ( Exhibit-Ja) in respect of 0.59 acre land was prepared and finally published in the name of defendant No. 34 and RS Khatian No. 134 [Exhibit-4 (Kha)] in respect of 0.23 acre land was prepared and finally published in the name of the plaintiff. Moreover, the courts below found that defendant No. 34 paid rent to the Jaminder and Government. The above facts lead to irresistible presumption that the sale deed dated 9-10-1952 has been acted upon. The plaintiff could not produce any evidence to discard the such presumption. 

22. Considering the evidences of the parties, it is evident that though total 0.89 acre land was recorded in CS Khatian No. 220 (Exhibit-1) in the name of Emran Sonar, the father of the plaintiff and others, as tenant under superior landlords but subsequently, Bashanto Kumar became tenant of 0.89 acre land under the superior landlords out of which he settled 0.23 acre land to the plaintiff and thus the plaintiff became under-tenant under Basanto Kumar and then Bashanto Kumar transferred 0.59 acre land under his khas possession along with rent receiving interest of 0.23 acre land to defendant No. 34 following which separate SA and RS khatians were prepared and finally published in their respective names and defendant No. 34 acquired title to 0.59 acre land and the plaintiff acquired title to 0.23 acre land. 

23. Apart from that, even if it is taken that the deed of 1952 was invalid but since the possession of defendant No. 34 in respect of 0.59 acre land has been proved since 9-10-1952, the date of execution and registration of the sale deed No. 7799, for more than twelve years before institution of the present suit, he acquired title to said land by way of adverse possession and, as such, the present suit which was filed in 1982 was barred by limitation. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties contended that defendant No. 34 did not specifically pleaded adverse possession in his written statement and, as such, he cannot get title by adverse possession. This submission of the learned Advocate has no leg to stand in view of the decision of our Apex Court reported in 17 BLC (AD) 300 wherein it has held that 'since the possession of the defendant No.1 has been proved for more than 12 years, he is entitled to get title even on the basis of invalid title though the defendant No. 1 did not specifically claim title by adverse possession'. 

24. The suit property is an agricultural land and that the defendant No. 34 is a stranger purchaser to the suit holdings and the tenancy of CS Khatian in respect of the suit holdings has been separated by preparation and publication of three sets of separate SA and RS Khatians in the name of the plaintiff and defendant No. 34. Accordingly, the plaintiff and defendant No. 34 are not co-sharers of the suit holdings. Moreover, in one part of the plaint, the plaintiff asserted that he has no community of interest with defendant No. 34 and in other part, he stated that cause of action of the suit arose in the event of pronouncement of judgment in the pre-emption case. Accordingly, the plea of the plaintiff is self contradictory leading to no cause of action for filing this suit. In view of the above, question of community of interest between the parties does not arise at all and the present suit for recovery of khas possession in the guise of suit for partition is not maintainable. 

25. Though the plaintiff contended that the possession of Bashanto Kumar and thereafter, defendant No. 34 was permissive but the plaintiff did not or could not adduce any evidence to prove that Bashonto Kumar and thereafter, defendant No. 34 was permissive possessor under the plaintiff. Even the plaintiff did not state anything from when defendant No. 34 got permission from the plaintiff to possess the suit land. On the other hand, possession by dint of a registered sale deed within the knowledge of the plaintiff has been proved and such possession can never be construed as permissive but it should be construed as adverse to the plaintiff. Accordingly, the courts below rightly held that the plaintiff could not prove the plea of permissive possession. 

26. I have already found that defendant No. 34 is a stranger purchaser to the suit holding and he is in possession since his purchase on 9-10-1952. To get a decree of recovery of khas possession by a suit for partition or recovery of khas possession, the plaintiff is required to plead that he was in possession before dispossession, the date of dispossession and that he filed the suit within twelve years from the date of alleged dispossession. In the plaint of this suit, the plaintiff stated nothing from when his predecessor/he was in possession of the suit property purchased by defendant No. 34 and when he has been dispossessed from the suit property and that he filed the suit within twelve years from the date of his dispossession. Since the plaintiff could not make out such case and failed to lead evidence in that regards he is not entitled to any relief of recovery of khas possession in respect of 0.26 acre land by way of partition. Moreover, since the plaintiff was out of possession, he was required to institute suit for declaration of title to and recovery of khas possession of the suit land on payment of ad valorem court fees but the plaintiff did not do so. Accordingly, he is not entitled to any relief as prayed for. 

27. However, since the plaintiff filed the present suit on the basis of observation made in the judgment of pre-emption case and indirectly seeking relief of recovery of khas possession of 0.26 acre land from defendant No. 34 in the guise of partition of the suit property, he was required to make specific statement and prove that his predecessor was in possession of the suit land and that the suit was brought within 12 years from the date of alleged dispossession. But the plaintiff did not make out such case and led evidence in this regards. 

28. It appears that the trial Court as well as the Court of appeal without resolving the above issues, erroneously held that the plaintiff is entitled to saham of 0.26 acre land as per judgment of pre-emption case and that the suit is maintainable and not barred by limitation. Moreover, the Court of appeal without evaluating and sifting the evidence on record came to its findings and upheld the findings and decision of the trial Court. 

29. Now question arises whether the High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the concurrent findings of facts of the Court of appeal. It is settled principle of law that the High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment of the courts below when the same has been made either upon mis-reading or non-consideration of the material evidence caused failure of justice; or when the same has been passed on the basis of evidence which cannot be considered legal evidence and had the same been not taken into consideration the judgment would not have been one as has been made; or when the appellate Court in giving a particular finding has committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice or such finding is found to have resulted from glaring misconception of law; or when the findings arrived at by the appellate Court is contrary to the evidence; or when there appears error of law apparent on the face of the record occasioning failure of justice. It is also of the view of the Apex Court that once the conditions in section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure are satisfied and the High Court's jurisdiction to interfere is established, the proceedings as a whole from start to finish can be scrutinized and any order necessary for doing justice may be passed. There is no limit to the area in which the revisional power is to be exercised by the High Court Division in the facts and circumstances of each case. When a finding of fact is based on consideration of the materials on record, those findings are immune from interference by the revisional Court and the High Court Division has no jurisdiction to sit on appeal over a finding of fact. [Ref. Md. Shajahan Khan vs Additional Deputy Commissioner II BLT (AD) 60; Md. Habibulla vs Sher Ali Khan 15 BLT (AD) 319; Md. Habibur Rahman Bhuiyan and others vs Mosanuhat Galman Begum and others, 2013 BLD (AD) 93; Government vs Golam Hossain Kazi and others 22 BLT (AD) 486; Kanchan Mallik and others vs Saleha Begum and others 22 BLC (AD) 254; Dr. Choudhury Mosaddagul Isdani vs Abdullah al Mansur Choudhury and others 70 DLR (AD) 168]. 

30. It appears that the impugned judgment of the court of appeal suffers from mis-reading and non-consideration of the material evidence and glaring misconception of law which caused miscarriage of justice and, as such, interference is called for by this Court. Since the plaintiff failed to prove his case, the Court of appeal should have dismissed the suit. 

31. In view of the above, I find no substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties. 

32. Accordingly, I find merit in this Rule. 

33. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgments of the Courts below are set-aside. The suit is dismissed with costs. 

34. The order of stay granted earlier is hereby vacated. 

Send down the LCR along with a copy of this judgment to the Courts below at once. 

End.

parties:

Vs.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozibur Rahman Miah, J. At the instance of the plaintiffs in Title Suit No. 876 of 2013, this appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 23.08.2016 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in the said suit dismissing the same holding that, the plaintiffs have failed to prove their title and possession in the suit property.

2. In a nutshell, the case of the plaintiffs-appellants is that the predecessor of the plaintiffs namely, Entaz Ali, Abdul Jobbar, Robi Ullah, Abdul Hamid and Jabed Ali got the suit property measuring an area of 3.06 acres of land by way of pattan appertaining to C.S Plot No. 3306 and that of 1.13 acres of land of C.S. Plot No. 3305 and accordingly, a khatian namely, B/1060 was prepared in their name. During the course of preparation of S.A. record, it was also prepared in the name of Entaz Ali and another and accordingly, each of the S.A. recorded tenant got 0.8380 acres of land. While they had been in possession one, Robi Ullah died leaving behind 5 sons and 5 daughters. After getting the property as of descendents of Robi Ullah, they then started enjoying their title and possession over their inherited land through amicable partition. Subsequently, 5 (five) daughters of Robi Ullah transferred their portion of land by way of oral gift in favour of their 5 full-brothers and accordingly R.S. record was prepared in the name of those 5 full-brothers in R.S. Plot No. 10107. Subsequently, while Md. Nurul Islam, Md. Dulal Miah had been enjoying title and possession over the property died leaving behind plaintiff nos. 1-5. But when the City Survey (সিটি জরিপ) came into operation, as the predecessor of the plaintiff no. 1, Md. Dulal Miah died, he could not remain present at the time of City Survey and accordingly, City Survey in respect of the suit land was wrongly prepared in the name of the defendant no. 1. The plaintiff no. 2 on 01.07.2013 went to the respective land office to pay the land development tax (খাজনা) and showed R.S. record when the respective official at the office disclosed that, the land development tax could not be taken on the basis of S.A. and R.S. record as the latest City Survey had not been prepared in the name of the plaintiffs. Then upon due search, the said plaintiff came to learn that the City Survey has been prepared in the name of the defendant no. 1 and upon obtaining respective porcha (পর্চা) of the disputed record he then apprised of the wrong recording and hence filed the suit for declaration of title in the suit property and that of declaration that the City Survey in respect of the suit land prepared in the name of the defendant no. 1 is illegal, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

3. On the contrary, the present respondent no. 1, namely, Land Reforms Board, Courts of Wards, Ministry of Land represented by its Manager as defendant no. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material averments so made in the plaint contending inter alia that, the land measuring an area of 4.19 acres of land of C.S. Khatian No. 646 comprising C.S. Plot Nos. 3306 and 3305 originally belonged to one, Kumar Robindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury and others whose favour the property was being enjoyed by the then Courts of Wards that is, Bhawal Raj Estate. After the demise of Kumar Robindar Narayan Roy Chowdhury, his three sons, Norendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury, Romendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury and Robindra Narayan Roy Chowdhury inherited the said property left by their father. Subsequently, the suit property was being possessed and supervised by the Courts of Wards and accordingly, C.S. record was prepared in its name and subsequently, its ownership was devolved upon the Board of Revenue. It has further been stated that, no authority has been bestowed to anybody else to transfer the suit property in favour of the predecessor of the plaintiffs and the said property has since been owned and possessed by the Board of Revenue for the Courts of Wards and when the City Survey came into operation, it was accordingly recorded in the name of the Courts of Wards vis-à-vis defendant no. 1 finding it in possession and the same was leased out to the lessees who has now been enjoying title and possession over the same. Lastly, it has been asserted that, the plaintiffs have got no title and possession over the same rather the defendant has been enjoying title and possession over the suit property and the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. Likewise, the defendant nos. 6 and 7 also filed a joint written statement denying all the material averments so made in the plaint contending inter alia that, the suit is not maintainable in its present form and the same is bad for defects of party as the plaintiffs have got no title and possession over the suit property and it is liable to be dismissed.

5. In order to dispose of the suit, the learned Judge of the trial court framed as many as 4(four) different issues and the plaintiffs in support of their case examined two witnesses and produced several documents which were marked as exhibit nos. 1-8. On the contrary, the defendant no. 1 examined one witness but no document was produced.

6. After taking into consideration of the materials and evidence on record, the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd court, Dhaka by his judgment and decree dated 23.08.2016 dismissed the suit.

7. It is at that stage, the plaintiffs came before this court and preferred this appeal.

8. Mr. Mohammad Kamrul Hasan, the learned counsel appearing for the appellants upon taking us through the memorandum of appeal and all the documents appeared in the paper book at the very outset submits that, the learned Judge of the trial court erred in law innot considering the facts that, the plaintiffs have been enjoying title and possession overt the suit property measuring an area of 16.76 acres of land on mutating their name in the record-of-right and by paying rent to the respective office and the DCR, S.A mutation khatian and all other relevant documents have been prepared in their name which is the proof of enjoying title and possession by the plaintiffs in the suit property but without considering such material aspect, the learned Judge has very whimsically dismissed the suit.

9. The learned counsel further contends that, since C.S., S.A. and R.S Khatian in respect of the suit land was prepared in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs and that of the plaintiffs but only for nonappearance at the time of holding City Survey, it was wrongly prepared in the name of the government but it does not ipso facto prove that the plaintiffs have got no title and possession over the suit property and therefore, the learned Judge has erred in law in dismissing the suit without considering the consecutive record of rights in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs.

10. The learned counsel by referring to the judgment also submits that, since the plaintiffs adduced two witnesses as well as produced several documents which were also marked exhibit nos. 1-8 but without considering those title documents, the learned Judge passed the impugned judgment and decree in a very perfunctory manner and therefore, the said judgment cannot be sustained.

11. The learned counsel by referring to the relevant documents annexed with the application for taking those as additional evidence also submits that, for the inadvertent mistake of the plaintiffs’ lawyer in the lower court, those vital documents could not be produced and had those documents produced, the judgment would have been otherwise, yet this Hon’ble court under section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure has got every authority to consider those documents as additional evidence and therefore, the judgment and decree of dismissal cannot be sustained in law.

12. When we pose a question to the learned counsel on the point of maintainability of the suit on the back of the provision provided in section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the learned counsel then contends that, since the suit has not only been filed for correction of the latest City Survey record rather for declaration of title in the suit property so the suit itself is well-maintainable and the learned Judge of the trial court while framing issue to that respect has found the issue of maintainability in favour of the plaintiffs having no scope to reopen the point of maintainability before this Hon’ble court as appellate court and finally prays for allowing the appeal by setting aside the impugned judgment and decree.

13. Conversely, Mr. Tassadder Raihan Khan, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent no. 1 opposes the contention taken by the learned counsel for the appellants and submits that, the learned Judge of the trial court has rightly passed the impugned judgment by dismissing the suit having no reason to interfere with the same by this Hon’ble court. The learned counsel then contends that, though the plaintiffs claimed the suit property to have obtained from the C.S. recorded tenant by way of pattan but since that very pattan has not been proved by any bilateral document and therefore, the learned Judge has rightly passed the impugned judgment dismissing the suit.

14. The learned counsel further contends that the chain of acquiring title by the defendant and that of the plaintiffs are totally different as it has been found by the learned Judge of the trial court below that the C.S. record has not been prepared in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs rather the record has been prepared in the name of the predecessor of the defendant and since the property belongs to the government finding the same to have recorded in the name of Courts of Wards so there has been no scope for the plaintiffs to claim the same as their own property and the learned Judge has rightly passed the impugned judgment.

15. When we pose a question to the learned counsel for the respondent no. 1 with regard to maintainability of the suit in view of the statutory provision as has been provided in section 145A of chapter XVIIA of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the learned counsel finds it difficult to say anything about it in spite of taking several adjournments to that effect though finally prays for dismissing the appeal.

16. Be that as it may, we have considered the submission so advanced by the learned counsel for the appellants and that of the respondent no. 1 at length. We have also gone through the impugned judgment and decree.

17. At the first instance, we would like to confine our discussion and observation keeping ourselves within the ambit of the provision of law guided in that respect especially the provision provided in section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and relevant provision which has been inserted in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act incorporating a separate chapter being no. XVIIA by Act No. 09 of 2004.

18. It would be expedient if we reproduce the provision provided in section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which runs as follows: 
“145A. (1) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, establish as many Land Survey Tribunals as may be required to dispose of the suits arising out of the final publication of the last revised record-of-rights prepared under section 144. 
(2) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, fix and alter the territorial limits of the jurisdiction of any Land Survey Tribunal. 
(3) The Government shall, in consultation with the Supreme Court, appoint the judge of the Land Survey Tribunal from among persons who are Joint District Judges. 
2[(3A) Until such judge is appointed under sub-section (3), the Government may empower a Joint District Judge in each district as the judge of the Land Survey Tribunal of the district. 
(3B) The Joint District Judge empowered under sub-section (3A) shall be deemed to be the judge of the Land Survey Tribunal appointed under sub-section (3). 
(3C) The Government may, if necessary, appoint one or more Senior Assistant judge or Assistant Judge as a judge of the Land Survey Tribunal to dispose of the suits transferred by the judge of the Land Survey Tribunal appointed or empowered under this section.] 
(4) No suit other than the suits arising out of the final publication of the last revised record of rights prepared under section 144 shall lie in the Land Survey Tribunal. 
(5) If any suit arising out of the final publication of the last revised record-of-rights prepared under section 144 is instituted in any civil court before the establishment of the Land Survey Tribunal under this section, such suit shall stand transferred to the Tribunal as soon as it is established. 
(6) Subject to the provision of sub-section (7), any person aggrieved by the final publication of the last revised record-of-rights prepared under section 144 may, within one year from the date of such publication or from the date of the establishment of the Land Survey Tribunal, whichever is later, file a suit in such Tribunal. 
(7) A suit may be admitted within next one year after the expiry of the period specified in sub-section (6), if the Land Survey Tribunal is satisfied with the reasons for delay shown by the plaintiff. 
3[(7A) The Land Survey Tribunal shall conclude the trail of a suit within 180 (one hundred and eighty) days from the date fixed for its final hearing.] 
(8) The Tribunal shall be competent to declare the impugned record-of-rights to be incorrect and further direct the concerned office to correct the record-of-rights in accordance with its decision, and may also pass such other order as may be necessary.”

19. On going through the provision of section 145A (4) of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act, we find that, challenging the propriety of the latest record be it City Survey prepared in City Corporation area and other than in the City Corporation termed as B.S record no suit shall lie in an ordinary civil court and for that obvious reason, the very word ‘shall’ has been inserted in that sub-section (4).

20. Furthermore, in section 145F of the Act, it also put a clear bar to entertain any suit in any civil court arising out of the final publication of the last revised record-of-rights prepared under section 144 of the Act in view of establishing Land Survey Tribunal under section 145A of the Act so for having such legal bar, no civil suit under the disguise of declaration of title ostensibly challenging the latest record can be entertained.

21. Further, section 145H of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act also postulates a non-obstante clause as well stating “Notwithstanding anything contained to the contrary, in this Act or any other law for the time being in force the provisions of the Chapter, shall prevail”. In all those provisions, the word ‘shall’ has been inserted making its compliance mandatory having no scope to override those provisions.

22. At this, the learned counsel for the appellant has very strenuously submits that, since the plaintiffs have not only challenged the propriety of the latest record rather they also prayed for declaration of title taking resort to the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, so the suit itself is well-maintainable. But that very submission does not stand since the plaintiffs sought remedy to correct the latest record namely, City Survey so until and unless, it is rectified through a proper legal forum no declaration of title in their favour can be passed where an ordinary civil court assumes no authority to declare title in favour of an aggrieved party even if, evidence is led favouring plaintiffs’ title to that effect. That said, in the four corner of plaint, we also don’t find any explanation as to what prevented the plaintiffs to seek remedy before the Land Survey Tribunal as per section 145A(6) and (7) of the Act. So no court of law other than Land Survey Tribunal can entertain a suit that actually challenges last revised record else, the very objective of legislating the provision incorporated in Chapter XVIIA in the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act will be redundant one.

23. At the fag-end of the submission, the learned counsel for the appellants contends that, if this Hon’ble court ultimately finds that the suit is not maintainable and the appeal dismissed in that event, the documents so submitted with the application praying for taking additional evidence dated 12.11.2017 may be allowed to take back, so that the appellants can produce in the proper forum. Since that very application for taking additional evidence has been kept on record vide order dated 14.02.2022, so we assume, a formal order is required to be passed to that end so that the appellants could take back the original copies annexed with the application by replacing the same with the photocopies duly attested by the learned counsel. Anyway, the submission has got substance and the learned counsel for the appellants is permitted to take back all the original documents annexed with the application filed on 12.11.2017 for taking additional evidence by replacing the same with photocopies duly attested by him.

24. Given the above legal aspect, we don’t find any substance to entertain the appeal. In any event, we are of the view that, under the provision of sections 145A, 145F and 145H of chapter XVIIA of the Act clearly put legal bar to file the suit by the plaintiffs challenging the latest record in ordinary civil court which is not maintainable.

25. In the result, the appeal is dismissed however without any order as to costs.

Let a copy of this judgment along with the lower court records be transmitted to the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka forthwith.

End.

full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque, J: In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh, a Rule Nisi under adjudication was issued on 01.03.2022 in the following terms: 
“Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to under what authority the respondent No. 13 is holding the post of Deputy Registrar of Bangladesh Nursing and Midwifery Council (BNMC) and as to why inaction of the respondent Nos. 1 to 9 and 14 in taking necessary actions against the respondent No. 13 and the Selection Committee consisting of respondent Nos. 10 to 12 for adopting unlawful and corrupt means by abusing their positions as public servants in the recruitment process of respondent No. 13 in the post of Deputy Registrar of Bangladesh Nursing and Midwifery Council (BNMC) should not be declared to be without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.”

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the Rule Nisi in short are that, Bangladesh Nursing and Midwifery Council (“BNMC”) is the statutory body which governs and administer the responsibilities that was conferred upon it vide বাংলাদেশ নার্সিং ও মিডওয়াইফারি কাউথিল আইন, ২০১৬ including nursing and midwifery education and practices. BNMC has the authority to affiliate such institutions who provide the academic courses and training programmes for nursing, midwifery and allied courses like community paramedics. Therefore, the involvement and role of BNMC is indispensable in enhancing nursing service by leading the profession towards constituting a significant force in the health care delivery system for achieving the goal‘Health for All’ congruent with national health goals of the Government.

3. Bangladesh Nursing Council issued an Advertisement Notice for appointment contained in memo No. বিএনসি/২০১৬/৫৬৭ dated 07.09.2016 under the signature of respondent No. 11 for appointment in the posts of ‘Deputy Registrar’, ‘Assistant Programmer’ and ‘Receptionist’ (Annexure-A to the Writ Petition). In order to complete the appointment procedure a 3 (three) member committee comprising respondent Nos. 10, 11 and 12 was formed. However, from the minutes of the Selection Committee dated 07.10.2016, it transpires that only 2 (two) members i.e. respondent Nos. 11 and 12 put their signatures in the said resolution but the Convener of the said committee, respondent No. 10, did not sign the resolution which indicates that the selection of the candidates, including the ‘Deputy Registrar’, was questionable from the beginning and was not done in accordance with law. Despite the said irregularity, respondent No. 11 vide memo No. বিএনসি/প্রশাঃ-৭০ (অংশ-২)/২০১৬/৬১৭ dated 09.10.2016 requested respondent No. 1 for approval of the result of the examination (Annexure-B-1 to the Writ Petition). Thereafter, respondent No. 1 vide memo No. বিএনসি/২০১৬/প্রশা-৭০ (অংশ-১)/৬২৯ dated 10.10.2016 appointed respondent No. 13, Mrs. Begum Rashida Akhter, in the post of ‘Deputy Registrar’ of BNMC (Annexure -B-2). Subsequently, the service of the respondent No. 13 in the post of Deputy Registrar was made permanent on 07.08.2017.

4. Thereafter, various other reports had been published in different national dailies and online news portal of the country regarding the illegal selection and appointment of respondent No. 13. For example, it has been reported in the daily newspaper namely the ‘Daily Inquilab’ and online news portals like, Banglanews24.com under the headline 'তথ্য গোপন করে রেজিষ্ট্রার হওয়ার চেষ্টা এবং কাউন্সিলের ডেপুটি রেজিষ্ট্রার হচ্ছেন আলোচিত সেই রাশিদা. The petitioners being conscious citizens of the country submitted 4 (four) applications dated 04.03.2020, 30.05.2020, 04.10.2020 and 03.01.2021 respectively, to the Hon’ble Minister, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Secretary, Medical Education and Family Welfare Division, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; the Registrar of BNMC and Chairman of Anti-Corruption Commission urging them to take necessary and appropriate actions against the illegal recruitment of respondent No. 13 in the post of Deputy Registrar (Annexure-C to C-3 to the Writ Petition). After receiving the complaints regarding illegal recruitment of respondent No. 13, the Anti-Corruption Commission, without taking any action referred the matter to respondent Nos. 1 and 9 vide memo dated 01.11.2021 and 05.12.2021 consecutively, in violation of section 17 and 28(Kha) of Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. Thereafter, respondent No. 1 formed a 1 (one) member enquiry committee consisting of respondent No. 8, namely Mohammad Daudul Islam, the then Deputy Secretary (Construction Wing), Medical Education and Family Welfare Division, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The enquiry was conducted in accordance with law with participation of both the parties, petitioners and respondent No. 13, and the report was submitted on 03.02.2022 (Annexure-F to the Writ Petition). The said enquiry report found the allegation brought regarding appointment of respondent No. 13 in the post of ‘Deputy Registrar’ of BNMC in violation of several Government Service Recruitment Rules and Regulations. The inquiry report also mentioned the fact of suppression of some material facts in order to secure the job and even the appointing authority deliberately and illegally avoided to obtain the police clearance about her antecedents.

5. After that, petitioners sent notice demanding justice to the respondent Nos. 1 to 9 and 13, to explain as to under what authority respondent No. 13 is holding the post of Deputy Registrar of BNMC. Nonetheless, getting no response from the respondents, petitioners filed the instant Writ Petition No. 2490 of 2022 on 17.02.2022 under article 102(2) of the Constitution and obtained Rule Nisi on 01.03.2022 in the manner as quoted hereinabove.

6. By filing supplementary affidavit dated 07.06.2023 the petitioners have stated that the recruitment notice dated 13.02.2013 and 21.04.2013, for the post of “Deputy-Registrar”, was published in the “Daily Ittefaq” (Annexure-N and N-1 to the Supplementary Affidavit). Similarly, BNMC for recruiting in the post of “Deputy Registrar” published the advertisement for the job in well circulated daily newspapers (e.g. Daily Ittefaq etc.) even after the recruitment notice dated 07.09.20216, vide which Respondent No. 13 was appointed. For example, recruitment notice dated 31.10.2019, for the post of “Deputy-Registrar”, was published in the “Daily Ittefaq” (Annexure-N-2 to the Supplementary Affidavit) and recruitment notice dated 13.01.2020, for the post of “Deputy-Registrar”, was published on the “Daily Ittefaq” (Annexure-N-3, Supplementary Affidavit). However, only in the instant case the advertisement, vide which Respondent No. 13 was appointed, was published on 07.09.20216 only in the website of BNMC, which converted the publication of the advertisement from public to private. It is also stated that the said advertisement notice dated 07.09.2016 was found in the website of the BNMC on 05.08.2020 long after the respondent No. 13 being appointment to the post of Deputy Registrar. It is also stated that the “সরকারি চাকরিতে নিয়োগের শিক্ষাগত যোগ্যতা নির্ধারণ (বিশেষ বিধান), বিধিমালা, ২০০৩” was not complied with in case of appointment of the respondent No. 13 in the post of Deputy Registrar (Annexure – O to the Supplementary Affidavit).

7. Respondent Nos. 1, 9 and 13 contested the Rule Nisi issued in the instant writ petition by filing affidavit-in-opposition.

8. Respondent No. 1 filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the writ petition contending inter-alia that the petitioners have no locus standi to file the writ petition. The allegation of appointing respondent No. 13 by adopting illegal and unfair means and violating the provision of the Service Rules is not correct and as such, the Rule Nisi is liable to be discharged.

9. Respondent No. 9 filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the writ petition contending inter-alia that the petitioner No. 1 is a businessman and petitioner No. 2 is an Assistant Professor in Holly Family Nursing College, Dhaka, claiming themselves as conscious citizens of the country filed the instant writ petition in the form of public interest litigation challenging the authority of appointment of respondent No. 13 long after 06 (six) years of the said appointment for achieving the dubious goal. As per the decision of 49 DLR (AD) 1, the petitioners have no locus standi to file the writ petition and as such, the Rule Nisi is liable to be discharged. Although, the petitioners made representations in the year 2021-2022 to the Ministry and Anti-Corruption Commission for taking appropriate action against respondent No. 13 for non-disclosure of fact of pending criminal cases during her appointment, they did not come before this Court to establish any public right but only to serve their selfish end which is not allowed in case of writ of quo warranto. It is also stated that the writ petition is admixture of quo warranto and certiorari and as such, it is not maintainable in its present form.

10. Respondent No. 13 filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the writ petition contending inter-alia that after getting appointment in the post of Deputy Registrar, the respondent No. 13 has been serving for more than five years but none of the contesting candidates has come to challenge the appointment of respondent No. 13. The petitioner No. 1 being a businessman and petitioner No. 2 being a lecturer of a Nursing College claim themselves as public interest litigants but they did not mention any reference of their earlier activities regarding filing any such case as PIL to prove their bona fide. Therefore, the claim of the petitioner is totally baseless one and they are not in any manner aggrieved persons within the meaning of article 102 of the Constitution, rather they are busy persons and purposely filed the instant writ petition to harass respondent No. 13. It is also stated that the appointment of the respondent No. 13 in the post of Deputy Registrar, the fundamental rights of the petitioners have not been affected in any manner. Since the petitioners neither represent a section of public nor claimed that any section of public has been aggrieved by the appointment of respondent No. 13 before five years back, as such they cannot be called as aggrieved person under article 102 of the Constitution. It is stated that since by operation of the judgment and order passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 48 of 2000 the Bangladesh Nursing Council Ordinance 1983 lost its force and repealed, the Government has decided to formulate a new law for the public interest to manage and maintain the Bangladesh Nursing and Midwifery Council and as such, it promulgated Bangladesh Nursing and Midwifery Council Act, 2016 and, before promulgation of such Act and in the absence of any recruitment Rules, to meet the legal necessity of the Council and to carry out its business, the respondent No. 13 has been appointed as Deputy Registrar in accordance with practice and procedure of the council being a statutory body. Regarding educational qualification it is stated that she passed S.S.C Examination in 1989 with Second Division from Joydebpur Government Girls High School, H.S.C Examination in 1991 with Second Division from a Government College, Dhaka, Diploma in General Nursing in 1992 from Holy Family Red Crescent Nursing Institute, Diploma in Midwifery in 1993 from the said institute, B.Sc. (Public Health) Nursing in 2003 from College of Nursing Dhaka under University of Dhaka and Masters in Public Health regarding Hospital Administration and Management in 2010 from the State University of Bangladesh and at present she is attending in Ph.D Program at American University and she also got license to perform as a Nurse from Bangladesh Nursing and Midwifery Council, Dhaka for the period from 11.11.2014 to 2025. Accordingly, it is stated that the respondent No. 13 has educational qualification for the post of Deputy Registrar. Regarding experience as stated in the recruitment notice it is stated that the respondent No. 13 started her carrier as a Medical Surgical Nursing in Holy Family Red Crescent Medical College Hospital from 1994 to 2005 and thereafter, she performed as a Guest Lecturer in United College of Nursing, Gulshan, Dhaka and she also performed as a Technical Supervisor of National Head Quarters Bangladesh and also performed as a Principal of Shahid Mansur Ali Institute, Uttara, Dhaka from 10.10.2010 to 15.11.2014. She also performed as an Assistant Professor in the International Nursing College, Gazipur from 16.11.2015 to 28.03.2016. She also performed as a Founder Chief Nursing Officer Co-ordinator of Asgor Ali Hospital, Gendaria, Dhaka from 01.04.2016 to 15.09.2016 with full satisfaction of the concerned authority. In such view of the matter, the respondent No. 13 has more than 15 years of experience to qualify to file an application for the post of Deputy Registrar of the Council.

11. It is also stated that the Government has approved the organogram creating different posts to carry out the business of Bangladesh Nursing Council treating the Council as Regulatory Body and such approval has been forwarded to the Registrar of the Council from the office of the respondent No. 1 by Memo dated 24.04.1994 (Annexure – 3 to the Affidavit-in-Opposition) including the post of Deputy Registrar, though there was no appointment Rules at the relevant time and as such, to carry out the business of the Council and to fill up the vacancy, a sub-committee headed by Additional Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (Discipline and Nursing) along with two other officers was formed who in a meeting held on 05.09.2016 decided that the appointment for the post of Deputy Registrar and other posts shall be made and accordingly, recruitment notice was published in the official website of the Bangladesh Nursing Council and also affixing on the official notice board on 07.09.2016. The respondent No. 13 having all requisite qualification applied to the authority concerned for the post of Deputy Registrar and she was issued admit card on 03.10.2016 and appeared in the written test on 07.10.2016 and stood first in the written test and viva voce, resultantly she was appointed in the post of Deputy Registrar exhausting all formalities and obtaining approval of the Executive Committee of the Council. Thereafter, the respondent No. 13 joined in the service on 16.10.2016 and her service was made permanent from 01.08.2017 vide office order dated 07.08.2027. It is also stated that the former Registrar Mrs. Suria Begum retired from the service on 19.01.2022 and the respondent No. 13 being Deputy Registrar filed application to the authority concerned for the post of Registrar by way of promotion and by order dated 18.01.2022 she was given additional charge of the Registrar until further order by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare Division. Accordingly, it is stated that since there is no illegality in the appointment of the respondent No. 13 the Rule Nisi is liable to be discharged.

12. Mr. Md. Imam Hossain along with Mr. Md. Selim Hasan, learned Advocates for the petitioners, submit that the instant writ petition is a writ of ‘quo warranto’ under Article 102(2)(b)(ii) of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality of holding the post of Deputy Registrar of BNMC by respondent No. 13 as well as writ of certiorari under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution of Bangladesh for abusing the position by the authority have been challenged. The challenge is made on various grounds, including the ground that the authority abused their position and the possessor of the office in question does not fulfill the requisite qualifications rather suffers from disqualification and holding the office without valid title, which debars the respondent No. 13 to hold such office. In this regard Mr. Hossain commenced his argument by referring a decision quoted in “Constitutional Law of Bangladesh” by Mahmudul Islam(3rdEdn, 2012, Paragraph 5.112) submitting that “The writ is used to ensure that no one can hold any public office without having a valid claim to that office (University of Mysore v. Govindrao, AIR 1965 SC 491).”

13. He submits that in the case of University of Mysore v. Govinda Rao, AIR 1965 SC 491 : [1964] 4 SCR 575 the Supreme Court of India observed that quo warranto proceeding affords judicial enquiry in which any person holding independent substantive public office or franchise or liberty is called upon to show by what authority or right he holds the said office or franchise or liberty and if the enquiry leads to finding that the holder of the office has no authority or title to it, issue of the writ of quo warranto for ousting him/her from that office is the right remedy. In other words, the procedure of quo warranto confers jurisdiction and authority on the Court to control executive action in the matter of making an appointment to public office against relevant statutory provision, as such the petitioners have rightly filed the writ of quo warranto as the instant writ petition has impugned the legal stance of holding the post of Deputy-Registrar of BNMC by respondent No. 13, with additional charge of Registrar at the time of filing instant writ petition, which gave her the sovereignty to exercise her power vested by বাংলাদেশ নার্সিং ও মিডওয়াইফারি কাউন্সিল আইন, ২০১৬. In support of his submissions he cited the reference from the book on “Constitutional Law of Bangladesh” authored by Mahmudul Islam (3rdEdn, 2012, Paragraph 5.113) in which the author opined that “If there was any complaint about the appointment of or promotion of an officer who was not eligible under the rules to be appointed or promoted, the proper remedy was to make an application for quo warrant (Ghulam Hussan v.
