case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 15-7-2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1653 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Abu Bakar Siddiquee, J: This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 15-7-2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1653 of 1997 making the Rule absolute. 

2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that the respondent, Md. Kandar Molla, the predecessor in interest of respondent Nos. 1(a)-1(i) and Md. Amir Molla, the predecessor in interest of respondent Nos. 2(a)-2(g) as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 89 of 1987 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Manda, Naogaon praying for declaration of title and confirmation of possession over the suit land contending, inter-aria that 0.80 acre land under CS Khatian No.109, Plot No.786 corresponding to hal dag No. 858, corresponding to SA Khatian No. 133 and RS Khatian No. 35 appertaining to Mouza Matgari belonged to Sobhan Sardar as Korfa Tenant under Rayati tenant Hossain Molla. On Chaitra 5, 1332 BS Sobhan Sardar being unable to pay rents surrendered the suit land in favour of Hossain Molla by executing an Istafa Patra. Hossain Molla took Possession of the suit land and transferred the same to Zamir Molla, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, by executing a registered kabala being No. 4665 dated 5-10-1918. Zamir Molla died leaving two sons Amir Molla and Kandar Molla and widow Afzan Bewa. SA khatian No. 133 was duly prepared in their names. During RS operation the field survey (parcha) was prepared in the names of Amir Molla and Kandar Mollah and while the defendants threatened to dispossess Amir Molla and Kandar Molla from the suit land they were constrained to file Other Class Suit No. 312 of 1974 which was renumbered as Other Class Suit No. 20 of 1984 praying for permanent injunction and during pendency of the said suit the defendants on 7-5-87 disclosed that RS Khatian No. 35 for the suit land was prepared in the names of the plaintiffs along with Pakalu Sardar, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 1 to 7, Baul Sardar, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 8 to 11 and Arsi Bewa, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 12 and 14 although none of them had right, title and possession in the suit land and as such, assuming that no fruitful result would come out from Other Class Suit No. 20 of 1984 due to wrong recording of RS Khatian No. 35, the plaintiffs on 19-5-1987 got the suit withdrawn with permission from the Court to sue afresh and being under apprehen-sion of dispossession from the suit land, the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 89 of 1987. 

3. Defendant Nos. 1 to 14 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter-alia, that the suit land belonged to Sobhan Sardar, the predecessor of the defendants, who was a Korfa tenant under Hossain Molla at Jama Rs. 3 in CS Khatian No. 109, Plot No. 786, area 0.80 acre. Sobhan Sardar died leaving two sons Pakalu and Baul one daughter Mani and SA Khatian was prepared in the names of Amir Molla and Kandar Molla wrongly and beyond the knowledge of the predecessor in interest of the defendant-appellants, however during RS Khatian No. 35 was prepared in the names of the contesting defendant-appellants along with the names of the plaintiffs for which the predecessor in interest of defendant-appellants filed Objection Case No. 12 of 1967 which was rejected by order dated 5-9-1967 against which Appeal No. 5331 of 1967 was filed by the predecessor in interest of the defendant-appellants and the same was allowed by the order dated 19-8-1968. Kandar Molla and the another filed other Class Suit No. 312 of 1974 in the Court of Munsif at Naogaon for permanent Action in respect of SA Khatian No. 133, Plot No. 786 area 0.80 acre and filed an application for temporary injunction was rejected on 18-12-1974. 

4. The further case of the defendant-appellants was that the plaintiffs of Other Class Suit No. 312 of 1974 again filed an application for temporary injunction and the same was allowed by order dated 26-7-1975 against which the defendants-appellants preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 111 of 1975 and the said appeal was allowed by the judgment and order dated 29-1-1976 in holding that though the plaintiffs filed Kabala of 1325 BS showing that Zamir Molla, the predecessor of the plaintiffs purchased the suit land from Hossain Molla, but they could not show how Hossain Molla acquired title in the suit land and the presumption of CS entry of the suit land was not rebutted and the established principle of law was that possession follows the title and as such, prima-facie case was that the defendants were in the possession of the suit land. 

5. The further case of the defendant-appellants was that plaintiffs of Other Class Suit No. 312 of 1974 did not mention the story of Istafa Patra dated 5-12-1323 BS executed by Sobhan Sardar in favour of Hossain Molla in respect of the suit land and the said suit was withdrawn with liberty to sue afresh by the order dated 19-5-1987 and the plaintiffs after creating forged Istafa Patra filed the present suit being Other Class Suit No. 89 of 1987 on 17-6-1957 and as such, Other Class Suit No. 89 of 1987 is liable to be dismissed on the ground of limitation and non-maintainability. 

6. The learned Assistant Judge on the basis of the plaint and written statement framed seven issues. The learned Assistant Judge, Manda, Naogaon, upon consideration of the evidence on record decreed the suit by its judgment and decree dated 31-7-1990. 

7. Against the said judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, the defendants as appellants preferred Title Appeal No. 239 of 1990 in the Court of District Judge, Naogaon which on transfer was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Naogaon who by his judgment and decree dated 20-3-1997 allowed the appeal reversing those passed by the trial Court and dismissed the suit. 

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge, the plaintiffs preferred Civil Revision No. 1653 of 1997 in the High Court Division, which after hearing the learned Advocate for the petitioners made the Rule absolute by the judgment and order dated 15-7-2010 thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 31-7-1990 in Title Appeal No. 239 of 1990 affirming those of the trial Court in Title Suit No. 89 of 1987. 

9. Against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division, the defendants filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 138 of 2011 wherein on 2-6-2014 leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners:—
"Mr. Omar Farooq, learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioner submitted that the appellate Court being the final court of facts, on proper appreciation of the evidence adduced by the parties, held that the suit was barred by limitation; that the 'estafapatra' (Exhibit-4) and the purchase deed of the plaintiffs dated 5-10-1918 (Exhibit-5) were not genuine; and that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their possession in the suit land so, without the prayer for recovery of possession, the suit was not maintainable. The High Court Division without reversing those findings of the last Court of facts exceeded its jurisdiction in setting aside the judgment and order of Appellate Court in a slipshod judgment which has caused a total failure of justice." 

10. Mr. Mansur Habib, Advocate, appearing for the appellants, submits that the High Court Division committed an error of law in reversing the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below without controverting the findings of facts in its proper perspective. He further submits that Istafa Patra Exhibit-4 by which Sobhan Sardar surrendered the suit land in favour of Hossain Molla dated 5-12-1323 BS was proved by PW2 Sadek Ali, who in examination-in-chief admitted that his eye-sight was so poor that he could not read out Exhibit-4 and the plaintiffs did not make any effort to examine any attesting witness or the scribe of Istafa Patra remained as not proved, the High Court Division committed error of law in reversing the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below relying on the Istafa Patra (Exhibit-4). He again submits that the High Court Division relying on the Istafa Parta which was inadmissible evidence, held by the Court of Appeal below that —"১৩২৩ সালের ৫ই চৈত্রের ইস্তফা পত্র খালি চোখে পর্যবেক্ষণ করে দেখা যায়, এটি একটি পুরাতন কাগজ ডেমিতে ভারতীয় রাজস্ব স্ট্যাম্পের উপরে লেখা হয়েছে। কিন্তু লেখাটি ফাউন্টেন পেনের নীব উল্টো করে লিখলে যেমন লেখা হয়, তেমনি চিকনভাবে লেখা হয়েছে। সত্যিকারে ১৩২৩ সালে লেখা হলে, তা ঐ আমলে আইডিয়াল বোতলের কালি ও হেন্ডেলের নীব দিয়ে লেখা হতো। ঐরূপ কলম দিয়ে লেখা হতোনা। তাছাড়া লেখার ধরণ ও লেখার কালি সম্প্রতিকালের ও মামলার উদ্দেশ্যে সৃজিত বলে প্রতীয়মান হয়।”was not controverted by the High Court Division, the judgment and order of the High Court Division suffers from gross illegality and is liable to be set-aside. He finally submits that the Court of Appeal below held that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land but the High Court Division without controverting the finding of facts of the Court of Appeal below reversed the judgment and thereby committed an error of law in making the Rule absolute and decreeing the suit. 

11. Mr. SN Goswami, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondents, made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and further submitted that the High Court Division has considered all material facts and has considered the evidence of PWs and DWs and rightly held that the trial Court on assessing the evidence available on record found that the Istafa Patra dated the 5th Chaitra, 1323 BS (Exhibit-4) was a genuine document. All the PWs corroborating each other proved the said Istafa Partra but the learned Judge of the appellate Court below without appreciating and misreading the evidence came to his decision that the Istafa Patra was not genuine which is against the evidence on record. Since the Istafa Patra was found to be genuine, transfer of the suit land by Hossain Molla, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, by the registered kabala (Exhibit-5) was also genuine and the High Court Division further he that the learned Judge of the appellate Court below while reversing those passed by the trial Court did not follow the procedures laid down in Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thus the impugned judgment and decree is not a proper judgment of reversal and made the Rule absolute He cited the case of Md. Nurul Islam and others vs Nipendra Pathak and others reported in 6 BLT (AD) 163, wherein their Lordships held that where there is a misreading of evidence or non-consideration of material evidence affecting the merit of the case, the High Court Division can review the evidence and correct the error in exercise of its revisional powers. He also cited the case of Md. Shajahan Khan vs ADC (Revenue) and others reported in 11 BLT (AD) 60 wherein their Lordships held that once the conditions in section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure are satisfied and the High Court's jurisdiction is established, the proceeding as a whole from start to finish can be scrutinized and any order necessary for doing justice may be passed and there is no limit to the area in which the revisional power is to be exercised by the High Court Division in the facts and the circumstances of each case. 

12. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants concerned, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

13. It is admitted by the parties that the suit land belonged to one Sobhan Mollah as Korfa tenant under rayati tenant Hossain Mollah. The present plaintiff-respondents have come with an allegation that Sobhan Sarder surrendered the suit land in favour of Hossain Mollah being unable to pay rent after executing an Istafa Patra. It has been further alleged that after taking over possession Hossain Mollah sold out the suit land in favour of one Zamir Molla who died leaving behind the plaintiffs as his heirs. It has been also alleged that the present plaintiff-respondents as heirs of Zamir Mollah has been possessing the suit land and SA Khatian was prepared duly in the name of the plaintiffs. On the other hand, the contesting defendants denied the contention of the plaintiffs and counter claimed that Sobhan Sarder never surrendered the suit land and never executed any Istafa Patra who as owner in possession died leaving behind the predecessor of the defendant-appellants and the defendants have been possessing the suit land. 

14. Let us proceed to examine the evidence on record and see therefrom as to how far the plaintiff-respondent has been able to prove the fact of execution of Istafa Patra and thereby surrendered the tenancy in favour of raiyat Hossain Mollah. 

15. Plaintiff No. 1 while deposing as PWlstated that Korfa tenant Sobhan Sarder being unable to pay the rent surrendered his Korfa right in favour of the raiyat Hossain Mollah after executing an Istafa Patra in the year 1313 BS and thereafter, Hossain Mollah took delivery of possession, sold out the same to his father Zamir Mollah in the year 1325 BS who died leaving them as sole heirs. One Sadek Ali has come forward to prove the written Istafa Patra who stated that the Istafa Patra was written by one Addyanath Dutta who is known to him and his hand writing is also known to him and the recital of this Istafa Patra was written by him. In cross-examination he deposed that Addyanath wrote out the same in his presence. He also deposed that one Arab Ali, Samir and Indu put their signatures on the Istafa Patra as attesting witnesses and all those witnesses and their signatures are known to him. On perusal of the testimony of PW2, it appears that nothing cogent could be elicited to disbelieve him. Moreover, the recipient of such to Istafa patra, Hossain Mollah after taking over possession, sold out the said land in favour of one Zamir Mollah by kabala dated 5-10-1918 PW6 Ekramul Haque appeared before the Court along with volume book of the aforementioned kabala dated 5-10-18 who deposed that he has come before the Court along with the volume book in respect of kabala dated 5-10-1918 and the page Nos.89 and 90 shows that Hossain Mollah executed the kabala in favour of Zamir Mollah and thereby sold out the suit land. This is a kabala the age of which is more than 100 years. This type of age-old document has come before the Court from proper custody which certainly carries a legal presumption of due execution and correctness under section 90 of the Evidence Act. But the lower appellate Court failed to notice this vital issue and committed flagrant violation of law resulting in miscarriage of justice. In this regard, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs, has cited a decision enunciated in the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) vs Md. Reazuddin 5 BLC (AD) 76 wherein it has been held that:—
"Once such a document more than 30 years old is produced from proper custody section 30 of the Evidence Act entitles the Court to presume that it is a genuine document." 

16. Not only that on the basis of kabala and Istafa Patra SA record in respect of this land has been prepared in the name of the plaintiffs who are the legal heirs of Zamir Molla. It is acceptable proposition that finally published record of right has presumption of correctness and that presumption continues till it is otherwise rebutted by reliable evidence. 

17. Those facts and circumstances and other material on record lead us to hold that the plaintiffs have successfully proved the fact that Korfa tenant Sobhan really surrendered his tenancy on executing the 'Istafa Patra'. 

18. As regards possession of the suit land, PW3, Islam Ali Sardar deposed that the suit land is contiguous to his homestead and the same is being possessed by the plaintiff and was never possessed by the defendant. PW4 Ayezuddin corroborated that he is also a contiguous land owner of the suit land and the plaintiffs are owner in possession of the suit land. PW5 Asher Mondal also supported that it is the plaintiffs who are in possession of the suit land and none else. We find no intrinsic weakness or blatant contradiction in the testimonies of PW3 and 4 and 5 and as such, they are able to earn the confidence of the Court. 

19. On the other hand, DW3, Nanda Mir is the lone witness of the defendants who deposed that he had a plot of land contiguous to the suit land and he sold out the same elsewhere and he cannot remember its plot number. He admits that he cannot say as to when Pakalu and Baul started to possess the suit land last. We find that the testimony of this lone witness of the defendant is impeachable and there is inherent infirmity in the same. 

20. On assessment of those testimonies of the PWs and DW, we have no option but to hold that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their possession over the suit land. 

21. On perusal of the impugned judgment passed by the learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division, it appears that he has considered the oral and documentary evidence of the parties and rightly held that the trial Court on assessment of the evidence on record found that the Istafa Patra (Exhibit-4) is a genuine document, and the PWs have successfully proved the Istafa Patra on the basis of which kabala dated 5-10-1918 has been executed by Hossain Mollah in favour of Zamir Mollah whose heirs are the plaintiffs and SA Khatian has been prepared in their names and RS Khatains also prepared in their names in preliminary stage. The learned Judge of the single Bench of the High Court Division further held that since the Istafa Patra was found to be genuine, transfer of the suit land by Hossain Mollah to Zamir Mollah, the predecessor of the plaintiffs by kabala dated 5-10-1918 is also genuine. The learned Judge of Single Bench of the High Court Division also held that the learned Judge of the appellate Court while reversing the judgment passed by the trial Court did not follow the procedure laid down in Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thus, the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below is not a proper judgment of reversal. Where there is misreading of evidence or non-consideration of material evidence affecting the merit of the case, the High Court Division can review the evidence and correct the error in exercise of its revisional power. 

22. We find that there is no illegality and infirmity in the impugned judgment. 

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Bazlur Rahman, J: In this writ, a Rule Nisi was issued at the instance of the petitioners calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 20-) 2020 passed by the learned District Judgo, Jamalpur, in Arpito Appeal No. 02 of 2018 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 14-11-2018 passed by the learned Joint District Judge and Arpito Sampotti Prottarport Tribunal, Jamalpur in Arpito Suit No. 75 of 2013 dismissing the Suit should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and/or passed such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Thereafter on 9-9-2020, an order of status quo was passed for an initial a period of three (03) months which was subsequently enlarged till disposal of this Rule. 

3. Admitted Facts: 
3.1. The suit property measuring 48 decimals of land appertaining to CS Khatin No. 1539 was originally recorded in the names of Shashi Mohan and his four (04) brothers in equal shares. The same land was recorded in SA Khatian Nos. 1828 and 1948 comprising of 34 decimals and 14 decimals respectively in the lone name of Dhirendra Mohan Dey, the son of Sree Sasi Mohan Dey. Thereafter, recent B.R.S Khatian No. 5023 was finally published incorporating the said suit land in the name of Abdul Aziz, the predecessor of writ petitioner Nos. 2-8 and Md. Zoynal Abedin, petitioner No. 01. Regarding the suit land, relevant government authority instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1974 for correction of BRS Khatian No. 5023 and Abdul Aziz and Zoynal Abedin instituted Other Classes Suit No. 136 of 1976 for declaration of title to the said land. Both suits were disposed of analogously by the then Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh vide judgment dated 31-5-1977 decreeing the Other Classes Suit in part declaring plaintiffs' title to 1 anna 12 gondas only of the suit land and the rest to be in the category of enemy property and thereupon, ordering to correct the BRS Khatian No. 5023 accordingly in the name of relevant government authority. The decree dated 31-5-1977 was challenged by the plaintiffs before the High Court Division in Appeal No. 74 of 1977 which due to establishment of Arpito Sampotti Prottarpon Tribunal under the Arpito Sampotti Prottarpon Ain, 2001 got abated in view of section 13 of the Ain. Be it noted, the entire quantum of suit land has been enlisted as vested property in Schedule-Ka vide gazette notification published on 9-4-2012. 
3.2. Subsequently, this petitioner instituted Arpito Sampotti Prottarpon Tribunal Case No. 75 of 2013 before the newly constituted tribunal seeking release of the suit land from the vested property category which on contest with the instant respondent Nos. 1-3 (being defendant No. 1-3), vested property government authority, was dismissed vide judgment and decree passed by the tribunal on 14-11-2018. Being disgruntled by the said judgment and decree, these petitioners preferred an appeal bearing Arpita Appeal No. 02 of 2018. The appellate tribunal hearing both the parties rejected the appeal on 20-1-2020. This appellate judgment of affirmance has been assailed in the instant writ at the instance of the petitioners who upon initial hearing of the writ application obtained the aforesaid Rule and then the ad interim order of status quo. 

4. Petitioners' Case: 
4.1. There was no reason to enlist the suit land as vested property as the petitioners have been althrough in peaceful possession thereof since 1975. The entire quantum of the suit land belonged to Dhirendra Mohan Dey by means of amicable partition amongst the co-sharers and, consequently, the Khatian No. 1948 and 1828 were published in his sole name. Dhirendra Mohan Dey transferred vide two registered sale deeds dated 1-10-1975 bearing No. 25175 and dated 5-11-1975 bearing No. 28129 incorporating 34 decimals and 14 decimals respectively in favour of the predecessors of these petitioners. Post-transfer necessary legal actions including mutation and payment of up to date land tax, holding tax etc. have been duly completed; even BRS Khatian No. 5023 also has been correctly prepared and published in the names of the recipients of the sale deeds. Those deeds and updated Khatian are still in force in petitioners' favour. They are the real owners or 'malik' of the land in question and the government authority never had possession in and control over the land by virtue of any title vested in it. Resorting to tricky device some colourable lease documents have been created and a sham lease has been shown to have been granted in favour of one Laxmi Rani, who, in fact, had been the tenant under Dhirendra Mohan Dey. The suit land during recent revisional survey was recorded in khas Khatian No. 01 which upon being challenged by the petitioners under Rule 30 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 was ordered to be released from khash Khatian and to open separate khatians also in their names. The tribunal or the appellate tribunal without appreciation of evidence adduced, whether documentary or testimonial, in its appropriate perspective, dismissed the Arpito Sampotti Prottarpon Case and the appeal upon misconception of law. Hence, both the judgments and the decrees passed by both the tribunal and appellate tribunal as mentioned hereinabove are nullity and are liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. 

5. Respondent's (No. 01) Case: 
5.1. CS recorded tenants Sree Shashi Mohon Dey and four (04) others used to reside on the land with their respective families. Sree Shashi Mohon Dey while possessing his respective share passed away leaving behind two sons, namely Shailendra Mohon Dey and Dhirendra Mohan Dey. Soon after the partition of India in 1947, Shailendra Mohon Dey migrated to India with all occupiers of his share. Only Dhirendra Mohon Dey remained in the erstwhile Pakistan. Hence, Shailendra Mohon's 8 Gondas share of the suit land was considered as "Evacuee Property" which gradually by operation of law stood vested in the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property. Dhirendra Mohon Dey used to own and possess only 8 Gondas of land. But the entire suit land of 48 decimals were erroneously recorded in the sole name of Dhirendra Mohon Dey. APWA (All Pakistan Women Association) of Jamalpur occupied 40 decimals of scheduled land setting up thereon an office, a girls school and a handicraft training center for women and the rest 8 decimals were leased out to Laxmi Rani Sen vide VP Case No. 71/69-70 dated 15-12-1976 which she continued to possess onward. The petitioners vide the said two sale deeds did not acquire the entire suit land, rather got 12 Gondas of land only belonging to Dhirendra Mohon Dey. The Arpito Sampotti Prattarpon Case No. 75 of 2013 and the Appeal preferred against bearing No. 02 of 2018 were rightly disposed of and dismissed on correct assessment of evidence with taking due consideration of all attending facts and circumstances as well. The judgment and decree assailed shall succeed in the long run. The Rule is, therefore, liable to be discharged. 

6. Submissions: 
6.1. First of all, petitioner's learned counsel Mr. Md. Bodruddoza, referring to an undisposed of local inspection application by the tribunal, submits that the same was brought to substantiate the existence of petitioners' having buildings on the suit land but neither of the tribunals below, trial or appellate, ever addressed the said application or the aspect of petitioners' possession over the suit land, rather both the tribunals disbelieved the factum of possession despite stronger basis thereof remaining present. The learned counsel further submits that the positive evidence of possession, both oral and documentary, .appearing in the testimonies of PW 1 and PW 2 was not appropriately analyzed in the judgments in its correct approach. The learned counsel emphasizes that the tribunal deliberately skipped DWI 's failure to substantiate government's case on evidence. He also underscores that unnecessarily emphasizing more on the CS Khatian while SA Khatian was finally published in 1962 in petitioners' predecessors favour was a futile and an uncalled for exercise. Since under the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance, 1965, government was only vested with the power of controlling the abandoned property, no title or ownership was created in favour of the government in respect of the vested and non-resident property. The learned counsel underscores that since the suit land has finally been published in BRS Khatian in the names of the petitioners, its inclusion in the vested property in 'Ka' scheduled list is a blatant illegality and a manifest indicia of executive high-handedness. Be it mentioned that the Government also lost in the proceedings under Rule 30 and 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 and the title deeds dated 1-10-1975 and 5-11-1975 cited by petitioners in the avbove proceedings were relied on upon by the survey authority. The learned counsel reiterates that petitioners' title document, being duly registered kabalas unless cancelled by competent Court and, a variety of legal documents of possession including finally published khatian and payment of land tax and holding tax etc. were adequate inter-woven evidence to pass an order of releasing the suit land from the impugned vested property list. But the tribunal and the appellate tribunal upon misconception of facts and of law concurrently arrived at a fallacious decisions which are liable to be set-aside. Learned counsel further submits that a construction plan has already been approved by proper authority at the instance of this petitioners upon a certain quantum of suit land. The learned counsel submits that Dhirendra Mohon Dey died in Bangladesh, and since then the petitioners have been in peaceful possession of the suit land by mutating their names and on payment of up to date rent to the government. It is stated that during enjoyment of peaceful possession of the predecessor of the petitioners, Abdul Aziz transferred certain quantum of land to petitioner No. 4 by way of registered sale deed bearing No 12363 of 1992 and thereafter, petitioner No. 04 by mutating his name has been paying rent to government regularly and enjoying its peaceful and uninterrupted possession therein. Learned counsel further submits that after the death of Abdul Aziz (predecessor of the petitioners), petitioner No. 08 inherited some quantum of land from the suit land as per his share and after having inherited the same he also has been enjoying peaceful possession and ownership by mutating his name and paying rent regularly. In view of the above facts and features of the circumstances, the learned counsel, however, urges the Rule to make absolute. 
6.2. Per contra, Mr. Md. Mohaddes-ul-Islam, learned Deputy Attorney-General on being assisted by Mr. Ashique Rubaiat, learned Assistant Attorney-General, frankly submits on behalf of respondent No. 01 that the SA Khatian in the lone name of Dhirendra Mohon Dey to the extent of whole of suit land and the subsequent BRS Khatian in the names of the petitioners have been wrongly prepared and published. The alleged deeds of sale dated 1-10-1975 and 5-11-1975 did not operate to create title to petitioners' predecessors or to the instant petitioners, as the case may be, to the extent of entire suit land; it only creates title in respect of Dhirendra Mohon Dey's proportionate share of 12 gondas only. Thus petitioners' claim to the entire 48 decimals of suit land does not bear any basis but a ficticin simpliciter. The Deputy Attorney-General further submits that in the case before tribunal the petitioner intentionally concealed the lineage of CS recorded tenants simply for apprehension of losing in the case. The learned counsel concludes that the tribunal upon detailed evidence and hearing disposed of and dismissed the Arpi to Sampotti Prottarpon Case No. 75 of 2013 which had been rightly affirmed in appeal. 

7. Deliberations and Decisions: 
7.1. We have extensively gone through the statements made and the grounds advanced in the writ application along with the contentions agitated in the affidavit-in-opposition. We have also scrutinized the documents annexed and considered the elaborated arguments of the learned counsels of both parties. 
7.2. It, however, appears that the tribunal while adjudicating the contentions raised in the Arpito Sampotti Tribunal Case held, Annexure-B-3, that the petitioners were not entitled to acquire title to the whole of suit land since their vendor, Dhirendra Mohon Dey, had no title to the whole amount of land as there were other co-sharers also as per CS Khatian. We find a specific case to have been demonstrated by the petitioners that Dhirendra Mohon Dey by way of amicable partition owned the suit land in the whole. Admitted publication of SA Khatian Nos. 1948 and 1828 in Dhirendra Mohon's single name including the suit land in its entirety excluding other co-sharers therein appeared to be prima facie evidence of his possession at the relevant time. None of the co-sharers ever challenged the correctness of the SA Khatians or the validity of the family partition as being never done by them. It is evident from the impugned Gazette dated 9-4-2012 that the suit property was enlisted as enemy property vide Case No. 71/6970. Till 1969-70, no other co-sharers came forward to resist the claim of Dhirendra Mohon and to refute sole possession of 48 decimals of CS recorded land in Dhirendra Mohon's name alone. But before the enemy list was done, the SA Khatian got finally published attributing thereto the presumption of possession in Dhirendra Mohon's favour. The incorporation of suit land in SA Khatians in Dhirendra Mohon's name reflects the initial basis of amicable family partition particularly when the Khatians continued to operate till further Khatian under new survey operation was published in ultimate conformity with the earlier Khatians. It appears from the lower court record that a number of co-sharers of Dhirendra Mohon Dey were impleaded as defendants in the Other Classes Suit No. 136 of 1976 which was analogously disposed of with Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1974. None of the co-sharers entered appearance to resist the family partition claim raised by Dhirendra Mohon Dey, rather impliedly allowed by their unopposed acts being ever raised in any legal action whatsoever. Unless a claim is controverted by persons directly affected or likely to be affected thereby, particularly when such claim is adjudicated with opportunities being provided to all concerned, such claim cannot be unilaterally deprecated on a mere hypothesis unattended by necessary surrounding circumstances. The exclusive and continued possession of one co-sharer over the land of other co-sharers for an unobjected and uninterrupted period of 12 years or more creates title by adverse possession in favour of the co-sharer possessing the land of such other co-sharers without material opposition. In the premises, the decision held either by learned erstwhile Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh in the said analogous judgment of Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 1974 and Other Classes Suit No. 136 of 1976 or the decision held by the trial tribunal (Annexure-B-3) in Arpito Sampatti Case No. 75 of 2013 or by the appellate tribunal, (Annexure-B-1), in Arpito Appeal No. 02 of 2018, whichever may be, that the basis of SA Khatians in the sole name of Dhirendra Mohon Dey to be absolutely wrong do not appear to us to be in any way logically acceptable. 
7.3. On the contrary, contesting respondent No. 01 states in the affidavit-in-opposition that only the respective share of Shailendra Mohon Dey to the extent of 12 gondas of suit land was considered as evacuee property after his migration to India with family members after the partition of India in 1947. The respondent althrough assailed to impair the credibility of the title of Dhirendra Mahon Dey as well as that of the petitioners claiming through Dhirendra Mohon relating to suit land but the respondent undertook no effort as to how, when and in what manner the government acquired title to the entire suit land or how that land of 48 decimals came under the control and management of the government. We are unable to detect any full-fledged legal proceedings at government's instance to claim the suit land, except the reference to the case bearing No. 71/69-70 appearing in the relevant column (No. 02) of the impugned Gazette notification dated 9-4-2012. The existence of registered title deeds dated 1-10-1975 and 5-11-1975 (Annexure-D and E), comprising of the suit land in petitioners'/their predecessor's name, the preparation and final publication of BRS Khatian No. 5023 in the names of the recipients of theses deeds (Annexure-G), acknowledge-ment of land tax, (Annexure-I-I series), and holding tax, (Annexure-M series), by the government, the striking out of the suit land from khas Khatian No. 01 and ordering the same to be recorded in separate Khatian in petitioners' name (Annexure-F), etc, are not liable to be knocked down by a simple and solitary assertion of fact that the suit land had been rightly included in the vested property list. 
7.4. The execution of the said sale deeds are not disputed, the only dispute is that those deeds did not operate to create title in favor of the recipients of the deeds in the lands more than the share the executant was entitled to transfer to the extent of 12 gondas of the suit land. It is a laid down principle that mere registration of a sale deed does not operate to pass title, the deed needs to be acted upon by delivery of possession. In the instant case, petitioners' complete possession is not alleged by the opponent. Rather, we have found a series of documents corroborating petitioners' possession in the suit land, not to speak of the testimonial evidence in this regard adduced before the tribunal, 
7.5. It has been remarked by the tribunal in its judgment, that the petitioners failed to prove exclusive possession over the suit land. Also held therein that the suit property was not identified and well demarcated by appending any boundary to the suit land. Where demarcation or boundary is indispensible to identify the property in question, only then such boundary requirement needs to be fulfilled. The SA suit plot Nos. 1483 and 1484 corresponding to BRS Plot Nos. 2375, 2376, 2377 and 2378 include the whole of suit land, no equivocation or unclarity appears to understand and indentify the property which were the subject matter of the case before the tribunal. The case before the tribunal was simply to release the suit property from the alleged vested property list and if released, its possession to be delivered accordingly. Whenever the whole quantum of land in a particular plot is the subject matter of relief, specification of its boundary is not necessarily fundamental and its absence in any way cannot forfeit the relief of the claimant. Moreover, boundary requirement has not been contemplated as pre-condition to file an application under section 10 of the Arpito Sampotti Prottarpon Ain, 2001 before the tribunal. 
7.6. It is apparent from the appellate judgment (Annexure-B-1) that the appellate tribunal on examination of the trial tribunal's judgment did not find any room to interfere with the judgment of the learned trial tribunal and, as such, the tribunal's judgment had been affirmed by the appellate tribunal. The powers of the appellate tribunal under section 20 of the Ain, 2001 may contextually be reproduced hereunder; 
"২০। (১) এই আইনের অধীনে দায়েরকৃত আপীলে উত্থাপিত তথ্যগত প্রশ্নে (question of fact) এবং আইনগত প্রশ্নে (question of law) আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল উহার সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদানসহ আপীলকৃত সিদ্ধান্ত সম্পূর্ণ বা আংশিকভাবে রহিত করিতে বা ক্ষেত্রমত অনুমোদন (confirm) করিতে বা উহা সংশোধন করিতে পারিবে:
তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, ধারা ১০ (৮) এ উল্লিখিত বিষয় এবং ট্রাইব্যুনালের রায় বা সিদ্ধান্তের বৈধতা ও যথার্থতা ব্যতীত অন্য কোন বিষয়ে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদান করিবে না।
(২) আপীল নিষ্পত্তির সুবিধার্থে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল এমন অতিরিক্ত সাক্ষ্য গ্রহণ করিতে পারিবে যাহা আপীলের বিষয়বস্তুর সহিত সরাসরি সম্পর্কযুক্ত এবং যাহা ট্রাইব্যুনাল কর্তৃক সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদানের পরে উদ্ভূত হইয়াছে।
(৩) আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল কোন আপীলে উত্থাপিত প্রশ্ন পুনঃশুনানী বা পুনঃসিদ্ধান্তের জন্য ট্রাইব্যুনালে ফেরত (remand) দিবে না, বরং নথিভুক্ত কাগজপত্র এবং সাক্ষ্যের ভিত্তিতে উহার সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদান করিবে তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, ট্রাইব্যুনাল কোন আবেদন শুনানির জন্য গ্রহণ না করিয়া সরাসরি নাকচ করিয়া থাকিলে এবং আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল উক্ত সিদ্ধান্ত রহিত করিলে আবেদনটির উপর শুনানির জন্য আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল নির্দেশ দিতে পারিবে।
(৪) একই সম্পত্তির ব্যাপারে একাধিক আপীল দায়ের হইলে আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল একযোগে ঐ সকল আপীল শুনানী ও নিষ্পত্তি করিবে এবং প্রয়োজনবোধে একটি রায় দ্বারা উহাদিগকে নিষ্পত্তি করিতে পারিবে"।
7.7. Sub-section (1) of section 20 clearly mandates that the appellate tribunal, while disposing of an appeal before it, has to discuss every question of fact and of law agitated in the application of appeal. Then the appellate tribunal will pass its own specific decision in order to either annul the judgment appealed against, whether in part or in full, or to confirm or correct the same. Even in case of concurring with the observation and for affirming the decision of the tribunal, the appellate tribunal is not exempted from discussing those question of fact and of law in its independent approach and to render its individual decision with reasonings therefor. Generally, the prime duty of the appellate Court should be to address the issues and redress the grievances of the appellant and to review the trial Court's decision to ensure that the law was applied correctly. The impugned judgment before us is far away from it. Any of the grounds raised here in the instant application of appeal, whether question of fact or of law, was ever attended, discussed or decided by the learned appellate tribunal in its judgment. This is a complete deviation of the provision of section 20 (1) of the Ain, 2001. Jurisdiction has been vested in the appellate tribunal to discuss every question of fact and of law raised in the appeal and to pass its own decision with reasonings thereon, but the appellate tribunal in the instant case has grossly failed to exercise such jurisdiction. This failure to exercise the jurisdiction palpably tentamounts to an error going to the root of the jurisdiction. 
7.8. In view of the above facts and features of the present circumstances and the relevant analysis of law, we, however, find substance in the contentions of the learned counsel for the petitioners. The Rule, therefore, deserves to be made absolute. 

8. Orders of this Court: 
8.1. The Rule is, accordingly, made absolute without, however, any order as to costs. 
8.2. The judgment and decree of affirmance dated 20-1-2020, as evidenced by Annexure-13- 1, passed by learned Arpita Sampotti Prottarpon Appeal Tribunal, Jamalpur in Artipa Appeal No. 02 of 2018 confirming the judgment and decree dated 14-11-2018 passed by the Arpito Sampotti Prottarpon Tribunal, Jamalpur dismissing Arpito Sampatti Suit No. 75 of 2013 is hereby declared to have been passed without lawful authority and be of no legal effect. 
8.3. The order of status quo passed in this writ is recalled and vacated. 
8.4. Let the record of the tribunal be sent back immediately. 

9. Communicate the judgment and order at once to all concerned. 

End.

full_judgment:
Partition Suit No. 38 of 2016 was dismissed on contest by the learned Assistant Judge, Kalihati, Tangail, vide judgment and decree dated 28.03.2021 (decree drawn up on 31.03.2021). Partition Appeal No. 83 of 2021 was dismissed on contest by the learned District Judge, Tangail on 06.04.2022. Challenging the same, the plaintiffs filed the instant Civil Revision and obtained Rule on 20.06.2022.

2. Defendant-opposite party Nos. 2-4 entered appearance in the Rule. During the pendency of the Rule, opposite party No. 4 died. His only son was substituted as opposite party No. 4(a). He also entered appearance in the Rule.

3. The plaintiffs filed the suit for partition simpliciter in respect of 75.333 decimals of land out of 209 decimals recorded in the C.S. khatian No. 92, plot Nos. 804 and 805. The defendant No. 1 filed an application in the suit praying for saham of 43 decimals of land. The defendant Nos. 2-4 (present opposite party Nos. 2-4) contested the suit by filing written statement denying the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land.

4. Admittedly, Taluk Sreenath Bhattacharya and Taraknath Bhattacharya were the rent receivers of 209 decimals of land of plot Nos. 72, 804, 805 and 583 of the C.S. khatian No. 92. It is recorded in the said C.S. khatian that Sutu Mali and others were the occupancyraiyats under the rent-receivers as ‘Chakran Paik’ without any rent (Niskar).

5. The plaintiffs’ case is that Sutu Mali, who subsequently inherited the entire portion of 209 decimals of land as legal heir of the C.S. recorded raiyats having occupancy rights, moved to another place along with members of his family due to loss of portion of the suit land including the dwelling house by diluvion. After death of Sutu Mali his only son Kalidas Chandra inherited the entire 209 decimals of land. Since Kalidas was not staying on the said lands due to loss of the land by diluvion, the land was recorded in the relevant S.A. khatian No. 126, plot Nos. 804 and 805 in the name of Santi Suda Nandi who was neither the owner of the land nor possessor of the same. After re-appearance of the lands, Kalidas returned to the reappeared lands and started living on the lands in plot Nos. 804 and 805 (suit plots) by erecting houses and cultivating the same. He sold the rest of 209 decimals of land in plot Nos. 72 and 583 to 3rd parties. Kalidas died leaving three sons plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and Goura Chanda who inherited the suit land in equal share. Defendant No. 1 is the son of Goura Chandra. He refused to partition the suit land. Other defendants, who are successors-in-interest of Suda Nandi in whose name the S.A. khatian was prepared, claimed ownership in the suit land. B.R.S. record was not prepared in the name of the plaintiffs. They are the owners and possessors of the suit land.

6. The case of the contesting defendant Nos. 2-4 is that by a partition through the civil Court, Durganath Paul, Krishnath Paul and Debidash Paul became the owners of 209 decimals of land and became the rent-receivers of the same. Thus, the rent-receiving interest of the C.S. recorded rent-receivers Taluk Sreenath Bhattacharya and Taraknath Bhattacharya, under whom the plaintiffs’ predecessors Sutu Mali and others were ‘Chakran Paik’ raiyats, ceased to exist. The subsequent owners of the land gave permanent settlement of the land in favour of Bhabani Kishore by a registered patta dated 28.04.1923. The S.A. khatian was correctly prepared in the name of daughter-in-law of Bhabani Kishore. The defendant Nos. 2-4 are successors-in-interest of Bhabani Kishore. They are the owners and possessors of the suit land.

7. Plaintiffs examined 2 witnesses while the defendants examined 4 witnesses. The plaintiffs produced the C.S. khatian (ext. 1) and the S.A. khatian (ext. 2). The defendants produced, inter alia, the registered patta dated 28.04.2023 (ext. Ga), rent receipts (ext. Cha).

8. Plaintiffs’ case is solely based on the C.S. khatian evidencing that their predecessors-in-interest were raiyats having the right of occupancy in the suit land as ‘Chakran Paik’ free of rent under the Zamindars. In Mridul Kanti Sarder and others vs. Krishna Charan Sarder and others, 14 BLC 848, it was held: 
“In view of the serious contradiction between the evidence of the PWs and the deed itself (Exhibit-2) in respect of source of interest of the inheritors and also on the vague point of Uma Charan's acquiring the occupancy right under section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and its legal implication, it cannot be held the vendors of the plaintiff inherited Chakran interest of Uma Charan or the plaintiff acquired any interest under his kabala, Exhibit-2.”

9. Relying on the above-quoted passage, the appellate Court below held that the right of occupancy of the Chakran land does not create any title and as such, the plaintiffs did not acquire any title in the suit land as successors-in-interest of the original Chakran tenants. The proposition of law based on which the appellate Court below dismissed the suit requires examination.

10. Under Section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (in short, the ‘SA & T Act’) a person possessing land as Chakran gets a right of occupancy from the date the Act came into force. The SA & T Act came into force on 16.05.1951. In Sakhina Bibi vs. Nazira Bibi, BCR 1985 (AD) 37 the plaintiff filed suit for recovery of khas possession of the suit premises by evicting the defendant therefrom on the ground that the latter was the permissive possessor of the land. The suit was decreed. The lower appellate Court dismissed the suit. The High Court Division dismissed the second appeal holding that the defendant possessed the land based on the Chakran right which became occupancy right after coming into force of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The Appellate Division observed that the important question was whether the defendant was holding the land as Chakran tenant when the Act came into force. The apex Court held that the answer was negative and allowed the appeal.

11. The above-discussed case does not answer the question of law as to whether the occupancy right of Chakran land creates any title and whether the same is transferable. Section 11(1) of the SA & T Act clearly states that the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 (in short, the ‘BT Act’) or the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 so far as they apply to occupancy raiyats known as Nankar, Chakran will apply. The term ‘occupancyraiyats’ was defined in clause 3(b) of Section 4 of the BT Act as raiyats having a right of occupancy in the land held by them. One of the incidents of occupancy-right under Section 26 of the BT Act is that on the death of the raiyat his right in the land devolves to his legal heirs in the same manner as other immovable property. Another incident of occupancy-right under Section 26B of the BT Act is that holdings of an occupancyraiyat or a share or portion thereof, together with the right of occupancy therein, is transferable. In Amal Chandra Dhupi alias Das and others vs. Lakshan Chandra Das and others, 10 LM (AD) 5, it was held that when land was given to a family on account of service rendered, i.e. as Chakran tenants, a part of that family does not lose their right of tenancy simply on the ground that part of the family ceased to render the service. If, in fact, the service to the landlord had ceased, it was up to the landlord to take action for his eviction. The tenancy of a particular member of the Chakran tenant family cannot cease automatically.

12. The above discussions on point of transferability of Chakran land based on Section 11(1) of the SAT Act, Sections 26 and 26B of the BT Act and case laws unequivocally establish that the rayati interest of Chakran land is transferable and heritable. Clearly, the appellate Court below was wrong on this point of law.

13. In the instant suit for partition simpliciter, although the point of law that Chakran land is transferable and heritable goes in favour of the plaintiffs, yet their title in the suit in land has to be considered in some more details than in a suit for permanent injunction.

14. In Rezaul Karim and others vs. Shamsuzzoha and others, 49 DLR (AD) 68, the apex Court held that in a suit for partition, the Court cannot convert itself into a Court for determination of the respective titles of the parties if a serious dispute emerges from the pleadings as to the title of the plaintiffs to effect partition without formally determining the plaintiffs’ title. In that case, the plaintiff is required to file a full-fledged suit for declaration of title to prove his claim. 49 DLR (AD) 68 was relied upon in Jotirmoy Datta and others vs. Mritunjoy Datta and others, 16 BLT 446 wherein it was held that a simple suit for partition without claiming declaration of title is not maintainable when a complicated question of title is involved in the suit for partition.

15. Reverting back to the case in hand, both the Courts below concurrently observed that the defendant Nos. 2-4 proved that the suit land was settled in favour of their predecessors-in-interest by the then Zamindars, vide registered patta deed No. 2754 dated 28.04.1923 (ext. Ga). In this regard, I note that PW1 (plaintiff No. 1) stated that they did not file any case against the patta. The patta executed in 1923 implies that the earlier grant of the suit land in favour of the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiffs as Chakran land had ceased to exist and the same was no longer valid. The relevant S.A. khatian was prepared in the name of the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 2-4. They filed rent receipts (ext. Cha) in support of possession of the suit land by them. The plaintiffs, on the other hand, did not submit any document in respect of possession. PW1 admitted in examination-in-chief that they had not paid any rent for the suit land. The instant suit for partition involves determination of complicated question of title which can only be resolved in a full-fledged suit for declaration of title. Therefore, the suit is not maintainable. Moreover, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant Nos. 2-4 rightly pointed out that the suit land sought to be partitioned has not been identified by giving boundaries. Reference of the C.S. khatian numbers and C.S. plot numbers are not sufficient to identify the suit land. Order VII rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires that where the subject matter of the suit is immovable property, its description must be sufficient to identify it and must not be vague and unspecified. In Md. Sorboddi Miah vs. Md. Serajul Haque and another, XII ADC 413, the Appellate Division held that when the land is vague and indefinite without any specific boundary, the plaintiff cannot get a decree in respect of any unspecified land and on this score alone the suit is liable to be dismissed. The observation made in XII ADC 413 squarely applies to the case in hand.

16. In view of the foregoing discussions, I do not find merit in the Rule.

17. In the result, the Rule is discharged.

Send down the LCR.

End.

Mr. A.R.M Qayyum Khan, Advocate ------ For the respondent No. 2
parties:

Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Jibon Bima Bhaban (3rd Floor), 10, Dilkusha Commercial Area, Dhaka-1000 an.d another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Momammed Tazrul Hossain, J: 1. This appeal under section 196D of the Customs Act 1969 has been preferred against the judgment and order dated 14.10. 2021 (communicated on 17.10.2021) passed by the respondent Number- 1, in CEVT/CASE(Cus)- 165/ 2021 allowing the appeal thus setting aside the order being number 347, dated 08.02.2021 passed by the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chattogram, contained in Nothi No. 100/বিবিধ/এপি/সেকশন-৯(বি)/২০১৭-২০১৮/১০৮৬৭(কাস).
 
2. Short facts relevant for disposal of the present appeal are that the Respondent No. 2 opened a letter of credit being number 00 134 1160 10857, dated 05.12.2016 for import of 200 reconditioned cars from Japan, part shipment was allowed and the petitioner imported 32 cars under two invoices in two consignments of 16 cars and both invoices were dated 14.12. 2016. After the cars arrived at Chittagong port the C&F agent of the responder number 2 submitted bills of entry being number C- 124 1980, C- 124 1981, C- 124 1982, C- 124 1983, C- 124 1984, C- 124 1985, C- 124 1986, C- 124 1987, C- 124 1988, C- 124 1989, C- 124 990, C- 1241991, C- 1241 992, C-124 19 93, C- 1241194 and C- 1241115, all dated 03.10.2017 and bills of entry being number C- 138 4692, C- 1384698, C- 138 4704, C- 13847 08, C- 138 4711, C-138 4717, C- 138 4724, C- 138 4731, C- 138 4736, C- 138 4741, C- 138 4747, C- 138 4753, C- 138 4759, C 138 4770, C- 138 4773 and C- 138 4779, all dated 05. 11. 2017 to the Commissioner of customs for assessment and release of the vehicles. The customs authority, upon receiving the necessary documents, proposed to assess the imported cars based on the minimum value fixed for each model. This valuation was determined by calculating the average of all prices quoted for each model code in the latest edition of the Yellow Book published in Japan. When it was found that the authority was taking an excessive amount of time in assessing and releasing the vehicles, Respondent No. 2 filed a writ petition No. 14684 of 2017, challenging the customs authority's inaction and failure to release some of the imported cars. Subsequently, Respondent No. 2 filed another Writ Petition, being No. 613 of 2018, seeking a directive for the customs authority to complete the assessment of the remaining cars. Both writ petitions were heard together, and a Division Bench of this Court, after considering the submissions of the parties, disposed of the cases with a directive to the writ petitioner to respond to the communications from the customs authority. In compliance with this directive, Respondent No. 2 submitted the required documents. During the assessment process, the customs authority discovered a discrepancy between the House Bill of Lading submitted by the importer and the Master Bill of Lading concerning the shipment dates of the vehicles. Based on this discrepancy, it was determined that the vehicles were over five years old and therefore import-prohibited under the applicable regulations. Consequently, Respondent No. 2 was issued a show-cause notice dated 05.11.2020 under Section 180 of the Customs Act, 1969. Respondent No. 2 replied to the show-cause notice, and the Commissioner of Customs upon conducting a hearing in presence of the respondent No.2 issued an adjudication order, vide order No. 347, dated 08.02.2021 and directed the confiscation of the imported vehicles and imposed a penalty of Tk. 32,00,000/- (thirty-two lacs) on the importer. Against the said order of the Commissioner of Customs, respondent No. 2 filed an appeal before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka (hereinafter CEVT). Upon hearing the parties, CEVT vide its order, dated 14.10.2021 allowed the appeal and set aside order No. 347, dated 08.02.2021 passed by the Commissioner of customs. Being aggrieved with the said order of the CEVT, Commissioner of Customs preferred the instant Appeal. 

3. Mr. Mohaddes Ul Islam, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing with Mr. Manjur Elahi Parag, learned Assistant Attorney General, placed the paper book and the relevant records. He submits that after the C&F agent of the respondent No.2 submitted two sets of bills of Entries dated 03.10.2017 and 05.11.2017 respectively, the customs authority opened a Note Sheet contained in Nothi No. 100/bbidho/ep/sekshon 9(bi)/2017 - 2018 for assessment of the imported vehicles. While the customs authority was in the process of the assessment, respondent No. 2, filed writ petition No. 14684/2017 and Writ Petition No. 613/2018 seeking direction upon the customs authority to complete the assessment and release of their imported vehicles. Both the writ petitions were heard analogously and were disposed of with a direction upon the respondent No. 2 to submit required documents before the customs authority. 

4. Then the respondent No. 2 submitted necessary documents and during scrutiny, the customs authority discovered that even though the House B/L submitted by the respondent was shown to be dated on 14.12.2016, but the corresponding Master B/L showed that the said consignments were laden on board the vessel on 06.09.2017 and on 26.09.2017 respectively, hence the said recondition vehicles imported by the respondent No. 2, being older than 5 years were import banned under the provision of Import Policy Order 2015-2018. Considering the above aspect, the commissioner of Customs by an order, dated 08.02.2021 confiscated the vehicles and also imposed a penalty of Tk. 32 (thirty two) lacs under Clause 9(i) and 14 of the Table under Section 156(1) of customs Act, 1969 for violation of Section 16 and 32 of the said Act. Against the said order, dated 08.02.2021, respondent No. 2 preferred Appeal before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka under the provision of Section 196A of the Customs Act, 1969 and the same was numbered as CEVT/CASE (Cus)- 1657/2021. Thereafter, the tribunal upon hearing the parties vide its order, dated 14.10.2021 on erroneous findings allowed the appeal. 

5. He submits that the Tribunal failed to realize the pertinent point in the instant case and failed to consider the mis-declaration made by the importer with an ulterior motive to defeat the legal provision under the Import Policy Order 2015 – 2018 banning the import of reconditioned vehicles older than five years into the country. 

6. He submits that the importer submitted 16 House Bills of Ladings, all dated 03.10.2017 and another 16 House Bills of Lading all dated 05.11.2017 for importing 32 reconditioned cars, but their corresponding Master Bills of Lading being 0087A53075 and 0087A53076 respectively were actually dated on 06.09.2017 and 26.09.2017; these facts were clearly established through undeniable documents which shows that the respondent No. 2 was involved in an attempt to bring import banned items within the country which is an offence under Section 32 of the Customs Act, 1969 and the Commissioner of Customs has correctly passed the order, dated 08.02.2021 by confiscating the imported vehicles and imposing penalty under the provisions of Table 14 of Section 156 of the Customs Act, 1969. The Tribunal failed to appreciate the said facts and relevant legal provision and reached to a wrong conclusion and allowed the appeal which is not at all sustainable. 

7. He submits that during the assessment process, the Customs authority conducted a thorough investigation in the matter and recorded in minute details in Note No. 74,75,76, and 77 of the Note Sheet about the suspicious activities carried out in relation to the instant consignments of the reconditioned vehicles, but the Tribunal completely overlooked the same and misdirected themselves and on wrong interpretation of the legal provisions allowed the appeal which is liable to be set aside. 

8. Mr. Islam further submits that the case references presented by the respondent No. 2; i.e. the judgments passed in Writ Petition No. 6224/2006, Writ Petition No. 3125/2015 and Writ Petition No. 3126/2015 are not applicable in the instant case and the Tribunal has fallen in severe mistake by allowing the appeal and hence instant appeal should be allowed and the order of the tribunal below should be set aside. 

9. Mr. A.R.M. Qayyum Khan appearing for the respondent No. 2 submits at the outset that the Tribunal upon properly appreciating the legal provisions and the applicable laws has rightly allowed the appeal and there is no reason for this Division to interfere with the findings of the Tribunal below. 

10. He submits that the respondent No. 2 opened Letter of Credit being No. 1341/16/01/0857, dated 05.12.2016 for importing in total 200 reconditioned vehicles from Japan and as part shipment imported 152 vehicles. Customs authority assessed and released 120 vehicles, but for no fault on the part of the said respondent refused to assess and release 32 vehicles. He submits that the respondent's freight forwarder issued House Bills of Lading, dated 14.12.2016 and accordingly it submitted the said Bills of Lading and other related documents for the Customs Authority to assess and release the vehicles of the importer but, the said authority arbitrarily refused to release the vehicles and the Tribunal below was correct to hold the view that the vehicles imported by the respondent No. 2 were not contrabanned and were required to be assessed and released. 

11. Mr. Khan Submits that it has been long established in our jurisdiction that for assessment of reconditioned vehicles, House Bills of Lading is to be taken into consideration by the customs authority in assessing the date of shipment and applicable duties and levies and the Tribunal below has been absolutely correct to upheld the said legal position and it has not at all committed any error in allowing the appeal. 

12. He submits that under the provision of Section 3 of the Bills of Lading Act, 1856, every bill of lading in the hands of a consignee or endorsee for valuable consideration, representing goods to have been shipped on board a vessel, shall be conclusive evidence of such shipment as against the master or other person signing the same, notwithstanding that such goods or some part thereof may not have been so shipped, Said provision of law has been repeatedly upheld and bolstered by this Division and our Apex Court in many cases. Mr. Khan submits the judgments passed in writ petition No. 6224/2006, writ petition No. 3125/2015 where similar issues as in the instant case was raised. The date in House Bill of Lading and the date in Master Bill of Lading differed, but in light of the provision of Section 3 of the Bills of Lading Act, 1856 this Division in the said matters found that the date appearing on the House Bill of Lading is to be considered in calculating the age of the reconditioned vehicles. Hence the order of the Tribunal below allowing the appeal has been based on proper appreciation of the provisions of law and as such instant appeal should be rejected. 

13. We have heard the learned advocates from both the sides, perused the paper book and the LCR, carefully gone through the materials on record, considered the applicable laws and case references produced by the parties. 

14. The point at issue in the instant case is very clear; whether the House Bills of Lading, dated 14.12.2017 presented by the respondent No. 2 in relation to the imported reconditioned vehicles should be accepted by the customs authority as the date of shipment in determining the age of the said vehicles and be accordingly assessed and released. 

15. A bill of lading is a crucial legal document in international trade and shipping. Its primary purpose is to serve as a receipt, a contract, and a document of title for the goods being transported. It acts as evidence that the carrier has received the goods in good condition or as described in the Bill of Lading. Bills of lading are primarily of two kinds; house bill of lading and master bill of lading. If the shipper takes assistance of a freight forwarder or a Non-Vessel Operating Common Carrier (NVOCC) for transporting its goods, the freight forwarder or the NVOCC finds a suitable shipping line and vessel for transporting the shipper's goods. Upon receiving the goods from the shipper, the freight forwarder or the NVOCC issues a bill of lading which is called a house bill of lading (HBL), it basically includes the shipper's details, consignee's details, notify party details, carrier information, description of goods, voyage and port details, marks or number on the packages or container, bill of lading number, freight charges, date of shipment, signature and seal, etc. on the other hand a master bill of lading (MBL) is issued by a ship owner or operator, known as a carrier. MBL is issued when the carrier receives the goods on board the vessel. Both the House and Master Bill of Lading contain the same accurate, precise, and detailed information about cargo (the number of containers, seal numbers, weight, measurements, etc.). The shipper, consignee, and notify party are the only details that might be different between the HBL and MBL. Another detail that may vary between the HBL and the MBL is the date. Because HBL is issued on the date the freight forwarder or NVOCC receives the goods at its premises or when the contract for transportation is concluded. On the other hand MBL is issued once the goods are received on board the vessel. In international trade usual difference of date of the HBL and MBL is 1-3 days, but at extreme circumstances, it could be even 10-15 days, because it might take longer than expected for the consignment to get to the port of lading provided the designated vessel and voyage is still on; otherwise, the HBL will have to be changed to reflect the variation. 

16. In the instant case, the respondent No. 2, opened Letter of Credit, dated 05.12.2016 to import reconditioned vehicles from Japan. At the relevant time, under the provision of Import Policy Order 2015 - 2018, reconditioned motor car, microbus, minibus, jeep and other such vehicles and tractor could be imported on the condition that on the date of shipment, the vehicle would not be older than 5 years; for determining the age of the vehicle, day will be counted from the 1st day of the immediate next year from the date of manufacture of chassis of the vehicle. Due to this restriction regarding the age of the vehicle, the date of shipment is of paramount significance to an importer of reconditioned vehicles, like the instant respondent No. 2. 

17. Learned advocate for the respondent No. 2, in his quest to impress upon this court and to show that the reconditioned vehicles imported by the said respondent were not older than 5 (five) years has shown that the vehicles were manufactured in the year 2011 and as per law, counting the age of the vehicles will start from 1st January, 2012 and they will complete 5 (five) years of age on 31st December, 2016. But the respondent No. 2 as per the Bill of Lading, produced by it, has shipped the vehicles on 14.12.2016, before the vehicles completed their 5th year from the date of manufacture and hence the said vehicles were not contrabanned under the provisions of law. In this regard learned advocate referred the provision of Section 3 of the Bills of Lading Act, 1856, which reads as follows: 
"every bill of lading in the hands of a consignee or endorsee for valuable consideration, representing goods to have been shipped on board a vessel, shall be conclusive evidence of such shipment as against the master or other person signing the same, notwithstanding that such goods or some part thereof may not have been so shipped, unless such holder of the bill of lading shall have had actual notice at the time of receiving the same that the goods had not in fact been laden on board; Provided that the master or other person so signing may exonerate himself, in respect of such misrepresentation, by showing that it was caused without any default on his part, and wholly by the fraud of the shipper or of the holder, or some person under whom the holder claims." 

18. Said Section of the Act, 1856 stipulates that every bill of lading in the hands of a consignee or endorsee for valuable consideration representing goods to have been shipped on board a vessel shall be conclusive evidence of such shipment as against the master or other person. Applying the aforesaid provisions to the facts of the present case, as already noticed hereinbefore, the bill of lading in question, produced by the respondent No. 2 it was shown that the vehicles are not older than five years and they are not import banned items and as such the vehicles imported by the respondent No. 2 should be assessed regularly and released accordingly by the customs authority. 

19. Learned advocate for the respondent No. 2 in support of his argument has also referred two unreported judgments, passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 6224 of 2006 and Writ Petition No. 3125 of 2015. In both the cases, the dispute was regarding the date of shipment and it was held that House Bill of Lading is to be taken into consideration for calculating the age of the reconditioned vehicles. In writ petition No. 6224/2006 as per the House bill of lading vehicles were shipped on 24.12.2005 but, the customs authority showed that as per corresponding Master bill of lading those vehicles were shipped on 06.01.2006 and as such the vehicles were older than 4 years on the date of shipment and hence were banned under the import policy order 2003 - 2006. This court, relying upon the provision of Section 3 of the Bills of Lading Act, 1856, held that house bill of lading is to be accepted as the date of shipment. In the case of writ petition No. 3125/2015 neither the date of House Bill of Lading nor the date of Master Bill of Lading was mentioned, nevertheless it was held that the date of HBL is to be considered as the date of shipment. 

20. Every case should be considered and judged in the light of its own facts and circumstances. It is clear that in case of both the above referred decisions, it was decided to accept the house bill of lading as the evidence of shipment solely relying on the 1st part of Section 3 of the Bills of Lading Act, 1856. But, in neither of the judgments the proviso of Section 3 of the said Act was raised or discussed. A bonafide consignee or endorsee for valuable consideration can hold a bill of lading as a conclusive evidence of shipment against the Master of a vessel; but under the proviso of the said section such presumption can be rebutted or shrugged off by the Master or the person signing the said MBL by showing that there has been a misrepresentation in the bill of lading and such misrepresentation was not caused by his fault, or that it was caused by fraud of the shipper or of the holder, or some other person under whom the holder claims. 

21. In the instant case, the customs authority found that the HBL submitted by the respondent No. 2 has shown that the vehicles were laden on board the vessel on 14.12.2016 but the MBL showed the vehicles to have been laden on board the vessel on 06.09.2017 and on 26.09.2017 respectively. This discrepancy in the lading dates of the vehicles show a significant difference of about 9 (nine) months. Upon finding this unacceptable difference of lading dates of the vehicles, the customs authority took steps to find out the reason for the said variation of dates. They contacted Columbia Enterprise Ltd., the local agent of the Main Line Operator that carried the vehicles. The information provided by the said local agent and from the information shown in the Import General Manifest (IGM) in the ASYCUDA World System submitted by the Main Line Operator of the vessel, it was discovered that there were two Master Bills of Lading being No. 0087A53075 and 0087A53076. As per said MBLs, vehicles of the respondent No. 2 were laden on board the vessel from Kobe, Japan and MBLs were issued on 06.09.2017 and 26.09.2017 respectively. It was also found that all the information of the HBL submitted by the respondent No. 2 including the name of the vessel, shipping lines, shipping agent, shipper, consignee, Notify Party, Voyage number of the vessel, country and port of lading, description of the shipped goods, chassis number of the vehicles, container number, etc. completely matched with the MBLS mentioned above, except the date of lading the vehicles on board the vessel and issuance of the HBL. 

22. In such a situation, if the date of HBL, i.e. 14.12.2016 is held to be a date of shipment; it will lead to an absurd conclusion. As per the said HBL, vehicles were laden on board the same vessel which carried the vehicles on 14.12.2016 and after more than 9 (nine) months said vehicles reached at Chittagong port. On the other hand if it is accepted as evidenced from the MBL Nos. 0087A53075 and 0087A53076 that the vehicles were laden on board the vessel on 06.09.2017 and 26.09.2017 respectively from Kobe, Japan and reached Chattogram Port on 02.10.2017 and 27.10.2017 respectively upon transshipment at Malaysia, it shows to be a more likely event that had actually taken place. 

23. It may be noted that apart from all other information contained in the HBL submitted by the respondent No. 2, which matched with the MBLS, the name and voyage number of the vessel that carried the vehicles also matched with the MBLS, it is not in the usual course possible to get the correct and matching voyage number and the vessel name about 9 months in advance. However, even if somehow it becomes possible to get correct voyage number and a vessel’s name in advance of a period of more then 9 (nine) months it does not look to be normal for the importer to do so. This fact sadly leads to the conclusion that the date shown on the HBL submitted by the respondent No. 2 may have been manipulated or distorted and hence became unreliable. The HBL, dated 14.12.2016, therefore, in our view brings the same under the proviso of Section 3 of the Bills of Lading Act, 1856 and it loses the legal value and cannot actually be used as a conclusive evidence of ownership and shipment of the vehicles against the Main Line Operator that carried the vehicles and as such cannot be accepted by the customs authority to determine the date of shipment of the vehicles to calculate the age of the vehicles. Accordingly, it is found that as per the acceptable date of shipment as evidenced from the MBL being 06.09.2017 and 26.09.2017 respectively, the vehicles imported by the respondent No. 2 have become older than 5 (five) years and as per Import Policy Order 2015 - 2018 have become contrabanned item. 

24. In the case of C.I.T. Vs. Sun Engineering Works Pvt. Ltd. Reported in [1992]198 ITR 297 (SC) the Indian Supreme Court has cautioned against reading its own judgment in a truncated manner in following words: "It is neither desirable nor permissible to pick out a word or a sentence from the judgment of this Court, divorced from the context of the question under consideration and treat it to be the complete 'law' declared by this Court. The judgment must be read as a whole and the observations from the judgment have to be considered in the light of the questions which were before this Court. A decision of this court takes its colour from the questions involved in the case in which it is rendered and, while applying the decision to a later case, the courts must carefully try to ascertain the true principle laid down by the decision of this court and not to pick out words or sentences from the judgment, divorced from the context of the questions under consideration by this Court, to support their reasonings. Again in Madhav Rao Jivaji Rao Scindia Bahadur Vs. Union of India, reported in 3 SCR 9, it was observed that "It is not proper to regard a word, a clause or a sentence occurring in a judgment of the Supreme Court, divorced from its context, as containing a full exposition of the law on a question when the question did not even fall to be answered in that judgment". 

25. In light of the above observations, it may be found that the Judgment passed by this Division in a case might not be applicable in a subsequent and seemingly similar case, but where the context and the questions raised is somewhat different. In writ Petition No. 6224/2006 and writ petition No. 3125-3126 of 2015 or even in case of the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 2768-2769 of 2015 even though the customs authority raised the issue of difference of dates between the HBL and MBL, but it appears that in those cases the authority failed to produce any evidence or record to show that there were cogent reasons not to rely upon the House Bill of Lading which was submitted by the importer and therefore it is found that the case references produced by the respondent No. 2 being the judgment, dated 08.02.2007 passed in writ petition No. 6224 of 2006, judgment, dated 08.07.2015 passed in writ petition No. 3125-3126 of 2015 by this Division and the order, dated 22.11.2015 passed in CP No. 2768-2769 of 2015 by the Hon'ble Appellate Division is not applicable in the instant case. 

26. Considering the facts and circumstances, provisions of law and decisions as referred to and the discussions made above we find substance to maintain the instant appeal. 

27. Accordingly, the Appeal is allowed and the order, dated 14.10.2021 (communicated on 17.10.2021) passed by the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal in CEVT/CASE(CUS)-165/2021 is set aside and the order No. 347, dated 08.02.2021, passed by the Commissioner of Customs, Chattogram as contained in Nothi No. 100/বিবিধ/এপি/সেকশন-৯(বি)/২০১৭-২০১৮/১০৮৬৭(কাস) is affirmed. 

28. Let a copy of this Judgment be sent to the Tribunal under the seal and signature of an officer of this court in view of Section 231 of the Customs Act, 2023. 

29. Send down the records to the concerned authorities.

End.
