full_judgment:
In this revision Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 28-7-2016 passed by the learned Special Judge (District Judge), Pabna in Other Appeal No. 109 of 2005 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 30-6-2005 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, lshwardi in Other Class Suit No. 206 of 

1998 dismissing the suit should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the petitioners, as plaintiffs, filed Other Class Suit No. 206 of 1998 in the court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Ishwardi, against the present opposite parties, as defendant, for a declaration of title contending inter alia, that the schedule-'Ka' property under DS Khatian No. 1237 originally belonged to Mofizuddin Sarder and others. The property was sold in auction in Certificate Case No. 237 of 1943. One Rahmat Ali Sarder purchased the same in auction from whom predecessor of plaintiffs named Rezia Khatun purchased the suit property by registered deed dated 20-3-1944. Property under DS Khatian No. 1364 originally belonged to one Jonaki Nath Paul under whom one Bolai Sarder was borgader, subsequently Jonaki Nath Paul evicted his borgader Bolai Sarder and took the property in his khas possession and sold out the same to Rezia Khatun by registered deed dated 5-5-1945. Rezia Khatun after purchase erected house on a portion of land and was residing therein with her sons and on a part of suit property planted different types of trees and was enjoying the property with the knowledge of all. The defendants have had no title and possession in the suit property.
 
3. Predecessor of the defendant named Azahar Ali Mridha was closely acquainted and related with the predecessor of the plaintiffs, resultantly, entrusted said Azahar Ali Mridha to look after the property and to get the SA khatian prepared in her name and to pay rents to the government. Said Azahar Ali Mridha ensured the predecessor of the plaintiffs that he took proper step for recording name of Rezia Khatun in SA Khatian. Believing Azahar Ali Rezia Khatun kept her relaxed thinking that everything were going well. In the month of August 1998 some of the defendants claimed title in the property saying that they purchased the same from the real owners. The plaintiffs made search to ensure with the concerned authority about the fact and came to know that SA and RS khatians collusively created in the name of predecessor of the defendants. SA and RS khatians wrongly prepared in the name of Azahar Ali Mridha who never acquired the property by any deed from Rezia Khatun. Azahar Ali Mridha taking advantage of looking after the property cunningly prepared the SA and RS khatians in his name instead of Rezia Khatun. Said Rezia Khatun died leaving husband plaintiff No. 1, sons plaintiff Nos. 2-5, grandson by predeceased daughter plaintiff No. 6 and daughter plaintiff No. 7 who inherited the property left by Rezia Khatun and have been possessing the same as their homestead on a part of the suit land and a part of suit land letting out shop to the tenant and running business themselves and planting various trees on the remaining portion of the land without any disturbance from any quarter, but for wrong recording of SA and RS khatians in the name of predecessor of the defendants, title of the plaintiffs have become clouded, hence, the present suit for declaration of title. 

4. The defendant Nos. 1-8 and 10-13 contested the suit by filing two separate written statements denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending inter din, that the suit is barred by limitation; defect of parties as well as under section 42 of the SR Act. Case of defendant Nos. 1-8 are that the predecessor of plaintiffs Rezia Khatun was owning the property by purchase from whom predecessor of defendant Nos. 1-8 took settlement of the property as agricultural tenant by dakhila. After obtaining settlement Azahar Ali Mridha constructed homestead on a portion of the property and the rest was possessing by planting various trees and cultivating the same. While he was in possession on the basis of settlement from Rezia Khatun SA Khatian correctly recorded in his name. Azahar Ali Mridha have six sons who after getting married, for their residence constructed 16/17 houses thereon and have been leaving with their family. Last RS khatian correctly recorded in the name of Azahar Ali Mridha in the field survey, but along with Azahar Ali Mridha on the back side of khatian name of Rezia Khatun wrongly mentioned for which Azahar Ali Mridha filed objection case under rule 30 of the SAT Rules before the Objection Officer. Rezia Khatun herself appeared in objection case and after hearing concerned Officer accepted the objection and corrected the RS khatian in the name of Azahar Ali Mridha. Thereafter, Rezia Khatun filed appeal case under Rule 31 of the SAT Rules before the Appeal Officer against the order of Settlement Officer. Said Appeal was rejected on contest by judgment and order dated 15-5-1980 affirming the order of Settlement Officer. Thereafter, Rezia Khatun gave up her claim in the property, accordingly, RS khatian finally published in the name of predecessor of the defendant. On the middle north portion of the suit plot Azahar Ali Mridha and his wife have been living by erecting homestead. Other houses constructed subsequently, were let out to the tenants. 

5. Other part of the property also have been possessing by his six sons constructing 16-17 houses thereon. Azahar Ali Mridha died leaving defendant Nos. 1-8, out of which defendant No. 4 sold 0.08 sataks land to Amjad Hossain and others. There are 23/24 houses, four tube-wells, three pucca latrines, kitchen, cowshed, palm trees, three coconut trees, bamboos dump, Tamarind trees and tea stall of defendant No. 5 are existing on the suit property some portion of the suit property has been acquired by the government for highway and notice of acquisition was issued by the government in the name of the defendants as heirs of Azahar Ali Mridha. Since settlement from Rezia Khatun Azahar Ali Mridha then his heirs continuously possessing the same without any intervention. The plaintiffs have had no right, title and possession in the suit property, but for illegal gain with ulterior motive filed the present suit. Defendant Nos. 10-13 filed written statement supporting the written statement filed by the defendant Nos. 1-8 and claimed that defendant No. 4 transferred 8 sataks of land to them by a registered deed No. 3568 dated 29-8-1986 and delivered possession of the same. All the defendants are in possession of the suit property and have been paying rents to the government, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

6. The trial court framed five issues for determination of the dispute. In course of hearing, the plaintiffs examined four witnesses as PWs and defendant Nos. 1-8 examined six witnesses as DWs and defendant Nos. 10-13 examined single witness as DW Both the parties submitted some documents in support of their respective claim in the suit properties which were duly marked as exhibits. The trial court after hearing by the impugned judgment and decree dated 30-6-2005 dismissed the suit. 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial court, the plaintiffs preferred Other Class Appeal No. 109 of 2005 before the learned District Judge, Pabna. Eventually the appeal was transferred to the court of learned Special Judge (District Judge), Pabna for hearing and disposal who after hearing by the impugned judgment and decree dated 28-7-2016 dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trial court. At this juncture, the petitioners moved this Court by filing this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 

8. Mr. Md. Alamgir Mostafizur Rahman with Mr. Md. Monjurul Hoque, learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners submit that the trial court as well as the appellate court in dismissing the suit and appeal committed illegality and error of law on misconstruction of evidences and relevant laws in this regard. He submits that the trial court and the appellate court wrongly decided the issue of limitation finding that the plaintiffs were aware about wrong record-of-right in the year 1980 as an objection case was filed by Azahar Ali Mridha against draft RS khatian prepared in the name of Rezia Khatun. 

9. He argued that cause of action for filing of suit depends on final publication of the record-of-right. In the instant case RS khatian finally published in the year 1992 and the suit was filed in the year 1998, it was very much within time. In support of his such submissions he has referred to the cases of Government of Bangladesh vs AKM Abdul Hye and others reported in 56 DLR (AD) 53 and Government of Bangladesh vs Har Chandra Nath and others reported in 10 MLR (AD) 313 . 

10. It is further argued that the courts below failed to find that the defendants could not submit any document before the trial court showing that Azahar Ali Mridha obtained settlement of the property from Rezia Khatun by any deed of settlement, kubaliyat or rent receipt and could not show the basis of SA khatian in any manner, but the courts below on an speculation observed that somehow Azahar Ali Mridha obtained the property by way of pattan, consequently, SA khatian recorded in his name which has no basis at all. 

11. He further argued that both the courts below put stress on the proceeding under Rules 30 and 31 of the SAT Rules initiated. by Azahar Ali Mridha in the year 1980, but in our jurisdiction it has been decided that unless the title of the plaintiff is invaded no cause Of action for filing suit arises. In the instant case after publication of RS khatian finally, the plaintiff came to know about wrong record and by such wrong record title of the plaintiffs have become clouded then they filed the present suit. 

12. Mr. Alatngir argued that both the courts below assessed the evidences of the defendants taking into consideration a series of rent receipts showing payment of rent, but failed to appreciate the provisions of law mere payment of rent to the government on the strength of unfounded entry in the record-of-right will not create valid tenancy in favour of the defendants. In support of his such submissions he has referred to the case of Md. Yasin and others vs Kamini Kumar Shome reported in BCR 1982 (HCD) 216 and Abdul? Noor and others vs Aziruddin and others reported in 21 BLT (AD) 161.  

13. Finally, he argued that by any record-of-right in particular recording of name of a person in SA and RS khatian having no basis at all, the defendants acquired no title in the suit property. In support of his such submission he has referred to a catena of cases Syed Abdul Hague and another vs Surendra Nath Majumder and others reported in IV ADC, 43, Lal Meah vs Haji Md. Ibrahim Meah and others reported in 28 DLR (AD) 61, Narendra Chandra Das and another vs Sree Sree Gopal Bigraha and another, reported in 3 XP (AD) 201, Government of Bangladesh vs Abdul Malek reported in 61 DLR 635, Sajeda Khatun and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 34 BLD (AD) 227, Abdul Aziz and others vs Hindu Deivy Luxmi Gobinda Jew and others reported in BCR 2006 (AD), 214 and Md. Motiruddin Mondal @ Matiar Rahman Mondal and others vs Full Mohammed Mollah and others reported in III ADC, 108. 

14. It is also argued that as decided by this Court SA khatian has no presumptive value and on the basis of SA Khatian nobody acquires title in the property, but both the courts below in one hand failed to appreciate the provisions of law, misread and misconstrued the evidences on record, as such, committed illegality and error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

15. Mr. Omit Roy, Advocate with Mr. Kawser Rahman Kafi, learned Advocates appearing for the opposite parties submit that admittedly the suit property belonged to Rezia Khatun by purchase, from whom predecessor of defendants named Azahar Ali Mridha obtained pattan by way of payment of rents and obtaining rent receipts, but said rent receipt (চেক দাখিল) could not be filed before the trial court as those dakhilas were not taken return from the office of the Settlement Officer, where Azahar Ali Mridha submitted those dakhilas before hearing of objection case and appeal case. 

16. He submits that SA khatian correctly recorded in the name of Azahar Ali Mridha as agricultural tenant under Rezia Khatun as appearing from SA khatian itself. It is argued that since 1957 the predecessor of defendants have been paying rents to the government continuously as tenant under the government, no objection whatever from plaintiffs or their predecessor Rezia Khatun ever raised till 1980. 

17. He submits that cause of action for filing of the suit lastly arises in the year 1980 when Azahar Ali Mridha filed objection case before the Settlement Officer in respect of wrong recording of name of Rezia Khatun at the backside of khatian which was sustained and accordingly, draft RS khatian was corrected, then Rezia Khatun filed appeal under Rule 31 of the SAT Rules which was rejected. The petitioners or their predecessor Rezia Khatun ought to have agitated the matter before the civil court within six years from rejection of the appeal on 15-5-1980, but after her death and after long time the plaintiffs filed this suit for simple declaration, as such, both the courts below rightly found that the suit is hopelessly time barred. 

18. It is argued that the defendants in their written statement categorically stated that the suit property is in exclusive possession of the defendants and they have been possessing the same residing thereon by constructing houses, by letting out shops to the tenants and planting various type of trees. To substantiate their statement and the evidences got the property locally inspected through court by appointing an Advocate Commissioner who submitted report in toto finding all the structures standing on the suit property. The plaintiffs objected the commission report, but after hearing the trial court accepted the report and finally at the time of hearing learned Advocate Commissioner deposed before the court as DW 6 and the report was marked as Exhibit-'Chha'. 

19. He argued that the plaintiffs though claimed their possession in the suit property, but PW 1 unequivocally admitted that he used to live in Sher Shah Road not in the suit area. None of the plaintiffs or their alleged tenant came forward to depose that the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit property by erecting houses or planting trees. Moreover, PW 2 after recording examination in chief did not appear before the court to face cross-examination. Consequently, the evidence so have been recorded by the court has become futile. Other P.Ws though stated in a lump that the plaintiffs are in possession, but one of the witnesses house is three miles away from the suit property and another witness is six miles away from the suit property. None of the PWs are inhabitant of suit area. Therefore, both the courts below rightly found that the plaintiffs are not in possession and in support of such claim they could not file even a single paper showing payment of rent to the government, payment of tax to the Union Parishad and showing voter list to substantiate their claim that they are voters of the suit area. Both the courts below rightly found that the defendants could able to prove that they have been paying rent since 1957 till today and paying taxes to the Union Parishad and also filed a certificate issued by the local Chairman who also deposed before the trial court saying that nobody in the name of Rezaul Karim is resident of the suit area or his Union Parishad. 

20. It is argued that though the defendants could not file any rent receipts showing payment of rent to Rezia Khatun which were submitted before the Settlement Officer, it is established from the judgment and order of the Appeal Officer that Azahar Ali Mridha filed rent receipts before them showing payment of rent to Rezia Khatun. That judgment passed by the Appeal Officer in Appeal No. 7163 of 1980 has not been challenged till today, meaning thereby, the predecessor of plaintiffs, Rezia Khatun conceded the fact that Azahar Ali Mridha was agricultural tenant under her. 

21. He submits that a portion of the property has been acquired by the government for construction of highway, acquisition notice was issued in the name of predecessor of the defendants and compensation award made in the name of Azahar Ali Mridha. Had the plaintiffs owned the property by inheritance from Rezia Khatun or Rezia Khatun had title in the property SA Khatian RS Khatian, and the notice for compensation would have been prepared and issued in the name of plaintiffs or their predecessor. Both the courts below considered series of exhibits filed by the defendants and finally found that the defendants are in possession and there was reasonable cause for preparing SA khatian and RS khatian in the name of Azahar Ali Mridha, as such, both the courts below committed no illegality or error of law in the, decision occasioning failure of justice. 

22. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, have gone through the revisional application, plaint in suit, written statement, evidences both oral and documentary available in lower court records and impugned judgment and decree of both the courts below. 

23. As admitted by both the parties the property in question along with vast property was purchased by predecessor of the plaintiffs Rezia Khatun by sale deeds dated 20-3-1944 and 5-5-1945. The plaintiffs claimed that predecessor of defendants Azahar Ali Mridha since closely related to predecessor of the plaintiffs, Rezia Khatun was entrusted to look after the property owned by Rezia Khatun and to get the record prepared in her name and payment of rents to the government. Taking advantage of having control and management of the property he with ulterior motive got the SA khatian recorded in his name for the suit plots measuring 66 sataks and also claimed that Azahar Ali Mridha was not raiyat under Rezia Khatun and he was not settled with the suit property by any settlement or issuing any rent receipt by Rezia Khatun. 

24. To appreciate the argument and the statement made by the petitioners. I have gone through the plaint in suit as well as judgment and order passed in Appeal Case No. 7163 of 1980. (Exhibit-Umo-3). From perusal of Exhibit-Umo-3, it appears that Rezia Khatun before the Appeal Officer claimed that predecessor of defendants Azahar Ali Mridha was borgader under her who used to cultivate the land before SA operation and at that time Rezia Khatun was out of that area. He had no adult son, consequently, she entrusted elder brother of her husband named Bilat Ali to look after the property on her behalf and to prepare SA khatian in her name. Bilat Ali informed her that SA khatian correctly recorded in her name, but she could not take any information about truthness of the fact as said by Bilat Ali and she came to know from objection case filed by Azahar Ali Mridha against draft khatian, which contradicts the statement made in the plaint by the plaintiffs and made before the Appeal Officer by the predecessor of the plaintiffs. 

25. Learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the defendants could not produce any document showing their settlement from Rezia Khatun before the trial court, as such, SA record has no basis. From perusal of exhibit-Umo-3, it appears that Appeal Officer in his judgment observed that Azahar Ali Mridha claimed that he obtained pattan from Rezia Khatun before the SAT Act came into force and he executed a kabuliyat before delivery of possession and after obtaining settlement he constructed homestead thereon and living with his family members, but Azahar Ali Mridha could not file kabuliyat before the Settlement Officer and Appeal Officer, however, he produced rent receipts showing payment of rent to Rezia Khatun and after SAT Act came into force he regularly made payment of rents to the government. 

26. From the aforesaid observations made by the Appeal Officer, it is found that Azahar Ali Mridha produced cheque dakhila before the Settlement Officer and Appeal Officer showing payment of rents to Rezia Khatun. Modified SA Khatian No. 1364/1 (Exhibit-Ka) supports the observations made by the Appeal Officer which was modified under Section 46 of the SAT Act, 1950 recognizing Azahar Ali Mridha as direct tenant under the government showing Rezia Khatun owner of the property as landlord under her Azahar Ali Mridha was agricultural tenant. Therefore, contention of the petitioners that the SA khatian has no basis at all has no substance and fact of acquiring title as agricultural tenant under Rezia Khatun was established in objection case and appeal case and it was also established that Azahar Ali Mridha was in possession. Fact of the cases referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioners regarding basis of SA and RS khatian are totally different from the fact of the present case. Both the courts below concurrently observed and found that recording of SA khatian and RS khatian in the name of Azahar Ali Mridha has basis and the documents like rent receipts showing payment of rents right from 1957 till today (Exhibit-Kha series), judgment and order of the Appeal Officer (Exhibit Umo-3), Advocate Commissioner report (Exhibit-Chha), notice of acquisition of property (Exhibits Umo-1 and 2) and the evidences led by defendants as DWs all corroborate each other supporting title of the defendants in the suit property. 

27. It is true that by wrong record-of-right the interest of true owner is not affected and for such wrong record-of-right the person whose interest is affected he is required to file the suit seeking declaration of title within six years from the date, the person in whose name record has been wrongly, prepared and finally published arises on the basis of wrong record. In the instant case, the invasion made on the basis of wrong record-of-right when predecessor of defendants Azahar Ali Mridha filed objection case under Rule 30 before the objection officer in the year 1979 or 1980. As per decision reported in 56 DLR (AD) 53, cause of action for filing of the suit arises on 15-5-1980 when the appeal case was rejected by the Appeal Officer in Appeal No. 7163 of 1980 filed by Rezia Khatun. The instant suit was filed on 29-11-1998 after about 19 years, therefore, the suit is barred by limitation. 

28. Apart from this, payment of rents by Azahar Ali Mridha to Rezia Khatun as agricultural tenant under her, payment of rents to the government after SAT Act came into force since 1957 till today, payment of taxes to the Union Parishad, Advocate Commission report supporting existence of structures thereon belonging to the defendants and all the evidences of DWs in its entirety support the case of the defendants. Therefore, the instant suit is also barred under proviso to section 42 of SR Act, as suit for simple declaration of title is not maintainable if the plaintiffs found out of possession. 

29. It is also true that mere payment of rents to the government by a person having no title in the property on the basis of wrong record-of-right does not create title in his favour unless he could show the basis of record-of-right, but the facts and circumstances of this case is totally different from the cases cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioners reported in 56 DLR and 10 MLR. All the decisions referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioners did not match with the facts and circumstances of the present case. Therefore, the trial court as well as the appellate court concurrently observed that the plaintiffs in suit failed to prove their title and possession in the suit property. On the other hand, the defendants by oral evidence, series of exhibits could able to prove that Azahar Ali Mridha acquired the suit property by way of pattan from Rezia Khatun and Rezia Khatun fought against Azahar Ali Mridha but failed. Where original owner Rezia Khatun gave up the claim during her life time conceding title and possession of Azahar Ali Mridha, her heirs, subsequently, after about two decades cannot come with the present suit claiming that they inherited the property from Rezia Khatun who purchased the same in the year 1944 and 1945. 

30. In view of the above, I find that both the courts below rightly dismissed the suit as well as the appeal and there is no illegality and error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

31. Taking into consideration the above, I find no merit in the Rule as well as in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners, though learned Advocate tried his level best to satisfy the court by referring various law and the decisions quoted above. 

32. In the result, the Rule is discharged however, without any order as to costs. 

Communicate a copy of this judgment to the court concerned and send down the lower court records at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why judgment and decree dated 17-5-2001 passed by learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Pabna in Other Class Appeal No. 123 of 1984 disallowing the appeal and affirming judgment and decree dated 30-5-1984 passed by learned Munsif, Ishwardi Upazila, Pabna in Other Class Suit No. 286 of 1983 dismissing the suit should not be set-aside. 

2. Facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule, are that the predecessor of the present petitioners, namely Most. Nurnahar Bewa as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 286 of 1983 in the Court of the then Munsif, Ishwardi, Pabna against the predecessor of opposite parties, namely Ataur Rahman for a decree of cancellation of registered deed of gift being No. 10426 dated 16-10-1978 in respect of 0.21 acre suit land along with its structure standing thereon. The case of the plaintiff is that the defendant is her younger brother and she looks after him from his childhood and he was residing with her. The plaintiff had no issues and she was dependent upon him for her regular livelihood. The plaintiff belongs to the suit property which was her self-acquired property situated within Ishwardi town and was a valuable property. She constructed a brick built house therein by spending huge amount of money. Considering the distressed condition of the defendant she brought up him and loved him very much and he was a peon of Railway Department of the Government. The plaintiff was an old lady of above 80 years of age and there was a close relationship between her and the defendant. The defendant advised the plaintiff to transfer the suit land in his favour with a condition that he would take care of her for the rest of her life and should do all 'possible domestic work for her. He also promised that he would do religious activities even after her death. Upon accepting such promise the plaintiff decided to transfer the suit property by way of gift with a condition that the defendant would look after her during her lifetime and the deed of gift would take effect after her death and with that conditions she decided to execute and register deed of gift in favour of the defendant. The defendant Ataur Rahman was a cunning and greedy man and with a view to cheating the plaintiff he took her to Bheramara Sub-registry Office situated within Kushtia district and without giving any opportunity to understand the contents of the deed, he took her LTI in the deed as an executrix. After the execution and registration of the deed of gift being No. 10426 dated 16-10-1978, the plaintiff used to live in the disputed house and collected rents from the tenants, took electricity connection and recorded in the Pouroshova and paid taxes and rents in her name. The defendant never claimed title to and possession of the suit property from the plaintiff but subsequently, the plaintiff came to learn that the defendant made an attempt to mortgage the suit property to the Agriculture Bank and he also claimed possession. Accordingly, the plaintiff on 28-11-1982 cancelled the deed of gift dated 16-10-1978 by executing a registered deed of cancellation. The possession of the suit property has never been handed over to the defendant. Thereafter, the plaintiff instituted the present suit for cancellation of the deed. 

3. The predecessor of the opposite parties as defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material averments of the plaint contending that the suit is not maintainable, barred by law and that after execution and registration of the deed of gift on 16-10-1978 the defendant got vacant possession of the suit land and he was looking after the plaintiff all through. He developed the suit land and thereafter, constructed a house therein by expending Taka 1,00,000 (Taka one lakh) and leased out a portion of the house to monthly tenant, mutated his name and paid rent and has been possessing the same peacefully. The plaintiff in her free will and upon under-standing the contents executed and registered the deed of gift and, as such, she lost her title to the suit property. Another brother of the plaintiff, namely Mojibur Rahman purchased another dwelling house from the plaintiff at a nominal price and upon his ill-advice the plaintiff has filed this suit with some false allegations and accordingly, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

4. Both parties adduced evidence, oral and documentary, in that the plaintiff adduced four PWs and the defendant adduced four DWs to prove their case. The trial Court, upon considering the evidence and materials on record, dismissed the suit by judgment and decree dated 30-5-1984. Being aggrieved by said judgment and decree, the plaintiff preferred Other Class Appeal No. 123 of 1984 before the learned District Judge, Pabna which Was transferred to learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Pabana for disposal who, after hearing the parties, disallowed the appeal by impugned judgment and decree dated 17-5-2001. It is to be noted that during pendency of the appeal the plaintiff died leaving behind two brothers namely Mojibur Rahman and the defendant Ataur Rahman who have been duly substituted in the appeal and thereafter, Mojibur Rahman and Ataur Rahman died and the heirs of Mojibur Rahman were substituted as appellants and those of Ataur Rahman as respondents. 

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and decree of the Court of appeal, the heirs of Mojibur Rahman have preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule. 

6. Mr. Md. Monzur Rabbi, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners made the following submissions: 
(1) The Court of Appeal committed an error of law in holding that the onus of proof was upon the plaintiff that the alleged deed of gift was collusively obtained from her. 
(2) Since the plaintiff was a pardanashin lady a special rule of onus is applicable and it is settled principle of law that a person claiming benefit under a document executed by a pardanashin lady, the burden of proof is upon the donee to show that the donor had independent advice and she properly understood the terms of the deed before its execution. 
(3) The possession of the suit property has not been handed over to the defendant but the Court of appeal, upon misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record, erroneously held that the defendant got possession of the disputed property from the plaintiff. 
(4) Though the plaintiff claimed that she was a pardanashin lady but the Court of appeal, upon assumption and presumption, illegally held that the plaintiff was not a pardanashin lady. 
(5) The Court of appeal, upon misreading and non-consideration of the evidence and upon misconception of law, arrived at its findings and decision and, as such, this Court has jurisdiction under revision to reverse those findings of the Court of appeal. 

7. In support of his submissions learned Advocate has referred to the cases of Niche Noriah vs Shaik Allie Bin Omar AIR 1929 Privy Council 3, Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury and others vs Gain Ahmed and Others 33 DLR (AD) 1, Most. Rokeya Khatun vs Alijan @ Alijan Bepari and others 1982 BLD (AD) 139 : 34 DLR (AD) 266, Smt. Andhi Kuer and another vs Rajeshwar Singh and others AIR 1972 Pat 325, Ashok Kumar and another vs Gaon Sabha Ratauli and others. AIR -1981 All 222, Md. Shaikh and another vs Maminuddin Shaikh and others 22 DLR 650, Abdul Manual: Shah and others vs Kafiran Nessa and others 46 DLR 103, Rangbi Bewa vs Md. Abed Ali and others 1987 BLD 319, Mohammed Aslain Khan vs Khalilur Rahman AIR 1947 PC 97, Sadik Hossain vs Hasim Ali (1916) IA 212. 

8. Mr. Md. Mucktadir Rahman, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties made the following submissions: 
(1) It is settled principle of law that burden of proof lies upon the plaintiff to prove his case and that who alleges forgery he must prove it but in the instant case the plaintiff has failed to prove her case. 
(2) Pardanashin lady theory is not applicable in this case because there was no fiduciary relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant and section 111 of the Evidence Act will not be applicable in this case. 
(3) Whether a woman is a pardanashin lady or not is a question of fact and it has been proved by evidence that the plaintiff was not a pardanashin lady which has been concurrently held by the Court of appeal and, as such, this Court under revisional jurisdiction has no power to reverse such findings of facts. 
(4) All conditions in respect of a gift under Mohammedan law have been complied with and the deed in question is a valid gift and a conditional gift, if made, the condition will be void and the gift will be valid. 
(5) The gift in question cannot be revoked as per provision of section 167 of the principle of Mohammedan Law (Molla). 
(6) Before amendment of section 28 of the Registration. Act the deed has been executed. and registered in the Sub-registry Office under. Kusthia district and, as such, though major portion of the property is situated under Pabna District the deed is valid as per section 28 of the Registration Act. 
(7) There is a presumption of a registered document under the Registration Act and since the deed in question is a registered deed it is presumed to be correctly executed and registered and since the plaintiff alleges that the gift was obtained by misrepresentation the burden was upon the plaintiff to prove her case but she failed to do so and accordingly, the Court of appeal rightly held that the deed of gift was a genuine document. 
(8) The Court of appeal concurrently found that the possession of the suit property has been delivered after execution and registration of the gift deed in favour of the defendant and this finding cannot be reversed in revisional jurisdiction and accordingly, interference is not called for by this Court. 
 
9. In support of his submissions learned Advocate has referred to the cases of Lutfur Karim and others vs Shahidullah and others 3 MLR (AD) 215 and Abdul Gafur and others vs Nizamuddin and others ILR (1893) 171. 

10. I have heard the learned Advocates, perused the revisional application, judgments and decrees of the courts below, pleadings of the parties, evidence adduced by them and other materials available on record. 

11. Admittedly, the predecessor of the present petitioners and opposite parties, namely Most. Nurnahar Bewa had no issue and she had some properties of her own. She brought the suit for cancellation of registered deed of gift No. 10426 dated 16-10-1978 in respect of the suit property, which was claimed to be transferred to her brother, the defendant Ataur Rahman, on the allegation that by taking advantage of her position her brother obtained the deed of gift by misrepresentation. It has specifically contended in the plaint that terms of the deed of gift were not read over and explained to her at the time of its execution and registration. Both the Courts below dismissed the suit taking the view that Most. Nurnahar Bewa was not a pardanashin lady and she executed and registered the deed of gift in favour of the defendant at her free will and the burden of proof was upon her that the impugned transaction was collusive and void. 

12. The main considerations before this Court are, whether the plaintiff was a pardanashin lady and whether the burden of proof was upon her that the impugned transaction was collusive and void. 

13. The expression pardanashin has not to be confused with a lady observing purda. A lady observing purda may not be a pardanashin lady in the legal scene of the term. The term pardanashin lady is not a term of art. It has special legal significance as one who is unable to understand the transaction by virtue of the manner in which she has been brought up. This view finds support in the case of Sint. Andhi Kuer and another vs Rajeshwar Singh and others AIR 1972 Patna 325. It is not merely by reason of purda itself that the law throws its protection around a pardanashin lady but by reason of those disabilities to which the life of a section of a people living in seclusion gives rise to disabilities and with which pardanashin lady suffers. Thus, the protection necessarily arises from causes such as old age, infirmity, ignorance, illiteracy, mental deficiency, experience and dependence upon others. This view finds support in the case of Ashok Kumar and another vs Gaon Sabha Ratauli and others AIR 1981 All 222. 

14. The object of the rule of law, which is applicable to pardanashin ladies is to protect the weak and helpless and consequently such a rule should not be restricted to that class only but should apply to the case of a poor woman who is equally ignorant and illiterate though not a pardanashin in the strict sense of term. This view finds support in the case of Md. Shaikh and another vs Mainimiddin Shaikh and others 22 DLR 650. In the case of Abdul Mannar Shah and others vs Kafiran Nessa and others 46 DLR 103 it has been held that 'of course, independent advice in case of transfer of property by pardanashin lady is insisted in case where transferee stands in fiduciary relation with the lady, onus in such 'circumstances is on the transferee'. 

15. In this regards section 111 of the Evidence Act is relevant which reads as follows: 
"111.—Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence—Where there is a question as to the good faith of transaction between parties, one of whom stands to the other in a position of active confidence, the burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the party who is in a position of active confidence." 

16. It is the mandate of section 111 of the Evidence Act that the burden of proving of good faith shall be cast upon the person who relies on the transaction if a relationship of 'active confidence' or 'fiduciary relationship' subsists between the parties. The word 'active confidence' in this section indicates that the relationship between the parties must be such that one is bound to protect the interest of the other. 

17. In the case of Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury vs Gard Ahmed, 33 DLR (AD) 1 it has been held as follows: 
"On a review of the authorities cited above it is manifest that this special rule of onus has been devised to give protection to certain categories of women in Indian sub-continent who suffer from some special disabilities because of purda system. Pardanashin women are excluded from social intercourse except with very near relation and communion outside the narrow family circle is barred to them. It applies to all pardanashin women illiterate or literate. The criteria is whether she is a pardanashin or not. It is, of course, a question of fact. Next we get that the protection granted to the pardanashin ladies has been extended to ignorant and illiterate women, though not strictly speaking pardanashin. 
If in a case of a transfer by a pardanashin lady a dispute arises as to its validity, the onus is always on the party who seeks to hold the transferor to the terms of the deed to satisfy the Court on evidence that she substantially understood the disposition and she executed the deed with full understanding of what she was doing and of the nature and effect of the transaction. It is to be observed that independent advice by itself is not an essential burden to be discharged, unless there are some Special circumstances calling for its application, in that the donee or the transferee stood in a position of active confidence or had fiduciary relationship with the pardanashin lady. It is only in such cases, the donee or transferee will carry the additional burden or to prove that the lady had independent and disinterested advice from persons other than the recipient of the document. 

18. Now it is well established that the person claiming benefit under a deed executed by a pardanashin lady is required to prove that she had independent advice about the transaction and that she understood the terms incorporated in the deed. 

19. To make the disposition by a pardanashin lady a valid one it must be proved that the disposition was substantially understood and it was really the mental act of the person who made it. The rule of law as indicated above is an exception of general rules. The rule of law has been codified in section 111 of the Evidence Act, which provides that where there is a question as to the good faith of a transaction between the parties, one of whom stands to the other in a position of active confidence, the burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the party who is in a position of active confidence. Relationship between the pardanashin woman and the person in fiduciary relationship, who is the donee, raises the presumption of influence upon the pardanashin lady and the burden is upon the donee to show that the act was spontaneous. 

20. This rule of law has been expanded to the legal heirs of such pardanashin lady in the case of Most. Rokqa Khatun vs Alijan, @ Alijan Bepari and others 1982 BLD (AD) 139 wherein it has been held that 'if the person upon whom the property of the pardanashin woman devolves by operation of law, and who in the facts represents her can challenge the legality of the disposition'. 

21. In the instant case admittedly, total 0.23 acre of land had been purported to be gifted by the plaintiff, Most. Nurnahar Bewa to her younger brother, Ataur Rahman. The plaintiff adduced four PWs including herself as PW1, who deposed on 8-1-1984 and 29-3-1984. In her deposition, she stated, "আতাউর রহমান আমার সহদর ছোট ভাই। আমার নিজের কোন সন্তান জন্মে নাই। আমি আতাউরকে ছোট বেলা হতে লালন-পালন করেছি এবং তার সকল ভরণ পোষনের খরচ বহন করেছি। আমার স্বামী মারা যাবার পর আতাউর রহমান আমার কাছেই থাকত। আমার সংসারের কাজকর্ম আতাউর আমার পক্ষে দেখাশুনা করত। আমার বাড়ী আতাউরকে লিখে দিয়েছিলাম এই চুক্তিতে যে আমাকে দেখাশুনা ও ভরন পোষণ করবে এবং আমার জীবিতাস্থায় নালিশী সম্পত্তি আমারই থাকবে এবং আমার মৃত্যুর পর আতাউর পাবে এই মর্মে আমি নালিশী সম্পত্তি আতাউরকে লিখে দিয়েছি। আতাউর বরাবর যে দলিল আমি করে দিয়েছিলাম তা রেজিস্ট্রারের সময় আমাকে পাঠ করে শুনানো হয় নাই। আতাউর মহুরির সাথে যোগাযোগ করে আমার ইচ্ছার বিরুদ্ধে অনেক কথা দলিলে লিখে নিয়েছে। নালিশী সম্পত্তি রেজিস্ট্রি করে দিলেও এর দখল আমি আতাউরকে ছেড়ে দেইনি। আমার বয়স ৯০/৯৫ বছর।" In cross-examination no suggestion was put to the plaintiff that the deed in question was read over or explained to her by any independent person to understand the contents of the deed by the plaintiff. Moreover, DW1 Md. Ataur Rahman, merely stated that his sister, the plaintiff, gifted the suit land to him. He denied the suggestion that the plaintiff did not willingly gift the suit land in his favour. In his testimony he did not state whether the deed had been read over or explained to the plaintiff at the time of its execution and registration.

22. Admittedly, the plaintiff was an old lady of above 80 years of age at the time of execution and registration of the gift deed and the plaintiff and the defendant, who are siblings, had a good relationship with each other. The plaintiff executed the deed by putting her LTI and admittedly, she was an illiterate lady. 

23. On perusal of Exhibit-(A), the deed of gift, it appears that out of 0.21 acre land 0.19 acre land covered by the disputed deed is situated within the lshwardi municipality under Pabna district wherein the plaintiff was residing and only 0.02 acre land is situated within Kushtia district but the plaintiff was taken by the defendant to Bheramara Sub-registry Office of Kushtia district wherein the impugned deed was executed and registered. Though as per section 28 of the Registration Act, there was no bar to executing and registering the deed of gift outside the territorial jurisdiction but the defendant could not explain as to why he took this old lady from Ishwardi to Bheramara for execution and registration of deed. Admittedly, another brother of the plaintiff, namely Mojibur Rahman was alive during execution and registration of the deed but he was not made as an witness of the execution and the three witnesses of the deed including the deed writer are not close relatives of the plaintiff and the defendant. All these facts indicate that the defendant was hiding something and he secretly obtained the deed from the plaintiff. Moreover, though the defendant adduced four oral witnesses to prove his case but they are not the witnesses of the deed. None of the witnesses of the deed of gift nor any other witness was produced to show that the deed had been read over or explained to the plaintiff or she understood the deed or the plaintiff had independent and disinterested advice from any person. Accordingly, it is clear that the impugned deed of gift was not explained by any disinterested person to the plaintiff and without understanding the contents and consequences of the deed the plaintiff executed it. Since the plaintiff was an illiterate and old lady of above 80 years of age, the Court of appeal should have held that the plaintiff was a pardanashin lady who had no independent and disinterested advice before she executed the impugned deed transferring her entire property. 

24. Whether the plaintiff was a pardanashin lady or not is a question of fact but the Court of appeal, upon misreading and non-consideration of evidence and misconception of law, came to erroneous finding that the plaintiff was not a pardanashin lady. The Court of Appeal should have came to the conclusion that the plaintiff was a pardanashin lady and the burden was upon the defendant to prove that the disputed deed of gift was explained to her, she understood the contents of the deed by disinterested person which is lacking in this case. 

25. Learned Advocate for the opposite parties tried to impress me that all requirements for a valid gift under Mohammedan law were complied with and, as such, it cannot be said that the deed was not valid one but his argument is not applicable in this case because this case is an exception of the general rules and it is the defendant to show and prove that the plaintiff was not a pardanashin lady and independent and disinterested advice was given to the plaintiff before execution and registration of the deed. Since the defendant failed to discharge the onus, the impugned gift is not valid in the eye of law. 

26. In regards handing over possession of the suit property to the defendant, learned Advocate for the petitioner has drawn this Court's attention to the oral and documentary evidence to substantiate that the actual possession of the property has not been handed over to the defendant. To prove her possession, the plaintiff herself stated in her deposition that she did not hand over physical possession of the suit property to the defendant and she herself was owning and possessing the suit property by residing herself therein and through tenants and the concerned utility bills and other taxes of the Government were paid by her. Other PWs supported this contention of the plaintiff. The defendant adduced four oral witnesses including himself to prove his possession in the suit property. Admittedly, the defendant was residing with his sister, the plaintiff from his childhood and the plaintiff looked after him but this fact of possession cannot be construed as possession of the defendant in the suit property on the basis of the disputed gift. Additionally, the plaintiff adduced some documentary evidence to prove her possession in the suit premises. It could not be proved by evidence of the defendant that after the execution of the deed of gift the plaintiff had left the disputed house and she was residing elsewhere. From the documentary evidence produced by the plaintiff it appears that though the gift was purported to be made in 1978, the holding of the suit property was in the name of the plaintiff [Exhibit-1(a)] after 1978, she paid holding tax [tax receipt number 16144 dated 18-3-1983, Exhibit-1(b)J. There was no separate holding in the name of the defendant and the suit premises existed as homestead even before the execution of the gift as evidenced by SA Khatian [Exhibit-2(b)). The electricity bills of the house stands in the name of the plaintiff (Exhibit-3) and municipality tax was collected from the plaintiff for the years 1983, 1984, 1981 and 1982 [Exhibit 4(a) and 4(b)]. The plaintiff also produced some rent receipts (Exhibit-5 series) showing that she was possessing the suit premises by leasing out the same to the tenants and PW 4 was adduced to prove the tenancy. The defendant produced a compromise agreement (Aposhnama) dated 18-2-1983 [Exhibit-(C)] entered into between the plaintiff and the defendant in which the defendnat admitted that the life interest of the subject matter of the gift would be retained by the plaintiff. Clauses (5) and (6) of the compromise agreement reads as follows:—
"১। অদ্য হইতে দানকারিনী মোছাঃ নরুননাহার জীবিত থাকা পর্যন্ত দানকৃত জমির উপর যে বাসা ভাড়া দেওয়া আছে সেই ভাড়াটিয়ার নিকট হতে ভাড়া পাইবেন এবং খরচ করিতে পারবেন।
২। আতাউর রহমান দানকৃত জমি নরুননাহারের জীবদ্দশায় কাহারো নিকট বিক্রয় করিতে পারিবেন না। কোথাও দায়বদ্ধ করিবেন না।"

27. On perusal of the আপোষনামা, it appears that a salish was held to resolve the dispute between the parties in presence of the local Councilor and other elite persons. The defendant signed the compromise agreement from which it appears that the plaintiff wanted to gift the property with a condition that she would retain the life interest in the gifted property. Accordingly, it is clear that if the plaintiff understood that such condition would not be embodied in the deed of gift, she would never execute and register said gift deed. Considering the evidence as a whole, I am of the view that the plaintiff could able to prove her possession in the suit property and the deed in question was not acted upon but the Court of appeal, upon misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record, wrongly held that the defendant could prove possession in the suit property. 

28. In view of the above the impugned deed is declared invalid and cancelled. The property immediately reverts back to the ownership of the plaintiff. 

29. Learned Advocate for the opposite parties contended that since the plaintiff died at appellate stage, the cause of action of the suit abated. This submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties is against the proposition of law because of the fact that as a general Rule, all rights of action and all claims existing in favour of or against a person at the time of his/her death survive to and against his/her representative. It is settled principle of law that the converse is that property rights in favour of and/or against any person continue to exist in favour of/or against the legal representative of a deceased party litigant. Admittedly, the plaintiff had no issues and she died after institution of the suit leaving behind two brothers, namely Mojibur Rahman (the predecessor of the petitioners) and Ataur Rahman (the predecessor of the opposite parties). Since the deed of gift is declared as invalid, the plaintiff's two brothers namely Mojibur Rahman and Ataur Rahman inherited the suit property in equal share. In the meantime, Ataur Rahman and Mojibur Rahman died leaving behind their respective heirs who are the petitioners and opposite parties in this Rule. Accordingly, the legal representatives of Mojibur Rahman and Ataur Rahman are entitled to get 50% share each from the suit property. 

30. Now question arises whether the High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the concurrent findings of facts of the Court of appeal. It is settled principle of law that the High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment of the courts below when the same has been made either upon mis-reading or non-consideration of the material evidence caused failure of justice; or when the same has been passed on the basis of evidence which cannot be considered legal evidence and had the same been not taken into consideration the judgment would not have been one as has been made; or when the appellate Court in giving a particular finding has committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice or such finding is found to have resulted from glaring misconception of law; or when the findings arrived at by the appellate Court is contrary to the evidence; or when there appears error of law apparent on the face of the record occasioning failure of justice. It is also of the view of the Apex Court that once the conditions in section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure are satisfied and the High Court's jurisdiction to interfere is established, the proceedings as a whole from start to finish can be scrutinized and any order necessary for doing justice may be passed. There is no limit to the area in which the revisional power is to be exercised by the High Court Division in the facts and circumstances of each case. When a finding of fact is based on consideration of the materials on record, those findings are immune from interference by the revisional Court and the High Court Division has no jurisdiction to sit on appeal over a finding of fact. [Ref. Md. Shajahan Khan vs Additional Deputy Commissioner 11 BLT (AD) 60; Md. Habibulla vs Sher Ali Khan 15 BLT (AD) 319 : 57 DLR (AD) 55; Md. Hahibur Rahman Bhuiyan and others vs Mosammat Galman Beguni and others 33. BLD (AD) 93 : 64 DLR (AD) 133; Government vs Golan, Hossain Kazi and others 22 BLT (AD) 486; Kanchan Mallik and others vs Saleha Begum and otherS 22 BLC (AD) 254, Dr. Choudhury Mosaddaqul Isdani vs Abdullah al Mansur Choudhury and others 70 DLR (AD) 168). 

31. It appears that the judgments of the courts below suffer from mis-reading and non-consideration of the material evidence and glaring misconception of law which caused miscarriage of justice and, as such, interference is called for by this Court. 

32. In view of the above discussion, I find merit in this Rule which should be made absolute. 

33. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs. 

34. The judgments and decrees of the courts below are set-aside. The suit be decreed in-part in favour of the petitioners (the heirs of deceased Mojibur Rahman) to the extent of 50% joint share in the suit property. The respective parties are directed to make partition of the suit property as per their respective share, as stated above, within 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment by the trial Court failing which the petitioners or the opposite parties, as the case may be, would be at liberty to get their share through execution process of the Court. 

Send down the LCR along with a copy of this judgment to the Courts below at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
At the instance of the petitioners, the Rule was issued with the following the terms: "Let the records be called for and a Rule issue calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-23 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 16-2-1997 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Cumilla in Title Appeal No. 204 of 1995 affirming those dated 12-6-1995 passed by the leaned Senior Assistant Judge, Daudkhandi, Cumilla in Title Suit No. 05/1994 should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper." 

2. The facts of the plaintiffs' case are that the opposite party Nos. 1-23 being plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 05 of 1994 initially for declaration of their raiyati right in the suit land but subsequently by amendment prayed for a declaration that the villagers have got customary right in the suit land impleading the petitioner and others as defendants alleging inter alia that the suit land measuring 2.70 acres of land in Plot No. 358 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 23 corresponding to SA Khatian No. 20 is a patito land for grazing the cattle. Urnacharan Aich and others were the owners of the suit land along with other lands in zamandari right. Haranath Roy and others were the owners in taluka interest under them. Under them, Kalu Bhuiyan was the owner and possessor in hawla interest. The CS Khatian was accordingly prepared in the names of all as mentioned above. Haranath Roy was the owner in 'Kha' and Udayatara Chowdhurani and others were the owners in 'Ka' group in taluka interest. Kalu Bhuiyan was the owner of the suit land under them in hawla interest. Crops did not grow in the suit land. Kalu Bhuiyan left behind the suit land along with other lands in favour of the general public of the village for their use some 100 years back. Even before that the general public used to graze their cattle in the suit land. At present, the people of the village graze cattle and the youngsters play in the suit land during dry season. During rainy season, water hyacinth and other weeds grow there and the people cut those things to feed their cattle. During the CS operation, the plots of Khatian No. 23 were recorded as being used by the general public except the suit plot in the remark's column of the khatian. The people of the village have no other land to graze their cattle. The people of the village have been possessing the suit land for more than hundred years as mentioned above by exerting their right, title and possession over the same. The possession as mentioned above was not obstructed by the defendants or anybody else. The title of the people has been perfected in the suit land by their uninterrupted peaceful possession therein. The defendant No. 1 has no title or possession in the suit land. He or his father or predecessor has/had no title in the suit land. The house is situated in the village of Ballai within the Police Station of Chandina. He in collusion with settlement officials got his name recorded in the SA Khatian along with others. He stays in Illiotgonj Bazar in connection with his business. The recording of his name in the SA Khatian is wrong, collusive and without any basis. During the recent settlement operation, the suit land has been recorded in the VP Khatian as being possessed by the general public. The defendant No. 1 raised objection against the said recording but the same was rejected. The defendant No. 1 thereafter filed Appeal No. 1213 of 1990 and in the said appeal, it was held on 22-9-1992 that the suit is a private property and the plaintiffs are in the forceful occupation of the same as mentioned in the remarks column of the khatian. The defendant No. 1 being emboldened by the said order is now claiming title over the suit land. For the reasons stated above, the plaintiffs have filed this under order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure on behalf of the general public. 

3. On the other hand, the petitioner being defendant No. 1 entered appearance in the suit and contested the same by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia the suit is barred by limitation and is not maintainable as per provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and also not maintainable in its present form. Haranath Roy had 6 annas 12 gondas 1 kana 1 kranti share in Khatian No. 23 as shown in group 'Kha' and the others had the remaining share and the khatian was correctly prepared and published in their names. In the said khatian out of eight plots, six were shown as paths and canals and those plots were used by general public. The land of the suit plot No. 358 is the gobam for grazing the cattle of the defendants. The defendant and his co-shares used the said land for grazing their cattle. This defendant purchased 1.50 acres of land of the suit plot for valuable consideration from other co-shares. The other co-shares after obtaining the consideration money amounting to Taka 2,000 executed a nadabi deed on 16-1-1990 in favour of the defendant. The defendant is the owner of 1.20 acres of land in the suit plot by way of inheritance and 1.50 acres of land by purchase in total 2.70 acres of land. It is to be mentioned here that Haranath Roy while owner in the possession of 1.20 acres of land died leaving behind four sons and by amicable settlement among the brothers Nibaran Chandra got, the suit land and he died leaving behind this defendant; Nethur Chandra Roy as his only heir. Nethur Chandra Roy got 1.20 acres of land by inheritance and 1.50 acres of land by purchase in total 2.70 acres of land and has been in possession of the same. The SA Khatian No. 20 in respect of the suit land has been correctly prepared and published in his name. This defendant has been regularly paying rents of the suit land. Neither the plaintiffs nor the predecessors had/have any interest or possession in the suit land. The plaintiffs never took any step to correct the khatian and had/have paid any rent of the suit land. The plaintiffs are terrorists and they have been trying to grab the suit land owned and possessed by this defendant on false claim. For the reasons stated above, the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs. 

4. On the pleadings, the Trial Court framed the following issues:—
i. Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form? 
ii. Whether the suit is barred by limitation? 
iii. Whether the suit is bad for defect of parties? 
iv. Whether the suit is barred by admission, acquiescence and estoppels? 
v. Whether the suit land is usable for the general public and whether the general public has easement right or customary right in the suit land? 
vi. Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to get the relief as prayed for? 

5. After considering the evidence on record, the Trial Court decreed the suit. Being aggrieved by and highly dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, the defendant preferred Title Appeal No. 204 of 1995 before the Court of the learned District Judge, Cumilla. After admitting the appeal and observing other formalities, the learned District Judge was pleased to transmit the record to the learned Additional District Judge, Fourth Court, Cumilla for disposal. Upon hearing, the learned District Judge was pleased to dismiss the appeal. Questioning the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the aforesaid Rule.
 
6. Mr. Md. Faruque Ahammed, the learned Advocate with Mr. Tajul Islam Miajee appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned Senior Assistant Judge without considering the materials on record and legal position critically involved in this case most illegally decreed the suit and the Appellate Court without independent assessment of evidence on record and considering the legal ramification relating to customary and easement right most illegally dismissed the appeal and thereby committed an error of law resulting in the decision occasioning failure of justice, therefore, the same is liable to be turned down to secure the ends of justice. He further submits that the concurrent findings of the Courts below are perverse, infirm and fragile and thereby suffer from misreading and non-reading of evidence. He further submits that the conditions which are essential characteristics of custom are absent in the suit, therefore, he added that to be a valid custom, it must have four essential attributes: (i). It must be immemorial, (ii). It must be reasonable, (iii). It must be certain in respect of nature generally as well as in respect of the locality wherein it is alleged to obtain and the persons whom it is alleged to affect and (iii). It must be continued without interruption since its immemorial origin. 

7. He further contends that those contentions have not been fulfilled in the aforesaid case. Nevertheless, the Trial Court declared a customary right of the plaintiff in the original suit. He further submits that reasonableness is the most essential element to ascertain customary right and it is a relative term and is always variable. A custom which was reasonable 100 years back may be unreasonable now therefore the Appellate Division in 40 DLR (AD) 143 rightly held that reasonableness is an essential clement of a valid custom and the period of ascertaining the reasonableness or a valid custom in the time of its possible inception, the court is not precluded from examining other dimensions of reasonableness. He next submits that now days, a radical change has occurred in the field of agriculture. The cattle grazing and ploughing have already fallen into disuse. Modern technology for tilling the soil has occupied the function of drawing plough by the cattle and chemical fertilizer already took place of the refuse from the cattle and now a days, cattle are brought up for supplying meat, milk and hide and in a nutshell in the modern world including Bangladesh, cattle are reared not for agricultural purpose but for the purpose as aforesaid and on the other hand, food crisis is acute throughout the world. He further adds that the area of the suit land is about 2.70 acres equivalent 8 bighas which can yield 24 mond rice per season and 72 month in 3 seasons per year. He further submits that it is strange that both the courts below failed to accommodate the testimonies of the witness and vetting the documents produced by the defendant and abruptly held the plaintiff to have customary right in the suit land. In support of his submissions, he has also referred to the cases reported in 8 DLR 464. 

8. None appears to oppose the Rule at the time of hearing. 

9. Heard the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and perused the materials on record with due care and attention and seriousness as they deserve. The convoluted question of law embroiled in this case has meticulously been waded through. 

10. The learned Senior Assistant Judge in his judgment clearly held that the suit plot is recorded as go-barn which means whereas cattle used to graze therein. In this respect, the learned Senior Assistant Judge held to the effect:— 
পক্ষদ্বয়ের স্বীকারোক্তি ও প্রদর্শনী-'ক' পর্যালোচনায় আরো প্রমাণিত হয় যে, নালিশী ৩৫৮ দাগটিসহ উক্ত খতিয়ানে মোট ৮টি দাগ আছে। তন্মধ্যে নালিশী দাগটি ছাড়া বেনালিশী অবশিষ্ট ৭টি দাগ পথ ও খাল শ্রেণীর জমি স্বরূপে উহাদের মন্তব্যের কলামে 'সর্বসাধারণের ব্যবহার্য" মর্মে রেকর্ড হয়েছে। অপরদিকে, নালিশী দাগটির শ্রেণী "গোবাম" হিসেবে রেকর্ড হয়েছে।"

11. PW-1, Abdul Mannan Sarker is the plaintiff of the suit. His abode is admittedly three miles away from the suit land. In his deposition, he stated:— 
"নালিশী ভূমি তাদের গ্রামের লোকজন পুরুষানুক্রমে শত বছরের ঊর্ধ্বকাল যাবৎ নালিশী ভূমি গোচারন ভূমি হিসেবে ব্যবহার করে আসছেন। শুষ্ক মৌসুমে নালিশী ভূমিতে জনসাধারণ গরু চড়ান। ছেলেরা খেলাধুলা করে। বর্ষাকালে নালিশী ভূমি পানির নিচে চলে গেলে তখন উহাতে কচুরিপানা হয় এবং জনসাধারণ উক্ত কচুরিপানা নিয়ে গরুকে খাওয়ায়। ১নং বিবাদী নালিশী ভূমি হতে তিন মাইল দূরে ইলিয়টগঞ্জ বাজারে বসবাস করে। ১ নং বিবাদীর কোন গরু নাই। নালিশী ভূমির ঘাস তিনি তার গরুকে খাওয়ান না।"

12. PW-1 in his deposition said, "আমি সাংবাদিকতা করি। ১৯৭৮ সাল হইতে সাংবাদিকতা করি। In another place, he says" "গ্রামবাসী কোন সাল হইতে নালিশী ভূমি ব্যবহার শুরু করে তা বলতে পারব না। .আনুয়া খোলা মৌজায় অনুমান ১,৫০০ লোক আছে। উক্ত ১,৫০০ জন লোকের মধ্যে কতজন পুরুষ কতজন মহিলা বলতে পারব না। PW-2 Siddiqur Rahman in his cross-examination said, "নালিশী ভূমি কোন সাল হতে এলাকার জনসাধারণ গোবাম হিসেবে ব্যবহার শুরু করে তাহা আমি বলিতে পারিব না।...... ১নং বাদীর কোন গরু নাই। ১নং বাদী চাকুরী করে ১ সপ্তাহে গ্রামের বাড়ীতে আসে।"

13. The learned Senior Assistant Judge without considering the evidence of DWs and documents submitted by the defendants in juxtaposition held to the effect that নালিশী ভূমি বাদীগণসহ এলাকার সর্বসাধারণের গোচারন ভূমি ও খেলার মাঠ হিসেবে ব্যবহার করার প্রথাসিদ্ধ (customary right) অধিকার আছে and accordingly, the learned Assistant Judge decreed the suit holding view that the plaintiff has got customary right in the suit land. The learned Additional District Judge without any independent assessment of the materials on record and considering the submissions and evidence on record adduced by the defendant held that the defendant has got no title and possession in the suit land. Therefore, the learned Additional District Judge was pleased to uphold the decree of the Trial Court. Admittedly, the suit plot measuring 2.70 acres was recorded in the name of Nethur Chandra Roy, son of Dr. Nibaron Chandara Roy and in the remarks column, the suit land was classified as gobam. In the case reported in 8 DLR supra, it was held: — 
"When a plaintiff sets up a prescriptive right he cannot be allowed to succeed on the basis of customary right. An easement right of pasturage cannot be acquired by an indefinite number of people of a certain village or villages on the basis of a lost grant or by prescription under section 26 of the Limitation Act but such a right can be acquired by custom when all the requisites of a valid custom are established." 

14. In the case reported in' 40 DLR (AD) supra, it was clearly delineated under what circumstances, a customary right may be acquired and in the aforesaid case, the Appellate Division considered a series of cases such as (1) 7 DLR 464, (2) 34 cm 319, (3) 42 CWN 1102 = ILR 63 Cal. 851, (4) AIR 1937 Cal 46 = ILR 653 Cal 851, (5) 7 DLR 464, (6) 42 CAL 455, (7) ILR 63 Cal 851=AIR 1937 Cal 46, (8) AIR 1937 Cal 245, (9)11904] 2 Ch. 534, (10) 46 RR 539, (11) AIR 1931 Mad 213, (12) ILR 42 Cal 455, (13) (1608) Danis 29, 37, (14) AIR 1937 Cal 245, (15) 54 CWN 143 (PC), (16) AIR 1968 SC 281, (17)11904] 2 Ch. 534, (18) ILR 61 Cal 45 (AIR 1934 Cal 461), (19)11904] 31 L.A. 75 & (20) 18 CWN 735. 

15. In the aforesaid case, the Appellate Division held: — 
"There is no dispute that reasonableness is an essential element of a valid custom and the period for ascertaining the reasonableness of a valid custom is the time of its possible inception. The proposition of law laid down in various decisions, some of them cited above does not preclude the Court from examining other dimensions of reasonableness viz reasonableness of the present exercise of a customary right. Considering changed circumstances, the Court may modify, extend or even disallow a right based on a custom that was otherwise reasonable at its inception, if it places an unusual and unjust burden on some individuals for benefit of others. 
In the instant case, the plaintiffs are claiming the grazing right over a vast land, 19.56 acres in all. The plaintiffs adduced no evidence about the reasonableness of their right of pasturage at its inception. They did not also produce any evidence to show what was the total land available in the village, the number of the cultivators, and the number of cattle-heads in order to justify the reasonablenes of the present exercise of their customary right. It appears that the plaintiffs a fluctuating body of persons were used to graze their cattle on the low waste land only in dry season for 4 or 5 months only. Such limited user on indulgence will neither make it a custom from time immemorial nor reasonable. When defendant No. I proceeded to bring the suit land under cultivation; the plaintiffs filed the suit in 1958. The trial Court found that the land had already been brought under mechanized cultivation by defendant No. 1. In the facts of the case, the impugned judgments do not call for any modification by way of allowing the plaintiffs' claim in part. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed with costs." 

16. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and considering the evidence on record, I am of view that the essential conditions of acquiring a valid customary right have not been proved. But the unfortunately, the Trial Court by gratuitous finding held that the plaintiffs acquired customary right over the suit land and the Appellate Court without any independent assessment of evidence on record and legal position critically involved therein most illegally dittoed the judgment of the Trial Court. By lapse of time, the use of the suit land as pasturage (গোবাম) has lost its validity specially in the context of Bangladesh, a densely populated country in the world and due to the advance of science and technology, the cows are brought up scientifically in the abode of the villagers. The plaintiffs claimed that the suit land is a vested property of the Government. But the Government did not claim any title over the suit land. The contention of the defendant is that by way of inheritance and purchase, the defendant became owner of 2.70 acres of land and has been possessing the same and his name has been correctly prepared in the latest khatian and he has been regularly paying rent to the Government. The title of the defendant could not be assailed by the plaintiffs. 

17. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the view that the Rule has got substance and therefore, the same is liable to be made absolute. 

18. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without passing any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of the Appellate Court affirming those of the Trial Court are hereby set-aside. Accordingly, the Title Suit No. 05 of 1994 is dismissed. The earlier order of stay passed by this Court thus stands recalled and vacated. 

Let a copy of the judgment with LCRs be transmitted to the Courts below at once. 

End.

lawyer: Fida M. Kamal, with Md. Momtazuddin Fakir Senior Advocates Md. Abdur Nur, Nahid Sultana SM Abul Hossain Md. Rohiul Alam M. Sayeed Ahmed Md. Sabbir Ibne Azam, Advocates—For the Contemnor-Respondent.
